en: Original Preface to the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* Compiled and Annotated The *Vajracchedikā* Sūtra encapsulates the profound meanings of all sutras.
It has been clearly stated within the scripture itself that all Buddhas and the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* (unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment) of all Buddhas emerge from this sūtra. Its greatness...

The essential point lies entirely in the eradication of self-clinging. Taking non-abiding as the fundamental essence and subduing [the mind] as the entryway, if one upholds this according to the Dharma, it can enable a person to forget desire while amidst desire and transcend the mundane world while dwelling within it, so that the self does not become an object for external conditions to exploit.
To bring one's surroundings under one's own mastery is truly like taking a cooling powder on a scorching summer day;
it is by no means a mere discourse on emptiness, but possesses practical utility. Yet there are those of good faith who merely recite this sutra while remaining ignorant of its meaning.
Furthermore, among scholars who have devoted themselves to the study of commentaries, some find them overly verbose, while others suffer from their brevity of meaning.
Regarding what is right or wrong, what may or may not be accepted, there is no direction to follow.

Even if one has a superficial knowledge of the meaning of the scriptures but fails to investigate their subtle and profound depths, seeking only to recite them as a means to expiate transgressions, yet lacking the sincere faith required for cultivation and realization, then one will ultimately have no way to even dream of the Tathāgata’s most wondrous Dharma of the mind.
Consequently, Buddhism appears clear on the surface but remains obscure in reality; this is truly deeply lamentable.

Alas! (Reflecting on my toil: My faculties are dull and my habits are deep-rooted; suffering entangles and obscures my accumulation [of karma]. In my later years and at the end of my path, every step I take is fraught with difficulty.
I have often felt indignation regarding this scripture, seeking knowledge where I knew not and seeking understanding where I did not comprehend, in order to dispel my own vexations and delusions.

Thus, I have taken the commentaries of various masters and, for them, excised errors and pared away the superficialities, extracting the essential principles and grasping the fundamental framework. Section...

I have sought to preserve the essential meaning; through cross-referencing, I clarify the fundamental substance; through repetition, I demonstrate the underlying implications; through focused recording, I reveal the profound mysteries; and by preserving both perspectives, I resolve doubts.
I believe that this exposition may perhaps approach the truth. It took three years of labor to complete and is titled *Huìzuǎn* (Compendium).

Although I exerted great effort and did not shrink from hardship, I hope that regarding this scripture— (Note: The provided source text ends abruptly. The translation above reflects the full intent of the preceding passage.)

In its general purport, there is nothing that is not detailed or inconsistent; this is what I dare not claim to know myself. Relying upon the collective efforts [of others], it has been carved into woodblocks to be shared with those of good faith.
Those of superior capacity may suddenly clarify their minds through it, while those of middling capacity may gradually exhaust the principles therein.
The world is beset by turmoil, its people drowning solely in profit and desire;
having lost their original nature and fallen into the obstacles of affliction without realizing it, why not seek a single *pāramitā* within the midst of purity and coolness?

Preface to the Re-engraved *Jingang jing hui zan* (Compendium of the Diamond Sutra), respectfully inscribed by the grandson Nianqu on the day of the full moon in the third month of the year of Gui-chou,
the fifty-eighth year of the Qianlong reign.
The textual teachings of the Tripiṭaka are none other than proofs of the essence of mind and serve as the rungs of the ladder to Buddhahood.

Only the *Vajra* Direct Pointing reveals the true wisdom and wondrous function of *prajñā* by indicating the abidingless fundamental mind; it neither discards a single dharma nor retains a single dharma.
From within this, all Buddhas are born and the life-force of wisdom remains unbroken. For those of the highest faculties, it is explained and elucidated according to their capacities.
If one accepts [the teaching] directly beneath, one will surely attain the Vajra Eye;

even those of inferior capacity, provided they know how to believe, accept, and practice it, can likewise shatter desire, leave behind the dust of the world, dispel all afflictions, cross over suffering, and rescue themselves from distress, with spiritual responses that transcend the mundane.

However, the commentaries on this sutra are as numerous as drifting clouds, making it difficult to discern its essential outline. Some exegeses are broad but lack core essentials, while others are too concise.
Yet much has been omitted. Sometimes characters are split while the chapters remain unlinked; sometimes chapters are linked while the meaning remains obscure.

If one were to follow exclusively a single school, those who discuss profound principles might find it a hindrance for beginners, while those who employ clear and simple language might fear being discarded by the highly intelligent.
Some works elaborate on phenomenal characteristics while neglecting the subtle essence; others point toward the ultimate source while omitting the detailed textual exegesis.

Each has its own strengths; it is difficult for them to excel simultaneously. (Nianqu) Not deeming myself presumptuous, I compiled various works from previous years into a single volume. However, being limited by my own learning and experience, my research and collection have not been extensive. I am particularly self-aware that my interpretations are superficial and my expositions lack thorough penetration. Nevertheless, as many like-minded colleagues from distant regions have requested this work, I have prepared it.

In the second month of spring in the year of the Tiger, this work was hastily committed to woodblocks. The collation was not thorough; errors in characters and omissions in phrases are beyond counting.

Therefore, after printing only two hundred copies, publication was immediately halted. Master Zhang, the Governor, with a sincere desire for goodness, nevertheless proceeded to carve and print this erroneous edition, and many copies have already been distributed.
(Nianqu) To err oneself and cause others to err is a karmic transgression no small matter. I rely upon the Buddha’s...

Ling: Within several years, I successively obtained excellent copies. As I perused them, a sense of regret and awakening pressed upon me simultaneously. Consequently, I extensively searched for and compiled materials, revising the drafts and re-engraving the blocks.
Wherever the original editions were superficial in their interpretation of the meaning or lacked thorough elucidation, I have provided supplementation for each deficiency.
By excising errors and pruning redundancies, I hope that this work will be refined, substantial, detailed, and comprehensive, ensuring its meaning is manifest and its logic is thoroughly integrated.
Grasping the collar and lifting the main framework, the beginning and the end were thoroughly penetrated; by this point, the manuscript had already been revised seven times.
Desiring to rectify the errors of the previous edition, the carving could not be delayed. It was completed during the second month of the year Ding-si.

To share it with like-minded colleagues, it has been increased by four-tenths compared to the original edition. For the profound depths of the meaning of this scripture cannot be reached without detailed examination; thus, for the sake of students—

One should possess a subtle and tranquil mind, repeatedly investigating and examining it to seek clarity regarding its own nature; thus, one may expound the numinous texts, resolve the delusions of the ignorant, and ascend the stages of the sages.
If one harbors a mind of false conceptualization, one enters the obstacle of words; if one harbors a coarse and superficial mind, [the same obstacle follows].
To enter into [the realm of] inviting blessings and creating obstacles is, in fact, to use the diamond-like seed-wisdom (*vajra-jñāna*) to cut oneself off from it.
Even if one recites ten thousand scrolls of scripture, how could one possibly perceive the Buddha-dharma? The Sūtra is the Buddha; the Buddha is the mind.
The non-abiding mind is the eternally abiding true mind. The eternally abiding true mind is the unborn and undying mind. The unborn and undying mind is the diamond-like [mind].
It is the mind. To attain the adamantine mind is called "abiding in the appropriate state of mind. To attain the appropriate state of mind is called "subduing the mind.
How does one abide appropriately? By attaining that which is unattainable; by abiding in non-abiding. Since there is no abiding, how could there ever be anything?
When that mind arises, how could it ever be non-existent? Let the reader study the Buddha with the mind, rather than studying the Buddha with the mouth.
See non-abiding within bubbles and shadows; do not see annihilation within non-abiding. See permanence within the diamond-like nature; do not see permanence within permanence.
When both annihilation and permanence are cast aside, and both person and phenomena are seen as empty, will one not reach the other shore and ascend together with all Buddhas to the state of peace?
How joyful! Recorded on the full moon day of the twelfth month in the year of Bingchen, the first year of the Jiaping era, by Sun Nianqu, the grandson of Shu Fu,
as a careful compilation of commentaries on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
General Principles:
Regarding the commentaries on this sutra, from the Jin and Liang dynasties down to the present, there have been no fewer than several hundred types.

Whether composed by great virtuous ones or by learned scholars, their exegeses are complete in meaning; nothing further can be added by later students. Nevertheless, those who provide such interpretations have increased daily.
Those who have observed this work daily have been numerous; their treatises, commentaries, and proofs fill many scrolls and are difficult to exhaust.

While there is much that clarifies doubts, reveals profundities, and brings forth the essential meaning, there are likewise no few instances of arbitrary annotations and divergent interpretations. This compilation gathers various editions, distilling the concise from the extensive and seeking commonality amidst differences.
Having discarded what is coarse and superficial and selected what is refined and essential, anything that is not accurate has been omitted in its entirety.
I have incorporated [these works]. Regarding the difficult and doubtful passages, I have sought out their correct meanings with meticulous care.
Although the commentaries on the sutras are numerous, those sufficient for transmission and preservation number no more than ten or so.
Among these, the most excellent are the sub-commentary by Guifeng of the Tang dynasty, the record by Changshui of the Song dynasty, and the resolution by Hanshan of the Ming dynasty.
There are doubts. Zeng Fengyi has the *Zongtong*; the layman Da Yuan Zhang Youyu has the *Yiqu zhi guangyan*;
and the layman Ruru Zhang Guowei has a commentary. These several works truly serve as wings to support the Mahāyāna.
In recent times, the layman Shengxian Gong Jicai has the *Zhengjie*, and the layman Chengzhai Sheng Fusheng has...
Regarding the five commentaries, this work further compiles the essential points from various schools; it may be called an excellent edition.
Among the aforementioned types of texts, this compilation contains the greatest number of excerpts.

Recently, various editions have been published and circulated; those who interpret the meaning according to the literal text may number eight or nine out of ten, yet those who grasp the main framework, coordinate the underlying structure, and elucidate the fundamental purport of the entire scripture are seen but two or three out of a hundred.
This compilation extensively sought out excellent versions, discarding the coarse and selecting the refined, ensuring that every interpretation seeks the most essential meaning.

Indeed, I have sought to penetrate the essential meaning throughout the entire scripture, elucidating its fundamental principles and structural connections, as well as the points of transition and mutual resonance.
Furthermore, I have provided explanations and citations for every chapter and every sentence, not daring to omit even the slightest detail.
In this compilation, whenever there is a discussion or citation of evidence, or when elucidating a fundamental principle, or when annotating points of agreement or difference,
each entry is prefaced by the author’s surname or, in some cases, the title of the original work. However, regarding the interpretation of specific words, phrases, and textual meanings,
these are drawn from various sources indiscriminately, and the titles of the works or the names of their authors are not listed.
The work consists of thirty-two sections, each with its own original title, serving as the very eyes of the scripture.

At the beginning of each section, the meaning of the title is first elucidated, and it is further prefaced by the essential purport of the sutra, so that the general intent may shine forth clearly and be easily understood by the reader.

In each section where the Chinese text contains extensive length, profound meaning, or deep significance, the annotations will necessarily be numerous. Now, I have provided separate annotations for each subsection to facilitate reading.
Furthermore, a general commentary has been added at the end of each section, ensuring that the essential purport is detailed and lucid, and that the internal connections are seamlessly integrated.
I have also marked the essential points above to clarify the structure.

The sequence of the collected commentaries proceeds from the shallow to the profound, following the meaning of the text rather than arranging them according to the chronological order of their authors.
Furthermore, regarding meanings within the commentary that require further explanation, these have all been supplemented and listed above.
As for the various editions where the discourses of the treatise are prolix, they could not be recorded in their entirety due to the constraints of this brief format;
thus, they have all been abridged. May readers kindly refrain from taking offense at such omissions.
In various editions, citations of supporting evidence frequently employ verses and poetic lines; this compilation generally does not include them.

(Maitreya composed verses to explain the sutras, while Asaṅga and Vasubandhu both composed treatises to explain those verses. Vasubandhu’s work is particularly clear and concise. If one were to list the verses, one would further need to explain them, which would be far too cumbersome. The verses themselves can be consulted elsewhere. As for citing poetry, it is utterly unworthy of inclusion.)

In various editions of this sutra, only punctuation marks are used; thus, it is difficult for those who have not yet attained clear insight to distinguish which passages are the words of the Tathāgata and which are the words of Subhūti.

To assist beginners, in this edition, all sentences spoken by the Tathāgata are marked with a circle (○), while all sentences spoken by Subhūti are marked with a pointed circle (◦). The passages compiled by Ānanda are left unmarked.
Use dots. By adding square brackets to mark the beginning and end [of a section], the questions and answers become clear and distinct, as if one were looking directly at the palm of one's hand.
In the various editions of this scripture, dots alone are used to explain the phrases;
however, in this edition, wherever there are subtle instructions on practice or essential points of view, a continuous circle is used, or a pointed circle, or dots are added within a circle.
This sutra has undergone a total of six translations throughout its history: first by Kumārajīva of the Later Qin; second by Dharmaruci of the Later Wei; third by Paramārtha of the Chen;
fourth by Jñānagupta of the Sui; fifth by Xuanzang of the Tang; and sixth by Yijing of the Zhou. All six masters were renowned as Tripitaka-masters.
The version currently in circulation is the translation from the Qin dynasty (the Later Wei version differs slightly from the Qin version).
This sutra consists of thirty-two sections. It was certainly established by Prince Zhaoming himself.
Wang Zhenru remarked that its chapter divisions are detailed and clear, and that it has rendered great service to Buddhism; yet some people conversely criticize it for being artificially partitioned.

However, even in the root text of Asaṅga’s commentary, it is already divided into eighteen "abodes," and in the root text of Vasubandhu’s commentary, it is already divided into twenty-seven "doubts. Thus, in total, [the division is inherent].
This is the compassionate heart [of the Master], wishing merely to provide people with a single point of entry. Now, the eighteen dwellings and twenty-seven doubts are explained above;
furthermore, the titles assigned by Prince Zhaoming for each section are listed here before the text.
This makes it easy for readers to memorize and does not contradict the meaning of the sūtras; thus, later students must not rashly give rise to criticism. (Master Zhuan-yu said:

"If the eighteen abodes are taken as the standard, then Vasubandhu should not have divided them into twenty-seven doubts. If the twenty-seven doubts are taken as the standard, then Asaṅga should not have judged them as eighteen abodes.

Since these two Great Beings cannot serve as the definitive standard, the others may be understood accordingly. Thus, each person simply follows their own insight to achieve their own segment of Vajra-wisdom, all of which is non-contradictory with the true nature (*dharmatā*). It is not...")
One excellence can cut off what follows it, yet one attainment does not entirely abolish what preceded it; for since principle is inexhaustible, wisdom is likewise inexhaustible.
The meaning of the Sūtra is established by its capacity to sever [doubt]. Therefore, within the fifth verse of Maitreya, there is already the teaching of severing doubt.
Vasubandhu, following this, divided them into twenty-seven doubts, all of which are comprised within the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. There is nothing [else].
It was not yet thorough. Therefore, he followed the traces of the previous words to sever the subsequent doubts. When such a statement exists, there must be a corresponding illumination.
Furthermore, this does not necessarily mean that he was anticipating this doubt within the Venerable One’s mind beforehand.

The questions and answers within this scripture span twenty-nine sections. Among them, twenty-four passages originate from the Buddha’s own words, while sixteen originate from the specific capacities of the listeners.
This collection seeks diligently to investigate the reasons for the calls and indications, the reasons for the responses, and the reasons for the elucidations;
it explains them sequentially according to their respective contexts, up until the main body of the scripture.
The phrases are frequently repetitive. Furthermore, if one seeks the reason for this repetition:

there are four instances of saying "one cannot see one another," four of "crossing over where there is nothing to cross over," four of "speaking where there is nothing to speak," and four of "enlightenment being unattainable.
There are nine instances of "the absence of the four marks" and nine of "the giving of treasures and the giving of life. Although the essential conclusion is one, [these are taken...]
The meanings differ; they are also distinguished and categorized according to their respective locations.

Within the phrases and characters of the sutras, there are variations in addition, subtraction, agreement, and difference, such that they have never been uniform. For example: "This is called the Prajñāpāramitā" (Thirteenth Division);

"This is called the Kṣāntipāramitā" (Twenty-fifth Division); and "This is called the phrase for ordinary persons," among others. There are instances where [words] have been omitted [in ancient versions]. (Ancient Version)

Furthermore, according to the meaning of the sūtra, [the character] "also" (亦) cannot be omitted. If it were not for the character "if" (若) being subtracted from "non-perception" (無想), then according to the principle of the nine categories, it should logically be removed; if it were present, it would seem to divide the heavens into two.

As for the three characters "Why is this? (何以故) appearing before the phrase "If there is another person" (若復有人)—this constitutes the sixth section—these three characters are certainly spurious text (衍文). In the seventh section, there is a Buddha... [text continues].
Regarding the five characters "Subhūti," beneath the phrase "is not a dharma of the Buddha," there are the four characters "this is named a dharma of the Buddha.
Both Master Cheng and Master Gong have corrected this in their definitive editions; I have not dared to alter it arbitrarily.

Furthermore, the textual meaning is certainly intended to be thus (beyond this, there are additional or omitted characters that do not significantly affect the sense, and thus they are not recorded in full).
The characters "zé" (則) and "jí" (即) frequently differ across various editions. Having examined the origin of this variation, it arose because the name of the Goryeo King was *Jik* (稷).
Desiring to avoid its pronunciation, people altered "jí" (即) to "zé" (則) within the scriptures; thus, the false came to displace the authentic.
Master Yan of Haiyu, synthesizing various arguments, maintained that "jí" (即) is formed by combining the meanings of both [characters].
The principle of "succession" (xiāngréng) serves as the standard. That is to say, where "succession" may be employed, "conjoining two" (héliǎng) is not to be used;
this explanation is most accurate.
This sūtra is divided into fascicles—sometimes one, sometimes three, or sometimes two—and each version differs considerably.

According to the general purport of the entire scripture, from the point where the Venerable One again makes his request, the depth and shallowness of the text differ from what precedes it. An ancient scholar once said:

"The former statements concern coarse attachments; the latter statements concern subtle attachments. The former were spoken for those who have newly resolved their minds, and thus they provide a detailed discourse on the generation of the bodhicitta."

Regarding those who have already resolved their minds [to attain enlightenment], it is simply stated that there is no mind to be resolved upon. Hanshan’s *Discrimination of the Upper and Lower Volumes* explains this very clearly; one should follow that.

The original edition of this book contained many errors, and the printing blocks have already been destroyed. If virtuous gentlemen from distant regions wish to print and circulate it, they must use...

This is the original version of this treatise; it does not follow previous errors. (Nianqu) It is hoped that this may remedy the faults of omissions and mistakes, so that one need not harbor regrets for all eternity.

The recitation and upholding of this sutra depend entirely upon reading its text aloud while contemplating its meaning with the mind, so that these subtle words may be thoroughly understood and the complete purport may be fully mastered.
Only through such faithful understanding, acceptance, and upholding will it be truly beneficial.

If one reads in a frantic rush, seeking speed at the expense of clarity, such that the mouth reaches the words but the mind does not, then even if one has read it ten thousand times, it is no different from not having read it at all.
Recorded respectfully by the lay practitioner Jiezhai.

Among the various sūtra commentaries, these several works are the most exquisite, inspiring a sense of wonder at their perfection.)

The commentaries by the two families of Zhang Youyu and Zhang Guowei are precise, substantial, penetrating, and illuminating—unprecedented in their excellence. Furthermore, Gongshi’s *Jijie* (Collected Explanations) is particularly clear, comprehensive, and detailed, successfully synthesizing the merits of all [previous works].

It is to be regretted that these three books were acquired last, resulting in the calamity of "disaster for the jujube and misfortune for the pear" (the destruction of the woodblocks), leaving me with the lament of having both harmed myself and misled others.

A general summary (compiled from various texts) of the essential meaning of this sutra consists of five points: first, its title is established through both dharma and metaphor; second, its essence is the discernment of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*);
third, its thesis is non-abiding; fourth, its function is the resolution of doubts; and fifth, its doctrinal classification is that of the Mahāyāna. If one is ignorant of the dharma...
The Master said: "The true wisdom of the Dharma-body is called Prajñā; the fruit of the principle of the Dharma-body is called the Other Shore (Pāra). One must take true wisdom as the precursor;
only then can one sever afflictions, transcend birth and death, and fully realize the fruit of the principle. Therefore it is said: 'Wisdom reaches the Other Shore.
Its essence is the eternal abiding of the True Mark (Lakṣaṇa), and this essence is the Dharma-body. Its school (Siddhānta) is the contemplative illumination that accords with the principle."
This is precisely Prajñā (Wisdom). Its function is to sever doubt through words and letters; this function is itself liberation.

The two characters "Prajñā" encompass the essence, the substance, and the function [of the Buddha-nature]. Yet, it is specifically designated by the name "Prajñā" because the Dharma-body is not manifested without wisdom, and liberation is not accomplished without wisdom.
The Great Master Zhi said: "There are three kinds of *prajñā*: the true aspect (*lakṣaṇa*), contemplative illumination (*vipaśyanā*), and words (*vyañjana*).
The true aspect is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Contemplative illumination is wisdom (*jñāna*). Words, which are able to provide expression, are also considered *prajñā*."

As Asaṅga says: "Vajra" means indestructible, which signifies firmness; "vajra" can also sever, which signifies sharpness. Firmness is a metaphor for the *prajñā* of original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*), while sharpness is a metaphor for the *prajñā* of initial enlightenment (*ādi-awakening*).
The record states that "original" refers to the *dharmatā* (the true mark), and "initial" refers to contemplative observation (*vipaśyanā*).

The *dharmatā* is the essence; the mind is originally without marks, taking the primordial truth as the *dharmatā*. (This is the wondrous understanding of the true principle that gives rise to the *dharmatā*). It is the self-nature of the *tathāgatagarbha*.

The pure mind is the essence (*tǐ*); contemplative observation (*guānzhào*) is its function (*yòng*). The mind inherently possesses awakening; that which is manifested by true wisdom (*zhēnzhì*) constitutes contemplative observation.

This is precisely the wondrous prajñā that accords with original awakening (one should read this as "body and function together elucidated, essence and wisdom mutually arising," clearly and fluently). Therefore, although essence and function are distinguished, essence-wisdom (*lǐzhì*) is one.

The commentary states: "The principle within wisdom is the true mark (*shíxiàng*); the wisdom within principle is contemplative observation" (these are definitive words). *Prajñā* is correctly translated as "wisdom" (*huì*). Now...
It is said that this is wisdom (*prajñā*). Wisdom is the essence of knowledge (*jñāna*), while knowledge is the function of wisdom.
The Record states: "There are two kinds of *Vajra-prajñā*: the Real Aspect (*lakṣaṇa*), which is principle (*li*); and Contemplative Observation (*vipaśyanā*), which is phenomena (*shi*).
Apart from principle there is no knowledge, and apart from knowledge there is no principle. Therefore, it is able to sever all things; thus it is both firm and sharp."

This sutra exists within the nature of sentient beings, yet people do not see it for themselves; they merely know how to recite and read the words, seeking the Buddha only outside their own bodies and searching for the sutra beneath the phrases.

If one awakens to the original mind, only then will one know that this sutra does not reside in written characters, and only then will one know that all Buddhas emerge from this very sutra. The student should uphold the sutra of the inner mind to establish true insight.
The Dharma of nature is precisely what this sutra does not establish as a provisional construct.
This entire scripture is dedicated to elucidating the principles of the Mahāyāna. Subhūti, feeling ashamed of the Lesser Vehicle and aspiring to the Great, specifically requested instruction;
his inquiry concerning how to abide and subdue the mind directly opens the gateway to the teachings for thousands of generations.
Regarding the Dharma, the Sūtra states: "This sūtra is taught for those who have set out upon the Mahāyāna; it is taught for those who have set out upon the Supreme Vehicle.
This clarifies that the Mahāyāna constitutes its doctrinal characteristic (*śāsana-lakṣaṇa*).
This sutra takes the ten characters "arousing the mind for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*" as its main axis.
A single point of bodhicitta is, in fact, the adamantine true eye (*vajranetra*) and the universal retention (*dhāraṇī*) of all dharmas; one must regard it with the utmost gravity.
Only then does one know the point where the practical application of effort truly begins. Once the bodhicitta is aroused, the light of wisdom immediately appears; this is called prajñā.
All myriad practices arise from this. Therefore, for those who study the Buddha-way—from initial pure faith until the attainment of Buddhahood—one can never be separated from arousing the bodhicitta.
(If one does not arouse this mind, then one will dwell where one should not dwell, and fail to subdue that which must be subdued.)
Thus, they fail to heed and receive the entrustment. For this reason, within the sūtra, the phrase "arousing *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*" appears twenty-nine times.
In the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the Buddha speaks of formlessness (*animitta*); he merely removes deluded thoughts, but does not remove the principle of Heaven (*tianli*).

If one were to eliminate the principle of Heaven as well, would this not be like a walking corpse or a wandering piece of flesh, living in the world in vain? Therefore, it is explained in the fourteenth section.

Regarding the three characters for "the true mark of arising" (*sheng shixiang*), those with the faculty of wisdom should fix their gaze upon them. (It must be understood that what is called the state of non-characteristics is, in fact, the state of real characteristics;

this is the very lifeblood of the Buddha’s teaching. Elder Zibo said: "Later generations have labeled the teachings of Śākyamuni the 'Gate of Emptiness' (*kongmen*), which is utterly contrary to the original intent of Śākyamuni.
Our Confucian scholars do not investigate this minutely, but merely say that the Buddhists advocate emptiness, nothingness, and extinction. Is this not a grave error?"

Yuanzhi said: "Although Prajñāpāramitā certainly resides in the detachment from signs, one must nonetheless employ this prajñā of detachment to penetrate through the midst of the other five perfections—generosity, patience, and so forth.
Only by practicing with genuine earnestness can they be forged into a single whole.

Therefore, when the sutras speak of prajñā, they invariably observe it within the context of generosity, patience, and the like. When a practitioner of the path attains understanding and realization..."

Yet, without applying oneself to the higher realization, what is seen will ultimately fail to fall into the reality of things. Once Śūnyatā-utpāda had awakened to the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*), the Buddha further expounded for him a major section of the sūtra on patience (*kṣānti*).
This was precisely because he wished for him to pass through each and every stage of the most difficult-to-endure conditions without a single thought of agitation;
only then is it the truly authentic *prajñā* of the true mark. This is the *prajñā* that is free from marks (*lakṣaṇa-vivikta-prajñā*).

If one originally perceives [the Buddha] within the myriad phenomena of the universe, it is by no means a mark of annihilation. The Buddha spoke exclusively of Prajñā-pāramitā as being free from marks;
yet after [Subhūti] had entered this state, he suddenly proposed that one "may view the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks," thereby testing Subhūti.
Subhūti replied directly, "He may indeed be viewed," precisely identifying the point where his vision was correct. Later generations do not understand the Buddha’s intent.

[The author] says: Upon seeing one difficulty regarding the Wheel-Turning King, [the opponent] immediately claims that Śūnyatā-utpāda (Empty Birth) does not encompass such a statement; thus, they have buried Śūnyatā-utpāda to a great extent.
Giving is the foremost of the six perfections and is a major matter among the practices. It is at the very beginning that he speaks of the nirvana of immeasurable beings.
"Countless and boundless sentient beings—yet in truth, no sentient being is there who attains deliverance. This is the Tathāgata’s Dharma-gift of Prajñā.
Every sentence of this sutra is such a gift of the Dharma of Prajñā. It differs from the giving of material wealth or the giving of one's body and life;
it is entirely free from dwelling or attachment and does not fall into the realm of sense bases and objects. Therefore, in the fourth division, it says: 'The Bodhisattva...'"

"One should practice giving without dwelling on anything within the Dharma. In the final age, people take mere giving as their cultivation, regarding the act of relinquishing as "giving," and further rely upon giving to seek blessings and profit. This is to seek Buddhahood while clinging to the four marks.
When the faculties and objects are impure and the ocean of nature is not clear, how could a practitioner be like this?
The sutras frequently speak of "purity. This is because all phenomena possess both clarity and turbidity, as well as defilement and purity.
Since the *prajñā* of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is free from all such things, the two characters "pure" (*śuddha*) can only be truly applied to the *prajñā* of the true mark.
When the Elder says that when the mind of faith is pure, the true mark arises, he means that if it is not pure, it cannot be called the mind of faith.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying: "Bodhisattvas have four dharmas of pure conduct:

purity of mind, purity of dharma, purity of vow, and purity of the merit that adorns the buddha-field. This sutra overturns everything to its very bottom, applying a single flavor of whip-like lash to deluded sentiments;
it is like a sudden thunderclap or the blazing sun, or the ancient sword Taie—nothing it does not shatter.
There is not the slightest thing that is not illuminated. (As it is said: Prajñā is like a great mass of fire; whatever touches it is immediately consumed.
This directly causes every dharma to be found to be unobtainable, so that in every instance one encounters the family treasure. Thus, the originally pure essence is revealed.
The Diamond Sūtra lacks a first half; its exposition is not fully unfolded. It lacks a second half; its comprehensive synthesis is not exhaustive.
From within the seventeenth fascicle, it further explains the section on "How one should abide," thereby gathering the complete purport.

Hereafter, that which was previously detailed is abbreviated, while that which was previously abbreviated is detailed. Each successive section follows upon the last, each possessing its own wondrous meaning.
The first half speaks of the signless samādhi; this is the Dharma of the Bodhisattva. The second half speaks of the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya);

this is the Dharma of the Buddha. The Bodhisattva is the cause of the Buddha, and the Buddha is the fruition of the Bodhisattva. Thus, it is said that the cause encompasses the ocean of fruition, and the fruition reaches back to the source of the cause.
The single character "faith" (信) in the sixth section and the single character "patience" (忍) in the twenty-eighth section correspond to one another as interior and exterior.
Faith is the gateway for entering the Way; patience is the root for guarding the Way.
Daiyuán says: Prior to the thirteenth fascicle, the text speaks only of fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), and the title of the sutra is established as *Prajñā*.
From the fourteenth fascicle onward, it begins with the six *pāramitās* and continues until the attainment of *bodhi*, clarifying that all phenomena (*sarva-dharma*) are Buddha-dharmas;
even the wisdom of differentiation (*pravicaya-jñāna*) is fully explained therein. This is because there may be those who suspect that there are wholesome dharmas existing apart from *prajñā*.

It can be cultivated. Therefore, the twenty-fourth section further extracts the name of the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* to demonstrate that the wisdom of differentiation (*viśeṣajñāna*) is contained within fundamental wisdom (*mūlaprajñā*), which is collectively termed *prajñā*. Consequently, the cultivation of the merit of wholesome dharmas is used as a comparison to conclude [the discussion].

(Before the sixteenth section, the "arousing of the mind through practice" (*caryā-prasthāna-cittotpāda*) is explained; this proceeds from the fundamental to the differentiated. After the seventeenth section, the "realized arousal of the mind" (*bodhi-prasthāna-cittotpāda*) is explained; these all proceed from the differentiated back to the fundamental.)
From the seventeenth to the twenty-fifth sections is the "Mind of Realization" (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
Its intent lies in the dissolution of all phenomena (*dharma*), by means of penetrating the *tathatā* (suchness) of non-self;

it takes the non-self of all phenomena as its meaning and the attainment of enlightenment through non-attainment as its goal. From the twenty-sixth to the thirty-first sections is the "Refutation of All Views. By...
This reveals the Tathāgata’s correct vision, which is the vision of no-vision; it is taught generally for those who have resolved to attain bodhicitta.

Its meaning is "knowing and seeing through non-seeing," and its purpose is the non-arising of dharmic characteristics (the first twenty-five sections teach people to penetrate the dharma of non-self, while the subsequent twenty-six sections teach people to destroy the view of self).
To penetrate the dharma of non-self, one must first destroy the view of a self. To penetrate the dharma of non-self, it must be realized as a seamless whole.
Only when it is realized as a seamless whole can one shatter all marks.

Therefore, the three phrases—"is," "is not," and "is called"—are spoken simultaneously to select against and destroy the view of a self; this must be distinguished with clarity. Only when it is distinguished with clarity...
It is able to shatter all views; therefore, it is taught by splitting the three phrases apart as "neither this nor that.
The view of self does not transcend existence and non-existence, or unity and difference. In the twenty-ninth section, it is stated that [the Tathāgata] comes from nowhere and goes nowhere;
thus he is named the Tathāgata. Only when these three phrases are spoken simultaneously are the fourfold views of existence and non-existence completely shattered.
Thus, the doubt regarding whether the Dharmakāya and Nirmāṇakāya are identical or distinct is resolved in thirty ways.

By stating that "dust is not dust" and "the realm is not a realm," and that "the unified is not unified," the view of selfhood within the four propositions of identity and difference is further shattered.

The two lines, "As it truly is, it is immovable" and "do not grasp at appearances," establish the method of teaching the Dharma: to depart from appearances in order to realize suchness. This is the fundamental...
Regarding this contemplation of the wondrous wisdom of dharmas: it cannot be accomplished unless both the fundamental and the differentiated wisdoms are perfected.
Therefore, the entire Prajñāpāramitā corpus concludes with this.
The distinction between the sages and the worthy does not reside in the essence of the reality-mark (dharmatā), but rather in the function of contemplative wisdom (prajñā).
It is said that "Prajñā is non-Prajñā," for even the act of awakening and illumination has no place of attachment; only then does it pervade all dust-motes and the entire realm.

The great body of non-characteristics as characteristics manifested all at once. Only then did Kūṇḍadhāna understand that the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is precisely non-characteristic, and that the mark of sentient beings is precisely non-characteristic. To be free from all marks is what is called the Buddhas;
the Buddha-eye and Dharma-eye opened simultaneously. It is only through the Prajñā that does not dwell on marks that fundamental wisdom (*mūlaprajñā*) is thoroughly attained.

It has already been attained. One can now proceed to practice the six *pāramitās*. Following the section on patience, he instructs others to take this "separation from all marks" and, by means of wisdom, thread it through the head of every affair. One must put this into actual practice so that all sentient beings may receive its benefits.
From here until the point of "inconceivable," everything is spoken of in terms of merit; this is what is meant by "dedicating."

This is turning principle toward phenomena. When he asked again how one should resolve their characteristics to generate the mind [of enlightenment], he spoke once more of saving sentient beings, stating that in reality there is no dharma by which one generates or attains bodhicitta.

From the seventeenth section up until "that which the Tathāgata has attained is Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi," this is turning phenomena back toward principle. It is neither real nor false; it is true suchness. This is the phenomenon.

The non-obstruction of principle (*dharmadhātu-pratisaṃvid*). The five eyes, the marks and signs of merit, and the discourse on the four chapters—these are "to depart from and yet not depart from," "to be and yet not be.

In the teachings (*śāsana*), this constitutes the simultaneous illumination and simultaneous negation; in the Gate of the Patriarchs (*zongmen*), it is what is called "living together and dying together.

Only upon reaching this point does one truly understand the practice of saving beings and bestowing gifts according to the three or four divisions, and the case of not abiding in appearances. Once one has passed through the Great... [text ends]
The essential meaning is now complete. Following this, the four propositions of existence, non-existence, identity, and difference are split apart.

This is precisely to reveal that the three phrases—“is,” “is not,” and “is called”—are spoken simultaneously as a wondrous principle. For when one sees them divided, they immediately become the four marks of self, person, sentient being, and life-span;
there remains a sense of a unified whole, and the four views have not yet been entirely forgotten. Only upon reaching [the analysis of] existence, non-existence, identity, and difference...
Free from both. Even a "unified mark" (ekapiṇḍalakṣaṇa) cannot be apprehended; this is precisely the right view that is free from all four views.
This is intended to show people the method for upholding [the teaching] and to instruct them in the manner of expounding it. (The above four explanations are excerpts from Zhang Youyu.)
Zongmi said: "This sutra is intended as an antidote for the two attachments—to self and to phenomena—and for the two obstacles—the afflictive and the cognitive.
If the two attachments are eliminated, the two obstacles will be severed accordingly; it is for the purpose of eliminating these two attachments that this sutra is taught.

Song Zhengyu said: "Ordinary worldlings conceive of the five aggregates as a self; this is called the attachment to self. Non-Buddhists and those of the Two Vehicles conceive of all phenomena as having an intrinsic nature; this is called [the attachment to phenomena]."

Attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) gives rise to afflictions through attachment to a self (*ātman-grāha*), which constitutes the afflictive obstruction (*kleśāvaraṇa*). Attachment to phenomena gives rise to the cognizable (*jñeya*), which constitutes the cognitive obstruction (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Therefore, it is said that if these two attachments are eliminated, the two obstructions are accordingly severed.
Chen Xiong said: "Those who plant roots of goodness begin by reciting the sutras and end by awakening to the principle.

That which provides the power of firmness is the *Vajra* [Sutra]. That which possesses great wisdom is the *Prajñā*. That which crosses the sea of birth and death to ascend the shore of Bodhi is the *Pāramitā*.

The Great Master, the Fifth Patriarch, constantly exhorted both monastics and laypeople: 'Simply uphold the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, and you will naturally be able to see [the Buddha-nature].'"
[One of] inherent nature will certainly attain Buddhahood.
Cheng Chengzhai said: "Observing the various sections of the Mahāyāna, many Bodhisattvas mutually corroborate one another;

yet in this sutra, which is suited to the specific capacity [of its audience], there is only the Venerable Subhūti alone—either requesting instruction, being exhorted and shown the way, or receiving the teaching. [The content ranges from] shallow to deep, and coarse to subtle."
The details naturally form a systematic order; one should seek them within the single thread that runs through the preceding and following sections.

In the question-and-answer passages of various sutras, [the Buddha] often employs "retrogressive inquiry" (*pratyāgamana*) to elicit proof, yet Subhūti receives these teachings by following each word in due order. Responding to whatever arises according to the capacity of his faculties, he resolves them as easily as a blade meeting a whetstone.

Therefore, there is no need for prolixity. As for what is discussed in the Mahāyāna—such as the five dharmas, the three natures, the eight consciousnesses, the two attachments, and the *dhātu*—it is all contained herein.
The *āyatanas* (bases of cognition) have various and manifold names; yet this sutra speaks only of the single mind (*citta*).
It begins with the phrase "the non-abiding arising of the mind" and concludes with the three words "unattainable. Thus, while the branches and leaves are all empty, it uniquely highlights the root;

this is therefore of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). Following the third period, there was a uniform discourse on emptiness, yet even the word "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*) is not established within what is taught in this sutra.
One takes only the signless as the true mark; thus, non-abiding is itself the proper abiding.
From the initial arousal of the mind until the mind has nothing further to arouse, one further clarifies this through the unification of the unreal and the non-illusory.
In the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the Buddha speaks of its greatness by comparing it to Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains;
he speaks of its abundance by comparing it to the sands of the Ganges River; and he speaks of its duration by comparing it to immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.

These are indeed numbers that are infinitely great, infinitely many, and infinitely long, representing an inexhaustible quantity. It is neither an exaggeration on the part of the Tathāgata, nor is it...
It is well that you have come to utter such words to startle the common world; readers should seek the underlying principle.

In the eighth section of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, "The Section on Birth According to the Dharma," it is stated that one might give as alms the seven treasures filling a trichiliocosm.

(11) It is not equal to the merit of upholding this sutra. Within the section on the superiority of unconditioned merit, even the seven treasures filling worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—and indeed more than those in a trichiliocosm—are still not equal to the merit of upholding this sutra.

(13) Within the section on receiving and upholding according to the Dharma, even if one were to give away as many lives as there are grains of sand in the rivers as an act of charity, it would not merely be the giving of the seven treasures; when compared to receiving, upholding, and explaining [the sutra], it ultimately does not [equal it].

It is superior. (Fifteenth) Within the section on the merit of upholding the sutra, it is stated that even if one were to give away one's body and life as many times as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River three times over, this would still be far surpassed by the merit of upholding the sutra;

the former does not equal the latter. Within the section on purifying karmic obstacles, the practitioner recounts the vastness of their own offerings to the Buddhas, which greatly differ from the giving of the seven treasures, the body, and life; likewise, these do not equal the merit of upholding [the sutra].
A mere fraction of the merit gained from explaining this sutra. (Twenty-fourth) In the section on the incomparable merit of wisdom, it is compared to the seven treasures of Mount Sumeru;
though they are vast and lofty, they do not equal the merit of upholding and explaining this sutra. Although these words are repeated, their meaning is increasingly profound with each step.
This collectively demonstrates that this sutra is the essential point for realizing one's nature, enabling one to see for oneself.

One immediately attains Buddhahood. How could the merit of giving ever be compared to this? (The Buddha knew that during the age of the Dharma’s decline, most would take giving as their primary practice while failing to understand the essential point of realizing the nature; therefore, he spoke of it with earnestness and repetition.)

Those who read the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* should first cultivate the four immeasurable minds of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Furthermore, they must sit in stillness and contemplate the mind; when the mind is found to be no-mind, one may then enter the Great Way and awaken to the meaning of the Vajra.

(The opening verses of the sūtra composed by the Seventh Patriarch first invoke the Eight Vajras, which represent the eight consciousnesses within one's own body. Next, he invokes the Four Bodhisattvas—Guanzizai, Suoxing, Aiyu, and Si—which represent the four immeasurable minds of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, the bodhisattvas within our own bodies. They are able to...)
To see one's own nature—why must one seek the Buddha outside of oneself? The essential framework of the entire sutra is this:
"If a bodhisattva has the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, or the mark of a life-span, then he is not a bodhisattva. (Part Three)
If one perceives that all marks are non-marks, one sees the Tathāgata. (The *Pañcavargika*) All noble and holy ones are distinguished by means of the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
(The *Saptavargika*) One should give rise to the mind without abiding anywhere. (The *Daśabhūmika*) When the mind of faith is pure, the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) arises.
If the mind has an abiding place, it is not truly abiding. This dharma is neither real nor unreal.
Empty. (Fourteenth section of the first fascicle) There is truly no dharma. (Seventeenth section of the second fascicle) One thoroughly penetrates the dharma of non-self.
(Eighteenth section) The past mind cannot be apprehended; the present mind cannot be apprehended; the future mind cannot be apprehended.
(Twenty-eighth section) By realizing that all dharmas are without self, one achieves patience (*kṣānti*). One should know thus, see thus, and understand thus.

Section Thirty-one: Faith and Understanding Do Not Give Rise to the Characteristics of Dharmas. Section Thirty-two: For the Sake of Others, One Expounds the Teaching Without Grasping at Characteristics, Remaining Immovable in Suchness.
The Essential Meaning of Each Section of the Scripture.

The first part is the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* Prologue of Testimony; the second part is the Inquiry into the Essential Meaning; the third and fourth parts are the Proper Response concerning Abiding and Subduing;

the fifth part clarifies that all things possessing marks are false, thereby revealing the true Buddha who is markless; the sixth and seventh parts clarify that all things not being dharmas are merely marks, thereby revealing the true Dharma which is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);
and from the fifth to the fourteenth parts, it clarifies that all Buddhas are, in essence, free from marks when one perceives the Buddha.
(90) This is the place where all sages and worthies have successively testified to and cultivated [the Dharma]. It cannot be grasped or described (11–13).
Comparing the excellence of the sutra (13), it reveals the name of the sutra and demonstrates the method for upholding it (14).

It teaches that one should give rise to practice from understanding, and generate the mind of awakening free from signs in order to benefit sentient beings (15–16). It clarifies the conduct of practicing this.
The Merits of the Sūtra, Difficult to Measure, Part Two (Seventeen Divisions): A detailed exposition that there is truly no dharma to clarify the meaning of the suchness (*tathatā*) of all dharmas;
concluding with the thorough realization of non-self in dharmas (Divisions 18–21). Correctly clarifying that all dharmas are without self (Divisions 23–24).
Stating that the cultivation of wholesome dharmas is not external to *prajñā* (Division 25). Exposition.
The Tathāgata delivers sentient beings; in truth, there is no extinction (from section 17 to 25). This is collectively titled "Forgetting Dharmas and Realizing Suchness" (from section 26 to 31).
This is entirely for the purpose of destroying views and manifesting wisdom: (section 26) clarifying that those who cling to existence follow a deviant path;
(section 27) clarifying that those who cling to non-existence fall into annihilationism; (section 28) clarifying non-self.
This merit alone is supreme. All dharmas are without self; this constitutes the perfection of patience (*kṣānti*). Without patience, one cannot maintain the Way.
(Chapter 29) Relying on the Dharma-body to refute existence and non-existence in order to clarify the absence of coming and going.

(Chapter 30) Relying on the realms of dust to refute unity and difference, thereby sweeping away for all people their attachment to phenomenal characteristics. Taking the realms as a metaphor for the Dharma-body...
The "Dust Simile" (Section Thirty-one) employs *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* to dismantle the two views of self and phenomena (*ātma-dṛṣṭi* and *dharma-dṛṣṭi*).

Because both self and phenomena are empty, one is able to abide nowhere; because one abides nowhere, one is truly able to abide. This is the ultimate realization of Prajñāpāramitā (Section Thirty-two), which concludes with its circulation.
General Preface to the Thirty-two Sections of the Diamond Sutra (Composed by Mingwanghua Long).

This single volume of sutra discusses entirely the true emptiness and formlessness. When the Buddha first turned the Wheel of the Four Noble Truths three times at the Deer Park, it was no more than to cause people to know that [phenomena] exist.
Yet deluded people hastily grasp at the existence of forms to practice; the Buddha further feared that people...
It is recorded that when this sutra was first preached, it was called the School of Destroying Marks (*xiang*). This was because it stated: "Whatever marks exist are all false and illusory.
Only by realizing that existence is not existence and emptiness is not emptiness does one attain the original true nature.
At the outset, the assembly of disciples gathered for the preaching of the Dharma (the section on the origins of the Dharma assembly), and Subhūti posed a question, saying: "This bodhi..."

"How should one stabilize the mind? How should one subdue the deluded mind? (The Section on Subhūti’s Request). The Buddha replied that [the four modes of birth—] womb, egg, moisture, and transformation;

as well as perceptions of form, perceptions of non-form, and so forth—all these are brought about by the habitual tendencies of the deluded minds of sentient beings, and all should be brought to extinction.
If one is free from the four marks of self, person, sentient being, and life-span, this constitutes the true orthodoxy of the Mahāyāna.
The Teaching. (The Section on the True Principle of the Mahāyāna) Therefore, in all acts of giving, one must not dwell upon signs.

(The Section on Sublime Practice Without Dwelling) Because they are empty, false, and unreal, one must perceive both signs and signlessness; thus, when the mind is illuminated and opened, the vision of the Tathāgata is attained.

(The Section on the Reality of Suchness) This principle is most worthy of firm faith, yet it is seldom found. (The Section on the Rarity of Right Faith) All of these are originally inherent within you.
Nature. To awaken and cultivate for oneself—what need is there for verbal expression? (Section on Non-attainment and Non-exposition) All Buddhas flow forth from this sutra.
(Section on Birth According to the Dharma) The four fruits of the path are all certified by this principle. (Section on the One Mark and Marklessness) When my mind is pure, it is only then adorned.
(Section on Adorning the Pure Land) When my mind is unconditioned, it is only then called merit. (Section on the Superiority of Unconditioned Merit)
[Section on the Most Supreme and First Rare Dharma] This is the most supreme, first, and rare Dharma; it is that which should be honored and revered.

[Section on Honoring the True Teaching] Furthermore, it is that which should be received and upheld. [Section on Receiving and Upholding According to the Dharma] When one is free from all marks (*lakṣaṇa*), then quiescent extinction (*nirvāṇa*) manifests before one.

[Section on Quiescent Extinction through the Absence of Marks] If one is able to recite, read, and expound it, then the merit will be immeasurable. [Section on the Merit of Upholding the Sūtra] For anyone who...
Karmic obstructions are all completely purified. (The Section on Purifying Karmic Obstructions) Ultimately, in the future, this is called the Bodhisattva’s Dharma of Non-self.
(The Section on Ultimate Non-self) The reason for this is that the minds of the past, present, and future are fundamentally ungraspable.

(The Section on Contemplating the Single Essence) Empty, luminous, profound, and still—this is the entirety of the single Dharma-realm. (The Section on the Universal Transformation of the Dharma-realm) Since these three minds...

When all is merged, both form and appearance are transcended (Section on Transcending Form and Appearance). When speech and what is spoken are both extinguished (Section on Neither Speech nor What is Spoken), how could a single dharma be apprehended?

(Section on Observing the Single Essence with Equal Vision). One should simply awaken to the nature of equality (Section on Cultivating Goodness with a Pure Mind) and bestow the merit of wondrous wisdom (Section on Inconceivable Merit and Wisdom).

Since ordinary beings and sages are mutually interfused, how could one know there are sentient beings to be transformed? (Section on Transforming Without Anything to Transform). How could there be a Tathāgata to be... [found]? (Section on the Non-existence of a Tathāgata).
They seek one another. (The Section on the Dharma-body being Without Characteristics) Now, to speak of "no-characteristics" would cause one to fall into a state of inert emptiness.

Therefore, regarding the Dharma, he does not speak of a characteristic of annihilation. (The Section on No Annihilation and No Extinction) Wondrously profound and perfectly penetrating, at times he practices giving, yet his mind does not crave receiving.

(The Section on Non-receiving and Non-craving) At times he responds to conditions, yet in principle there is no coming or going. (The Section on Dignified Deportment and Quiescence) Thus, principle and characteristics merge, and the inner and outer are unified.

Comprehensive and inclusive. (Section on the Rational Characteristics of Reality) Delusory views are entirely dissolved. (Section on the Non-arising of Knowledge and Views) Nevertheless, this scripture teaches people to recite and expound it;
it is simply this one nature of true emptiness. As for its applications and transformations, how could they ever possess any reality?
(Section on Manifestations Not Being Real) To summarize it in a single phrase: do not grasp at appearances; remain as such, unmoving. This is it.
The words are ultimate and exhaustive. If one can directly accept and take responsibility for them, there is not even a single character; what need is there for the thirty-two divisions?
Otherwise, one relies on rafts to cross a river and requires a boat to traverse the sea; this sutra should be upheld in all such cases. I pray that you will contemplate it with careful attention.
General Outline of the Entire Sūtra (Compiled by Shufu).
This sūtra’s initial introduction consists of two parts: first, the presentation of faith, hearing, time, the teacher, the location, and the assembly to establish credibility;

second, the presentation of precept, concentration, and wisdom to initiate the discourse. From the second division through the thirty-first division constitutes the main body (*samyak-artha*). The Buddha addressed Subhūti...
From "The Bodhisattva should abide as instructed" (the second to the fourth sections) is the brief exposition of Prajñāpāramitā. From "Subhūti, what do you think?

to "One should contemplate it in this way" (the fifth to the thirty-second sections) is the extensive discourse on Prajñāpāramitā; these correspond to what the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* calls the two gates of the extensive and the brief.

Within the brief exposition, there are three parts. The section from "The Buddha said to Subhūti" (the third part) briefly explains subduing [the mind], which internally comprises four [sub-sections].

The mind is that which the bodhisattva cultivates as contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*). Furthermore, Subhūti, [in the] fourth section (upper part), it is briefly stated that one should abide in the external practice of the six perfections;
this is that which the bodhisattva cultivates as active practice (*caryā*). Why is this? [In the] fourth section (lower part), this is a comparison of merits.
In order to refute the view of annihilation, it is said that merit and so forth are like space; this is the retribution obtained by the Bodhisattva.

This is divided into seven parts within the extensive [treatise]. The three sections of the first fascicle concern the Bodhisattva’s signless samādhi (*animitta-samādhi*), which is what he should properly abide in, yet he subdues [afflictions] while remaining therein.
Initially, the signless is elucidated in terms of the Bodhisattva’s fruit: the manifestation of the Tathāgata’s form is signless (Fifth Division), and his teaching of the Dharma...

This is the seventh section on signlessness (*animitta*). Next, signlessness is elucidated in relation to the stages of a bodhisattva; the teaching applies throughout the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), which constitute the rank of a bodhisattva.
First, it is stated that the four fruits [of the śrāvaka] are realized through signlessness (the ninth section). Second, it is stated that the pratyekabuddha is realized through signlessness.

Third, it is stated that the bodhisattva is realized through signlessness (the tenth section). Fourth, it is stated that the Buddha is realized through signlessness. Third, [this is] in relation to the bodhisattva.

To practice by means of clarifying signlessness (*animitta*)—practicing the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) and cultivating patience (*kṣānti*)—is precisely the practice of a bodhisattva (the Fourteenth Section). First, the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) clarifies signlessness;

next, the perfection of patience clarifies signlessness; furthermore, this is further elaborated through the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), which speaks to the ultimate extent that signs have no basis for abiding.
This constitutes the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) of the ultimate departure from signs, thereby concluding the preceding section.

After the [preceding] section, at that time, there is a passage where Subhūti addresses the Buddha; this serves to refute the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) and enter the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*).

It is a textual device for connecting the preceding and following sections, and thus it is restated. (This restatement is recorded by the scribe of the scripture; it is not a repeated question by Subhūti himself.
The lower fascicle is divided into four sections, which constitute the Tathāgata’s ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), providing the formal answer on how to subdue [the mind] and abide [in it].
Cultivation is contained therein. First, based on the Tathāgata’s vision and wisdom, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is established.
The five eyes are able to see; this is "clear seeing" and "purity" (Chapter 18). The three minds are unattainable; this is "clear wisdom" and "purity.

Next, based on the Tathāgata’s three karmas, the ultimate truth is established as "non-characteristic is characteristic," which constitutes the perfection of body (the twentieth division). There is no dharma that can be spoken; this constitutes the perfection of speech (the twenty-first division). Attainment...

Non-attainment constitutes the twenty-second part of the perfection of the mind. Third, regarding the establishment of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) through the Tathāgata’s deliverance of sentient beings:

to perceive the existence of sentient beings is the partial conceptualization (*parikalpa*) of ordinary worldlings; not to perceive the existence of sentient beings is the empty contemplation (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*) of the two vehicles.

In reality, there are no sentient beings who attain parinirvāṇa. To deliver them in this manner—namely, that which is simultaneously empty, provisionally existent, and the Middle Way—is precisely what it means to be a Tathāgata.
The First Noble Truth (in twenty-five sections). Fourth, establishing the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) in terms of the coming and going of the Tathāgata:
the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata pervades all places; how, then, could there be coming or going? When the conditions of sentient beings ripen, they perceive his coming (in twenty-nine sections).
It is like the aggregation of atoms forming a world. When the conditions of sentient beings are exhausted, they perceive his going. It is like the disintegration of a world into [atoms].

[It is like] a mote of dust. Therefore, the motes of dust in the world are used as a metaphor. Vasubandhu’s commentary explains this in terms of "one place" and "different places," which may be considered a refined formulation of the thesis.
Segment by segment, one measures the merit; this is what the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* refers to as "non-empty according to reality.
The conclusion states: "One should know, see, believe, and understand thus," which properly concludes the response to the previous question, "How should one abide?"
What is meant by "subduing" and so forth? Because the view of a self is shattered and the view of phenomena (*dharmadṛṣṭi*) is absent, one is able to abide nowhere.

Because there is no abiding, one is truly able to abide. This sutra, being without marks (*animitta*) and without a master, gathers the entirety of the scripture within the non-arising of dharmic characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).
At the end, it again highlights "not grasping at marks" as the essential point of its exposition, illustrating this through six metaphors as the true Prajñā.
The Gate of Essential Contemplation: All practitioners should enter by way of this. The thirty-second section is the Section on Dissemination, which has two parts:
first, the comparison of the excellence of merit; second, the joyful acceptance and practice.
The Compendium of the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra (The title of this sūtra contains both metaphor and dharma; this sūtra combines the dharma and the metaphor in its title).
"Vajra" is the metaphor; "Prajñā" is the dharma. The metaphor is employed to manifest the dharma. The "vajra" among metals is the most solid and firm.
"Most beneficial. "Gold" takes the meaning of being unchanging, which is a metaphor for the essence of *prajñā*. It is truly eternal and pure;
although it has passed through many lifetimes and scattered across the six realms of existence, it neither shifts nor changes—this is the *prajñā* of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*).
"Hardness" takes the meaning of cutting through, which is a metaphor for the function of *prajñā*. When this wisdom manifests, one sees that all phenomena of the five aggregates are...
Emptiness severs all outflows, afflictions, and karma; it is the wisdom of contemplation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-prajñā*). In Sanskrit, *prajñā* means "wisdom" in Chinese.
It is the light of immovable wisdom, the true vision that is free from marks; it is what is called the Buddha’s wisdom.
Wisdom is not deluded by various marks (*nimitta*); rather, it is able to shatter them all. The *vajra* is like this. In Sanskrit, *pāramitā*;
in the language of China, "reaching the other shore. This refers to the ultimate limit of cultivating the Path. People, however, remain attached to these various marks.
It is like entering a sea of suffering: when traversing the middle currents and encountering wind and waves, one is most easily submerged and drowned.
If one possesses wisdom, remains free from all marks (*nimitta*), and keeps the mind ever pure, one will immediately ascend to the other shore—this is what is called *nirvāṇa*.

*Jīng* (Sūtra) means "correct. It is ultimate correctness, devoid of error. *Jīng* also means "constant. It is the constant Way that does not change. *Jīng* also means "path" or "track. It is that which all people should exhaustively follow.
[The character for] "practice" (*xing*). Explanation of the Text: "Vajra. This is the name of a precious substance in the heavens; Śakra possesses it.

It is also said that it is the same jewel as the *vajra* (pestle) wielded by the *Dharmapāla* (Protectors of the Dharma) *Ṛṣis*. Weng Jiying says: "All five metals are called 'gold' (*jin*). Generally...
The term "gold" (jin) refers to iron. This [term] "vajra" refers to the hard iron found in swords and blades. The Commentary states:
"Prajñā is the untainted noble wisdom (*anāsrava-ārya-jñāna*) that is the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the fundamental mind;

it is not the deluded wisdom of conceptual inference (*anumāna*), intellectual discernment, or speculative estimation. For this reason, the scriptural text does not translate the term into Chinese; thus, it is distinguished from worldly things."
This is what is commonly referred to as "wisdom. [From] the *Jíjiě* (Collected Explanations): Prajñā is the true dharma for attaining Buddhahood.
Chen Xiong said: There are six pāramitās. Generosity transcends stinginess and greed; ethical discipline transcends lust and depravity;
patience transcends anger and resentment; vigor transcends indolence and retreat; meditative concentration transcends distraction; and only prajñā can give rise to the eight [liberations].
There are fourteen thousand types of wisdom. Therefore, by the power of wisdom, the Tathāgata hews away the mountain of self and personhood;
by the cause of wisdom, he extracts the ore of afflictions; and by the fire of wisdom, he smelts it into the refined gold of Buddha-nature.

Now, for those who plant roots of goodness, they begin by reciting the sutras and ultimately awaken to the underlying principle, thereby attaining firm and steadfast power—this is what is meant by the *vajra*. Possessing...
Great wisdom is precisely *prajñā*. Crossing the sea of birth and death and ascending to the shore of *bodhi* is precisely the *pāramitā*.

The Great Master of the Fifth Patriarch constantly exhorted monastics and laypeople: "If you simply uphold the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, you will naturally be able to see your own nature."
One will certainly attain Buddhahood.
Regarding the purport of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*: the single phrase "to give rise to the mind by dwelling nowhere" is the essential tenet of the entire scripture.
What is meant by "dwelling" and "subduing" is, first, not to cling to appearances (*nimitta*), and second, not to become mired in dharmas (*dharma*). This is its merit.
Now, abiding in non-self, its ultimate state lies in suchness, which is immovable. The first half of this fascicle explains the samādhi of emptiness; this is the Dharma of the Bodhisattva.
The second half of the fascicle explains the Middle Way, the primary truth; this is the Dharma of the Buddha.

The Bodhisattva is the cause of the Buddha, and the Buddha is the fruition of the Bodhisattva. Thus, it is said that the cause encompasses the ocean of fruition, and the fruition reaches back to the source of the cause.
Section One: The Origin of the Dharma Assembly.
From this, the cause arises. This entire sutra is merely a single discourse.
Prince Zhaoming divided this into thirty-two sections, intending to provide people with a single path of entry and also to facilitate memorization.
As it has been transmitted for a long time, I have retained its original form.
This section consists entirely of the words compiled by Ānanda and Kāśyapa.
*Evam mayā śrutam*.
"Thus" (*evam*) means "this," referring to what is stated in this sutra. "By me" (*mayā*) refers to the compiler of the scripture speaking of himself;
it signifies that this Dharma of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* is not my own speculative fabrication, but was heard directly from the Buddha by me as I compiled it.

Explanation: Regarding the four characters "Thus have I heard" (evam mayā śrutam), the emphasis lies on following what preceded and believing what followed, so that one may know the Dharma has its own source of transmission and is not a concealed or hidden teaching;
this is because it directly reveals that Prajñā contains no secrets. Regarding the word "thus" (evam) throughout the Sūtra, one must pay the utmost attention.
It uprightly and directly unveils the central theme of the entire scripture. What follows is called "abiding thus" (evam viharati).
Thus subdued; thus giving rise to a pure mind; thus knowing; thus seeing;

thus believing and understanding—each of these corresponds to these two characters, *ru* (如) and *lai* (來), which together form "Tathāgata" (如來). The character *ru* (如) also corresponds to this [same] character *ru*:

"as it is," the meaning of the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena, and "suchness as immovable. All instances of the character *ru* likewise correspond to this character *ru*. "As" (*ru*) means immovable; "is" (*shi*) means not...
It is not so. According to its true nature, the unchanging essence itself is "is" and not "not-is.
This is a remote indication of *prajñā*, yet it is also a direct pointing to the present moment.
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
It was at this time that he spoke this Prajñāpāramitā. The Buddha is Śākyamuni. "Buddha" is a Sanskrit term; in the language of China, it means "Awakened.
Internally awakened, he is free from all deluded thoughts; externally awakened, he is untainted by the six sense objects. He is fully endowed with awakening.

There are three meanings [to this]. First, self-awakening distinguishes one from ordinary people (*pṛthagjana*). Second, awakening others distinguishes one from those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).
Third, the perfection of awakening distinguishes one from bodhisattvas. Śrāvastī is the capital of King Prasenajit, who resided in Central India.
As for Jeta, he was the crown prince of King Prasenajit. The trees were planted by Jeta; therefore, it is called Jetavana. Prince Jeta possessed a park.
It was eighty *qǐng* in area, square, vast, and magnificent. There was an elder named Sudatta who provided for the orphaned and the solitary;
thus he was called the Elder Anāthapiṇḍada. Desiring to select an auspicious site to invite the Buddha to preach the Dharma, he went there to make his request.
The Prince said in jest, "If you spread gold to fill the entire garden, I shall grant it to you. Sudatta did not begrudge the expense.
The prince, perceiving their sincerity, offered them the garden along with its trees at a high price. Together they constructed a vihāra and invited the Buddha to reside there and preach the Dharma,
accompanied by a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
"Bhikṣu" refers to the Sangha. In Sanskrit it is *bhikṣu*; in the language of China, it is translated as "mendicant" (*qǐshì*).
This means that above, one begs the Dharma from the Buddhas, and below, one begs for food from the people of the world. Begging for food sustains the body; begging for the Dharma sustains the mind.
A "Great Bhikṣu" is one who has attained a profound realization of the Way, such as a Bodhisattva or an Arhat. Li Wenhui says: "To depart..."
One who wrongly grasps at goodness is called a "small bhikṣu"; one who casts away both good and evil is called a "great bhikṣu. [The] Extensive Commentary [states]:
Although the Buddha ordained a great many bhikṣus, he singled out these one thousand two hundred and fifty people because they were the very first to take refuge in the Buddha.

Furthermore, he was never separated from the Buddha; therefore, at the beginning of various sūtras, the great assembly is enumerated, stating that they were "accompanied by one thousand two hundred and fifty people.
According to the ancient explanation, when the Buddha attained enlightenment, he first ordained the five men, including Kauṇḍinya;
next, he ordained the three brothers of Kāśyapa along with their thousand followers; and subsequently, he ordained Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, each [with their own retinues].
