Together with one hundred followers, he next ordained fifty people, including Yaśas, the son of a householder, making a total of one thousand two hundred and fifty-five persons.
The omission of the word "five" is an abbreviation. "Together" (俱) means at the same time and in the same place.

This section constitutes the *Saddharmapratyayopadeśa* (Preface for Establishing Faith). Among the eleven wholesome dharmas, faith (*śraddhā*) stands at their head. "Thus" (*evam*) serves to establish this faith.
The term "hearing" (*śruta*) refers to both auditory consciousness and mental consciousness. This introduction contains six factors of accomplishment:
faith, hearing, time, the teacher, the place, and the assembly. It is only when these conditions are complete that the teaching arises.
At that time, at the hour for eating, the World-Honored One donned his robes and took up his alms bowl.
At that very moment, because the Buddha is the Honored One of the three realms, he is called the "World-Honored One" (*Lokanātha*), which is one of the ten epithets of a Buddha.
"The hour for eating" refers to the time when he was about to eat, not the time when he had already received the food. As the Sūtra says: "The various devas..."
The various ghosts eat in the evening; the Buddhas eat at midday. Begging for food occurs during the hours of the Dragon (辰) and Snake (巳);
receiving the meal is at the hour of the Horse (午). As for the robe, it is the twenty-five-fold *kaṣāya*, its pattern modeled after a water field.
The alms bowl is a bowl of deep blue lapis lazuli, a vessel of appropriate measure. The Sixth Patriarch said: "Wearing the robe and holding the bowl is to manifest the traces of the teaching."
He entered the great city of Śrāvastī to beg for alms.
Since the monastery was outside the city, he would enter from the monastery into the city; it was essential that he beg in places where crowds of people gathered.
As the Buddha was the son of a Golden Wheel-turning King, how could there be no one to offer him sustenance? This was all the more so in the presence of Prince Jeta and Anāthapiṇḍada.
"Elder, we have jointly constructed this vihāra and invited the Buddha to preach the Dharma. How could our Buddha be one who lacks food? Yet he still practices begging;

this is because he wishes to undergo the ascetic practices of a dhūta to show himself as equal to ordinary monks, and so that future followers of the black robe may not accumulate assets, abandon their greedy minds, subdue their arrogance, and thereby refine their spiritual natures."
Having completed his alms-round in the city in successive order, he returned to his original location.
The Buddha’s mind was impartial and free from discrimination; he did not bypass the poor to go first to the wealthy, nor did he abandon the lowly to seek out the noble.
Thus it is called "successive order. As for "having finished begging," he stopped according to what was needed and did not seek more than that. His "original location" was the Jeta Grove.
Having finished eating, he put away his robes and bowl, washed his feet, spread out a seat, and sat down.

The character for "food" (*bān*) is interpreted as the character for "cooked" (*shí*). "Finished" (*jì*) means completed. "Put away" means to collect and store his *kāṣāya* robe and alms bowl, setting aside his requisites.

Because the Buddha walked barefoot, he washed them; this is the purification of physical action (*kāyakarman*). Whenever the Buddha preached the Dharma in an assembly, he would invariably [do so himself].
He spreads out his sitting mat. By means of Prajñā (wisdom), he gives birth to all Buddhas; this signifies his reverence for the Dharma. Among the four modes of deportment, sitting alone is supreme.
Speaking from within meditative concentration, his words are never inappropriate. This section constitutes the Prologue of the Preface.
Begging for alms is the precept (*śīla*); sitting cross-legged is meditative concentration (*samādhi*). The precept can support concentration, and concentration can give rise to wisdom (*prajñā*).
Therefore, through precept and concentration, one brings forth the true teaching of *prajñā*. The Commentary states:
"The Dharma assembly at Jeta Grove symbolizes the equality of the Buddha and the great multitude, as they fully possess the ineffable Vajra-prajñā-pāramitā; and by wearing robes..."
Begging for food is listed at the beginning of the sequence of sūtras to demonstrate that profound Prajñā is not separate from ordinary daily life.
The *Yuanzhi* states: "The Buddha’s movement and stillness are non-dual; how could he wait to return to the meditation grove to enter meditative concentration?
The Buddha-body is itself the vajra; it has no raw or cooked internal organs, so why would he need to eat? The Buddha is wondrous, perfect, and luminous; his nature is fundamentally without action."
The mind is fundamentally without attachment; how could it wait until one has gathered up robes and bowl before ceasing the pursuit of external objects?

When the Buddha walked, his feet were four finger-widths above the ground, supported by lotus flowers; how could they be stained by dust or filth? All of this was a manifestation in accordance with worldly conventions, displayed as a model for others.
△ This first section is the introduction explaining the causes and conditions for preaching the Dharma. Dayuan says: "In the 'Certification of Faith,' it is thus:
the Dharma, the Buddha, and the great bhikṣus—the Saṅgha. If these Three Jewels were not complete, the Dharma assembly would not be established;
therefore, these few words must invariably appear at the beginning of a sutra. Regarding the "Initiation," there are alms-seeking, dignified deportment, and the precepts.

The "spreading of the seat" refers to meditative concentration (*samādhi*). From the perspective of the World-Honored One himself, however, these are all wisdom (*prajñā*). Precept, concentration, and wisdom are inseparable.
Although this sutra specifically addresses wisdom, it begins by speaking of upholding the precepts and cultivating merit, and encourages the practice of the six *pāramitās*;
thus, it effectively encompasses both precept and concentration. Therefore, these are used to introduce the subject. As the commentary states: "Intending to expound the *prajñā*..."
The preceding introduction describes the Tathāgata’s conduct while begging for food, so that one may see that supreme wisdom does not reside within words and letters,
but exists solely within the midst of ordinary daily life. It requires people, in the very acts of dressing and eating,
moving and sitting, and during the transitions of time and seasons, to recognize their own original face amidst commonplace speech and common actions.
Mujaku’s *Kankyō* (Notes on the Sutra) states: "The Buddha preaches the Dharma based upon human nature; it is not that there is some other Dharma to be preached apart from human nature.
Human nature is the 'Sutra of No Words. The Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma is nothing more than a commentary.

To know that the Dharma is not separate from nature, and to cultivate and deliver oneself through this, rather than obtaining it from another—this is precisely what it means to interpret one's own nature."
Kāya! This sutra is spoken as it is swept away, and swept away as it is spoken. Why is this?
It is solely for the sake of guiding those sentient beings who have not yet realized their own fundamental nature; one cannot help but provisionally establish written words to explain them in detail.
It is like having no raft—how could one cross over? Once one has reached the other shore by means of the raft, one leaves it behind and does not use it.
Indeed, for those who awaken and attain liberation through self-realization without relying on language or written words, this is the highest way.

Next best is to rely upon the Dharma. For one who has already awakened, the Dharma is not required; yet for one who has not yet awakened, the Dharma is still necessary. How could the Dharma not be taught?
It is simply that one must know that what is taught ultimately returns to the state of no-teaching. Thus, there was Subhūti’s request at the lower level, and the Buddha’s desire [to respond].
When it reached the thirty-second division, the preaching of the Dharma was finally completed.
○ The Second Division: The Request of Subhūti.
"Subhūti" is the name of Śāriputra; he rose from his seat to inquire about the Buddha-dharma. ○ This is the inquiry for the essential [teachings].
Master Dayuan said: "The entire *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* is initiated by a single question arising from emptiness.
This true emptiness of *prajñā* cannot be vigorously expounded with the Buddha by one who merely understands emptiness intellectually;
therefore, this sūtra takes Subhūti as its primary interlocutor."
At that time, the Elder Subhūti, being among the great assembly, rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground,
joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
One who is long in virtue and long in years is called an *Elder* (*sthavira*). Subhūti is translated as "Understanding Emptiness" (*Khai-k'ung*).

He is also called Shan-hsien (Good Manifestation), Shan-chi (Good Auspiciousness), and K'ung-sheng (Birth from Emptiness). When the Elder was born, physiognomists divined his fate and found it to be exclusively auspicious and fortunate.

Furthermore, because he benefits others according to conditions and can manifest to benefit people, he is called Shan-hsien; because the nature of emptiness gives birth to the myriad dharmas, he is called K'ung-sheng. [The above] is the full [explanation].
The nature of emptiness is truly bodhi; therefore, he is named Subhūti. Baring the shoulder, kneeling on the ground, and joining the palms are all gestures of reverent worship.
These are all performed from the right side, for in their custom, the right is considered auspicious and the left inauspicious.

The commentary states: "The right represents the correct, while the left represents the deviant. This demonstrates the meaning of abandoning the deviant and returning to the correct. [He] bared his right shoulder entirely...
To "shoulder" means to bear the burden upon one's person. To place the right knee on the ground is to humble oneself and receive [the teaching] with compliance.

To join the palms is for the mind to accord with the Way and the Way to accord with the mind. Thus, by withdrawing and manifesting reverence, one altogether rectifies one’s deportment to extend one’s inquiry.
"Rare, World-Honored One!
'Rare' is a term of praise for the Buddha, meaning that which is difficult to encounter. A Tathāgata is difficult to meet throughout vast eons;
thus, the time is rare. Within the trichiliocosm there is but one Buddha; thus, the place is rare. The prajñā of the true mark belongs to the Buddha alone."
Reaching the ultimate depths, his merit and wisdom are transcendent and beyond compare; such virtue is rare.

Having realized true wisdom, he possesses the utmost great compassion and skillfully delivers sentient beings by expounding immeasurable Dharma gates; this matter is rare. He now protects and entrusts [this teaching] from below.
This is indeed a rare and marvelous matter. Explanation of the text: The Buddha has ten titles: first, Tathāgata; second, Arhat;
third, Samyaksaṃbuddha; fourth, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna; fifth, Sugato lokavidū; sixth, Anuttaraḥ puruṣadamyasārathiḥ;
seventh, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām; eighth, Buddha; ninth, Bhagavān; tenth, World-Honored One. In the sutra, Subhūti [says] together with...
He is called the World-Honored One and the Tathāgata; indeed, the Buddha’s own self-designation is also "Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata skillfully protects and sustains all bodhisattvas, and skillfully entrusts all bodhisattvas.

These two lines initiate and lead into the entire sutra. Hereafter, whatever the Buddha has spoken constitutes both "skillful protection and mindfulness" (*sugopanā-susamādāpanā*) and "skillful entrustment" (*suparīndanā*).
"Tathāgata" is a general designation for a Buddha: "Tathā" means that true nature is as it is, free from obstruction; "Āgata" means that true nature manifests according to conditions.
"All Bodhisattvas" refers to those who study under the Tathāgata. "Skillfully protecting and mindfully guarding" (*sugopanā*) means to protect...
"Mindfulness of the present" refers to the "good entrustment," which means entrusting [the teaching] to the future. Regarding the commentary on "entrustment":
"entrusting" (fu) means to place a junior bodhisattva under the care of a senior bodhisattva; "instructing" (zhu) means commanding a senior bodhisattva to transform a junior bodhisattva.
The Sanskrit term for bodhisattva is originally *bodhisattva*; for the sake of brevity, it is abbreviated and simply called "bodhisattva. *Bodhi*...
"Bodhi" means awakening. "Sattva" refers to sentient beings. Sentient beings are unable to awaken by themselves;
a Bodhisattva is able to awaken themselves and can also cause all sentient beings to awaken. "Great Perfection" says:

"Skillfully protecting and mindful of" means protecting and being mindful of those in the present whose faculties of faith are matured and who will never regress, granting them the power of true wisdom.

It causes them to realize *tathatā* (suchness) and bestows the power of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*), enabling them to transform sentient beings. Regarding "entrustment" (*parindanā*): this refers to entrusting future bodhisattvas whose faculties are not yet matured.
For those who have already attained the Mahāyāna, it ensures they do not abandon it; for those who have not yet attained the Mahāyāna, it causes them to apply themselves with diligence.
This is because if one were not to guard and mind them, evil Māras might come to disturb and trouble them; thus, [the Buddha] does not fail to entrust them.
Fearing that the supreme Dharma might at some time be severed, Subhūti, at the beginning of the assembly’s hearing of the Dharma, had no leisure for other speech;
he did nothing but wish for the Tathāgata to protect, mindfully attend to, and entrust [the teaching] to him. As it is understood:

although Gautama established the teachings extensively for the sake of all sentient beings, why is this protection, mindful attention, and entrustment focused specifically upon the bodhisattvas? It is because of sentient beings.

Those with inferior faculties have not yet realized the Supreme Vehicle. Bodhisattvas, however, possess both profound compassion and wisdom; they are able to believe and understand what is taught, and are further capable of expounding it for others.
For the sake of sentient beings, the World-Honored One has thus carefully guarded and entrusted [this teaching] to them.

"Guarding" means to prevent deviation and error. "Mindfulness" refers to the urgency with which one protects it. It involves the power of both manifest and hidden grace. "Entrusting" means to transmit it through the Right Path.

"Entrustment" (zhù) refers to the earnest transmission [of the teaching], encompassing both oral and mental instruction. "Skillfulness" (shàn) refers to the mutual application of provisional and ultimate truths, wherein the boundaries between the sacred and the mundane are equalized;
it is the method that exhaustively provides benefit and salvation for all sentient beings.
“World-Honored One, when good sons and good daughters resolve their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they say that this vast mind is what a bodhisattva first cultivates. ‘An’ means ‘no.
‘Uttara’ means ‘above,’ ‘unsurpassed,’ meaning there is nothing that can surpass it. ‘Samyak’ means ‘correct. ‘Saṃ’ means ‘equal. ‘Bodhi’ means ‘awakening. All these are Sanskrit [terms].”
It is speech. The mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is precisely the Buddha-mind; it is the true nature of humanity.
This true nature encompasses the great void (*mahā-ākāśa*) and there is nothing that can surpass it; therefore, it is called "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*). Thus, from the Buddhas above...
Reaching down to the most minute of moving creatures, this nature is perfectly equal in its true aspect; therefore, it is called "Perfect Equality" (*samyak-sam-bodhi*).

Its awakening is perfectly luminous and shines universally, being without partiality or deficiency; therefore, it is called "Perfect Awakening" (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). As the Layman Ruru said: "The student realizes the fruit."
First, he rectifies the cause; therefore, he begins by questioning the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*).

Previously, it was stated that "Bodhisattvas are entrusted with protection," yet here he instead questions "good sons and good daughters. This is because all sentient beings are capable of realizing the state of a Bodhisattva.
One who arouses the mind toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* does not seek Buddhahood outside of their own mind, but rather arouses it within themselves.
This is the bodhicitta that is fully present at this very moment. Unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is the fruit of all Buddhas;
how could it be already possessed by one who has not yet practiced? For the mind is the essence of awakening;
it encompasses all phenomena, being limpid, translucent, and all-pervasive. It is fundamentally most correct and most pervasive; only bodhi can truly be called the mind.
It does not reside within the mind; rather, there is bodhicitta within the *antarābhava*. It is simply because sentient beings are shrouded by ignorance that it remains hidden.

Yet, upon a single moment of awakening, its entire substance manifests all at once. For Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, their practice consists of nothing more than this; for those who attain the fruit of fruition, they obtain nothing more than this.
"How should one dwell? How should one subdue the mind? It is said:

"O sons and daughters of good family, when first setting out on the path of learning and giving rise to this unsurpassed bodhicitta, how should one abide so as to prevent it from regressing? When deluded thoughts arise, how should one subdue them?"
"May it not delude or confuse my true mind. (Extensive Commentary) These two lines constitute the essential framework of this sutra. They ask:

when one has not yet resolved to attain enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), one dwells within the realms of the six sense objects; once the resolve has been made, in what realm does one dwell? When the resolve has not yet been made...
The mind follows along with delusions. Once the resolve has been generated, those delusions should be pacified and subdued. Regarding this, the Bodhisattva Qufu (俱切) said:
"Wuzhuo (無著) says that Subhūti’s question involves six causes and conditions: first, the severing of doubt; second, the arising of faith and understanding."

Third, entering the profound meaning; fourth, non-retrogression; fifth, the arising of joy; and sixth, the long endurance of the True Dharma—all these serve to ensure that the lineage of the Buddhas is never severed.
To resolve doubts: those of the Lesser Vehicle abide in emptiness, knowing only how to deliver themselves but not knowing how to deliver others.

Having now awakened the Great Mind, one shall descend to transform sentient beings below and ascend to achieve the fruit of Buddhahood above. However, one must relinquish the former [Lesser Vehicle]...

"Emptiness. Having not yet attained true emptiness, one fears that by clinging to the Buddha-fruit as something to be sought, one will instead take the seeking of the Buddha-fruit as a place of dwelling.
Furthermore, seeing sentient beings filling one's eyes, one wonders how one can achieve Buddhahood without first delivering them; thus, in the haste to seek a dwelling, the mind becomes unsettled.
Therefore, he asks for the method of settling the mind (*anxin*), so that those who have resolved to attain enlightenment may know what to practice. Suchness.
The lay practitioner said: "The three phrases regarding the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) flow together in a single breath.
The meaning is: how should the aroused mind abide? How should the abiding mind be subdued? To say 'subdue' and 'not act' is merely a provisional teaching for restraining delusion.
For if the aroused mind has no place of abiding, it falls into one-sided emptiness; yet, an abiding mind cannot be absent either."

One must not become attached; therefore, one must employ subjugation and maintain it within meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Therein lies the subtle excellence of being neither identical nor separate, as expressed in the following passage:
"Do not conceive such thoughts. That Subhūti raised this question demonstrates that he has profoundly grasped the meaning of Prajñāpāramitā.
The Layman Faren visited [the Master]. The two characters for "mind" (*citta*) above and below correspond to one another. The *bodhicitta* is the original, primordial true mind;
it was originally the rightful master, yet now, having been displaced by external objects, it has become a transient guest.
If it does not abide securely, it will vanish and reappear in an instant. That [other] mind is the deluded mind of afflictions and inversions; it is fundamentally external.
The thief is mistakenly recognized as one's own son; he is my closest relative. If he is not subdued, he will become entangled like a knot that is difficult to untie.
He is the greatest obstacle to Bodhi; therefore, those who give rise to this mind must abide in subduing him, allowing no room for self-indulgence.
In reality, although afflictions and Bodhi differ in terms of truth and falsehood, the mind is fundamentally one and the same.
When deluded, awakening itself becomes affliction; when enlightened, affliction itself becomes awakening.
Therefore, the method of practice is not of two kinds. If one can subdue [the mind], one will dwell securely within it. Thus, the heading below is marked as "Subduing."
The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent, Subhūti! It is just as you have said:
the Tathāgata well protects and sustains all bodhisattvas, and well entrusts all bodhisattvas. Listen attentively now; I shall speak for your sake."
Subhūti’s inquiry perfectly accords with the Buddha’s mind; therefore, the Buddha praises him by repeatedly saying, "Excellent! and confirms his discourse on mindful protection and entrustment.
He then instructs him to listen with thorough investigation of the truth, saying that one must not listen to the true Dharma with a mind of arising and ceasing.
This means one should not listen to the true Dharma with a mind characterized by birth and death.
Good sons and good daughters who have resolved to attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi should abide in this manner and subdue their minds in this manner.
The arousal of the bodhicitta is the general gateway through which the thousand Buddhas enter the Way.

"Thus" (*evam*) refers precisely to this; it points directly to the bodhicitta. Changshui said: "The two characters 'thus' constitute the text that provides a comprehensive answer by pointing downward from above.
The correct interpretation states: these two phrases, "thus," serve to connect what precedes with what follows. They first take up the arousal [of the bodhicitta]...
The Bodhicitta comes forth; it descends to illuminate and deliver sentient beings, yet it must be maintained with inner containment and not revealed.

Only then can the meaning of the words be grasped. Dayuan said: "Once one has generated the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, one should abide in accordance with that generated awakened mind, and subdue [the afflictions] in accordance with that generated awakened mind. These two [points].
It is thus. To say "this very place is it" means that there is no need to seek it elsewhere. Abiding is the fundamental essence; descending is the practice.
The fundamental essence itself is the practice; the initial resolve itself is the ultimate realization. A fire that consumes a vast plain originates from its first spark;
a spring that pours into the ocean results from its first flow. There is nothing to rely upon or cling to apart from bodhi.
This is the practice of cultivation. Master Lianchi said: "These two phrases should be viewed as a single thread.

If one dwells in that which is appropriate to dwell upon, then that which is inappropriate to dwell upon will naturally be subdued. It is not a matter of dwelling in this way and then proceeding to subdue in that way.
As the commentary explains: "This sutra opens the Buddha’s knowledge and vision for the sake of the末代 (mòdài, final age). Its...
That which you have asked about is precisely the characteristic of the practice of bodhicitta. The Tathāgata has answered that non-abiding in any dharma is true abiding;
subduing all minds that grasp at signs is true subduing; and not abiding in any dharma is [true subduing].
One immediately subdues the mind that grasps at signs. Once the mind that grasps at signs has been subdued, one does not dwell in any phenomena.
One should know that this is indeed the intention within the World-Honored One’s mind; yet he did not explicitly state it in words, but answered with general, figurative expressions.
That he did not speak in detail was to treat the teaching with gravity, desiring that his listeners listen with focused attention.
“Certainly, World-Honored One. We wish and desire to hear it.
We wish to hear the details regarding how one dwells in subduing [the afflictions]. Subhūti, having grasped the general meaning, responded with “Certainly.
Furthermore, desiring to know the details, he requested again, saying, “We wish and desire to hear it,” as he sat thus.

The scholar said: "Hearing is the most subtle of characters; it is to speak without anything being spoken, and to hear without anything being heard—this alone constitutes the transmission within this realm.
The three characters 'willing,' 'delighting,' and 'desiring' are the magnetized needles that guide one toward hearing the Way.
'Willing' is the sincere heart, like a poor scholar’s urgency for fame and office. 'Delighting' is the inspired heart, like a connoisseur of sound listening to drums and music."
Desire is a pressing state of mind, like a person suffering from hunger or thirst seeing a plate of food.
Since these three states of mind exist, if you can listen with earnest attention, you will consequently proceed from weeping to ultimate joy.
△ Dayuan said: "The question regarding the arousal of the bodhicitta is the essential gate for entering the Mahāyāna.
The question regarding where the bodhicitta should abide is the means to accord with the originally inherent awakened essence (*bodhi-tattva*).

The question regarding how to subdue [the mind] is the means to manifest the inherently possessed function of wisdom. Because these questions are asked with such extreme sincerity and precision, they are like..."

He comes directly to point it out, saying: "Abide thus; subdue thus. This is identical to the abiding and subduing of Bodhi—what is called the union of initial awakening (*ādikṣānti-bodhi*) with original awakening (*mūla-bodhi*), which is termed "Buddha. Later, he says: "The Tathāgata has nothing to preach," and further says:
"In truth, there is no dharma by which one sets forth for Bodhi; in truth, there is no dharma by which one attains Bodhi. This is precisely [the meaning].
This clarifies the purport of these two characters. The *Zongjing* (Mirror of the Source) states: "The bodhicitta is the adamantine true eye.
The place where this mind arises is precisely the dwelling place of the Buddha. To abide therein without shifting is itself subjugation."
Therefore, subduing is contained within abiding and cultivation; and abiding and cultivation are contained within the arousal of the bodhicitta.
The Sūtra states that the two characters "thus" (*evam*) answer the question "how. Furthermore, these two characters "thus" should open the chapter to introduce the subsequent text.
These two characters "thus" already encompass what follows: non-abiding, as well as abiding by means of non-abiding.
Non-abiding is signlessness; signlessness is the absence of all signs. The absence of all signs is the true mark (dharmatā), which is the fundamental nature of sentient beings.
○ Section Three: The Orthodox Lineage of the Mahāyāna.
The Supreme Vehicle; the Ultimate Doctrine of Correctness. ○ This answers the question regarding subduing.

○ This chapter answers the question regarding subduing, yet abiding is contained therein. Although it answers both subduing and abiding, it is in fact a formal exposition on generating the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. [Maitreya’s Verses] Section.
It gives rise to four states of mind: namely, the vast mind, the foremost mind, the constant mind, and the non-erroneous mind; that is, the bodhicitta.
It is a vehicle, meaning it carries; it carries across all sentient beings, yet perceives neither the one who crosses nor those being crossed.
This is the orthodox lineage of the Great Vehicle.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should thus subdue their minds.
The meaning of these words extends directly through to the phrase "In reality, there is nothing to be attained," at which point the sense is complete. *Mahā* means "great."
This refers to the vastness and greatness of the mind. Such a person possesses the nature of Great Enlightenment and stands one head above even the high-ranking Bodhisattvas.
Those who have not yet resolved their minds are called "good people," while those who have already resolved their minds are called "Bodhisattvas.
"One should thus subdue the mind" is a reiterative statement; its details are explained in the following text. Indeed, this subduing does not pertain merely to one's own person.
If you examine this within your own mind, you will already have become a self-enlightened person. There is no distinction between the Bodhisattva and sentient beings;

there is no distinction between the aspiration for Bodhi and the deliverance of sentient beings. To subdue [the mind] is precisely to see it in the context of delivering sentient beings. As stated in the passage below:
"When all sentient beings have been delivered, yet one does not perceive that any sentient being has attained extinction. Only then...
Only when one is free from the four marks does one subdue the mind and become a bodhisattva.
"All classes of sentient beings" refers to the nine types mentioned below;
as the extensive commentary states, sentient beings within the three realms do not exceed the five destinies. There are...

There are twelve categories, which are subsumed within these four modes of birth (*yoni*). Within the four modes of birth, there are no phenomena that transcend the two dharmas of form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*);
therefore, they are divided into nine types. This is the general heading; what follows is the detailed analysis.

If born from an egg, one is shrouded by ignorance and arises due to conceptualization. The Sixth Patriarch said: "This is delusion regarding one's nature. Because of delusion, one creates all manner of afflictions.
If born from a womb, [the same applies].
Enveloped by afflictions, they exist because of emotional attachments. The Sixth Patriarch said, "It is habitual nature. Because of habituation, one constantly transmigrates.
The commentary states that this refers to the profound depth of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).

If one is born from moisture, one is drenched by the waters of craving; through this union, one is moved [to rebirth]. The Sixth Patriarch said: "To follow what is perverse is the nature [of such beings].
To follow what is perverse means the mind is not settled. The commentary states that when the mind follows false views, it sinks into delusion without awakening.

If one is born by transformation (*upapāduka*), afflictions suddenly arise; one responds by detaching from them. The Sixth Patriarch said: "The tendency toward views is the nature. To have a tendency toward views is to fall into the Avīci Hell;

this means that when the mind perceives objects and tends toward them, it undergoes shifting changes and gives rise to illusions, frequently resulting in spiritual downfall. These four types [of birth] are...
This is the distinction regarding rebirth within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

As for "if there is form," the Sixth Patriarch said: "To give rise to the mind to practice is to cling to a mind that perceives existence; it is to falsely perceive right and wrong. Internally, one does not accord with non-existence (*anupalabdhi*)."
Regarding the principle of marks:
if there were no form,
the Sixth Patriarch said, "To guard the truth within the mind while clinging to the mark of emptiness, and failing to cultivate merit and wisdom."

If there is conceptualization (*saṃjñā*), the Sixth Patriarch said: "The mind thinks and reflects, becoming attached to the marks of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*); the mouth speaks of the Buddha’s conduct, yet the mind does not conform to that conduct.
If there is no conceptualization:
The Sixth Patriarch said: "To practice seated meditation for the purpose of eliminating delusions is to be without active function, like wood or stone;
it is not to learn compassion, joy, equanimity, wisdom, and skillful means."
If it is neither with thought nor without thought—Sixth Patriarch Huineng said:
"Not clinging to the perceptions of these two dharmas, yet seeking the principle within the mind. A sutra in the teachings says: "Both existence and non-existence are cast aside;
speech and silence are both forgotten. To have a mind of grasping and rejecting, of love and hatred, is not to understand the Middle Way.
These five types all refer to the distinctions within mental conceptions. **The Correct Meaning:** Regarding the four modes of birth (*yoni*):

birth from an egg arises through conceptualization; birth from a womb arises through emotional attachment; birth from moisture arises through the response to union; and transformational birth arises through separation. These are the distinctions in taking birth within the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*).
"Possessing form" refers to the heavens of the Four Dhyānas, where there is a physical body but no emotional desire. "Formless" refers to the [Four Formless Heavens].
The Ākāśānantyāyatana (Sphere of Infinite Space) takes feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as its body; this is the distinction of its basis.
Within the Formless Realm (ārūpyadhātu), the two spheres of Infinite Space and Infinite Consciousness are "with perception" (*saṃjñin*), corresponding to the first and second heavens.

The Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) is "without perception" (*asaṃjñin*), corresponding to the third heaven. That which is "neither with perception nor without perception" (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) is at the summit of the three realms and constitutes the fourth.
"O Heaven! This is the differentiation of realms. The old commentaries all agree on this; only the Sixth Patriarch points to the mind in his explanation.
According to their names, they are called "sentient beings" (*sattva*) because they undergo birth within the phenomena of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

Once the true nature is deluded, one becomes subject to birth from a womb, an egg, moisture, or transformation, wandering through the cycles of existence without end. The Sixth Patriarch, however, analyzes and reveals this very point based upon the nature and its habitual tendencies.
The reason for such transformations in the nature of sensation is that its meaning requires one to awaken to it personally;
it does not mean that if a person's mind is like this, they are called egg-born, or if a person's mind is like that, they are named moisture-born or transformation-born.
The Commentary states: "The minds of the nine kinds of sentient beings are all not the true mind of Bodhi.

At most, they may exist for a time, but upon death, they follow their respective categories to take birth, falling among those born from wombs, eggs, moisture, or by transformation; or among spirits such as those of empty space, or ghosts such as celestial Māras.
Thus they revolve through the six realms of existence, making it difficult to enter Nirvana. Juefei said: "All sentient beings..."
All arise from karma. As it is said: "It is simply because of one mistaken thought that ten thousand forms manifest.
I shall cause all [the aforementioned nine types] to enter nirvana without remainder and attain liberation.

"I" (Aham) is a term used in reference to the assembly; it is a designation employed by Bodhisattvas who vow to save sentient beings as their own responsibility, not a self-reference used by the Buddha himself.
"Entering" (Praveśa) means to enter into that which is within. "Great Nirvāṇa" (Mahāparinirvāṇa) is the refuge and ultimate resort for all practitioners;
it refers to the fundamentally pure state of the mind-ground of true emptiness. The Commentary states: "Non-arising is..."

*Nir* means non-extinction; *vāṇa* means perfection. This is complete purity in which both subject and object have entirely vanished. It is the transcendence of saṃsāra and the departure from birth and death;
it is the ultimate attainment of the state of the other shore. To mistakenly identify this as death is a great error.
"Without remainder. The Sixth Patriarch provided the interpretation: "without remaining habitual tendencies or afflictions. Master Lianchi provided the interpretation:

"the meaning of having nothing left over. Jinguan provided the interpretation: "wisdom without remainder or surplus," which is the ultimate limit of realizing the Way. This is according to the explanation of the meaning.
The two vehicles also possess *nirvāṇa*. They are able to destroy the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), but cannot destroy the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

They are able to transcend birth-and-death through segmented divisions (*paricchinna-jarāmaraṇa*), yet have not transcended birth-and-death through transformation (*pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa*). Thus, there still remains a residue of body and cognition, which constitutes *nirvāṇa with remainder* (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*).

Only when both obstructions are entirely exhausted and one is forever separated from the two types of death, such that no residue of body or cognition remains, can it truly be called [nirvāṇa without remainder].
Nirvana without remainder: there is no delusion to be severed, and no truth to be realized. It is neither attached to existence nor attached to non-existence;
this is precisely the skillful means by which our Buddha transforms and delivers sentient beings. "Extinction" (mie) means to eliminate and extinguish all ignorance and afflictions.
"Deliverance" (du) means to transform and deliver, to cross over and escape from the bitter sea of birth and death.
In this way, although he brings immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings to extinction, in reality there are no sentient beings who have attained extinction.
Although the Mahāyāna Buddha-dharma consists in saving sentient beings, the Buddha is absolutely free from any attachment to the mark of saving sentient beings. This is because...
Sentient beings possess Buddha-nature by their very nature; they are inherently capable of saving themselves.
Even if one were to deliver all sentient beings, it would merely be a restoration of their original state, and I would have no merit therein. Master Shuji said:
"All sentient beings manifest from karma, yet the conditions of karma possess no real nature; they are empty in their very essence. Since the conditions of karma..."
Emptiness. How can there be sentient beings? Since there are no sentient beings, what is there to bring to parinirvāṇa?

By subduing the four marks, one immediately attains abiding in the nirvana without remainder for oneself, and is likewise able to cause sentient beings to abide securely in the nirvana without remainder.

△ This section provides the direct answer to the question of how one should abide: it is the simultaneous cultivation of the contemplation of principle (li-guan) and the contemplation of phenomena (shi-guan).

The preceding chapter spoke only from the perspective of principle (*li*) and never from the perspective of phenomena (*shi*).

Distinguishing the Vision According to Reality.
This section refutes the attachment to the delusive habit-energies of appearances and first awakens to the principle of True Suchness (Tathatā), seeing the true nature as it truly is.
"Come. This means not dwelling upon the marks of the body. Juefei said: "The form-body (*rūpakāya*) has marks; the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is without marks.

To have marks is to see the form; to be without marks is to see the principle. Therefore it is said, 'seeing according to the principle as it truly is,' which means seeing the Tathāgata of one's own original nature as it truly is.
Correctly explained: the physical forms and colors of ordinary people all belong to the realm of delusion."
This is not reality; what is seen is not true seeing. Only this principle of suchness (tathatā) is the original nature of humanity;
it is what is truly real. It is not seen with the eyes, but seen with the mind; one does not seek to see it through forms.
To seek the vision of principle is to possess true vision. This chapter clarifies that all phenomena possessing marks are illusory, thereby revealing the true Buddha who is markless.
It requires people to possess the correct view of marklessness. Dayuan remarked:
"The preceding passage spoke of 'not abiding in marks,' yet it had not yet explained the reason why one ought not to abide in marks."
One obtains immeasurable merit; this merely speaks of obtaining the fruit of signlessness (*animitta*), which pertains to the level of provisional transformation.
It has never been said that one obtains the source of signlessness. At this point, it is explained separately that whatever possesses signs is entirely illusory.
How can one dwell upon what is illusory? If one perceives that all signs are non-signs, only then does one know.
This state of signlessness is the Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata. This sutra belongs to the school that refutes signs (*lakṣaṇa-vināśaka*).
Signlessness is the true Buddha. Thus, from the very source, it refutes the fear that the Two Vehicles might perceive the Buddha through signs;
for they might harbor doubts regarding non-abiding in signs. Therefore, he raises the fruit of Buddhahood as a question, so that they may know that the fruit itself is signless, naturally so.
One who has no doubt regarding causes abides nowhere.
Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of physical marks?
"Physical marks" refers to the thirty-two marks of the Buddha’s *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body). "Seeing the Tathāgata" refers to speaking of the *dharmakāya* (dharma body).
The correct explanation says: The Buddha feared that although Subhūti had heard the purport of signlessness (*animitta*), his realization was not yet entirely thorough.
Therefore, he raised the subject of physical marks (*lakṣaṇa*) to interrogate him. Dàyuán said:

The previous teaching on giving without abiding in signs and subduing the mind was the cause for attaining Buddhahood; [Subhūti] likely feared that the fruit of Buddhahood might be conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Regarding the physical marks (*lakṣaṇa*), he raised this as a question. The *Ji jie* (Collected Explanations) states: "This 'Tathāgata' refers to the Dharma-body;
it is what is called the Buddha of True Nature. Because the Buddha wishes for people to see the Buddha of their own nature, he calls out and questions them.
This is the Buddha’s first question. Ruru Jushi says: "In this question, the Buddha specifically brings forth the seeing of Suchness (*tathatā*)."
These three characters, "Come" (Lai), are the guide for the ten thousand practices of the six perfections. Those who enter the Dharma-gate must first realize their meaning.

Among all phenomena, the reason the physical body (*rūpakāya*) alone is singled out is that sentient beings, since beginningless time, have been deluded by mistakenly identifying with the physical body;
they must recognize this illusory body in order to realize the *dharmakāya*. This is a detailed explanation of the manifestation of the body in teaching.
"One might think that by seeing the marks of the body, one can perceive the Tathāgata; yet all such marks are non-existent and cannot be a basis for abiding.
"No, World-Honored One. One cannot see the Tathāgata (this refers to the Dharma-body) by means of the marks of the body. Why is this?
Because the 'marks of the body' spoken of by the Tathāgata (this is the Buddha's title) are not, in fact, marks of the body."

Subhūti understood the Buddha’s intention and replied immediately, “No. This is because that which the Tathāgata has described as the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body) is subject to arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing;
the Buddha-body is different from this. It is a manifested form (*māyārūpa*) and not a true physical characteristic.
The body should not be grasped according to its corresponding phenomena, just as a mirror cannot be grasped by its reflection.

When it comes to light, how can one respond to it with the physical body? Since the characteristics of the body are originally but a provisional combination of the four great elements, it cannot be seen through its physical characteristics.
This is what Subhūti explains by means of his own questions and answers.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "Whatever has marks is entirely empty and false.
This explains the Buddha’s confirmation of those words and their further elaboration; he stated that it is not only the Buddha-body that is thus.
All conditioned phenomena arise from deluded thoughts. Since the deluded thoughts that give rise to them are fundamentally empty, how could the various phenomena produced by them be real?
These two sentences constitute the essential core of the entire sutra. Yet, this does not mean that apart from these phenomena there exists a separate, signless Dharmakāya;
therefore, it is further said: "To see that phenomena are not phenomena is to see the Tathāgata."

As he understood it, Subhūti already knew that the characteristics of the body are illusory. The Buddha, responding to his capacity, expanded upon this by saying: "All that has marks is entirely illusory.
Once the illusory body is extinguished, all illusions are likewise extinguished. Furthermore, he offered another turning word, saying:
"If you see that all marks are no-marks, then you see the Tathāgata. To know illusion is to be detached from it.
To depart from illusion is awakening. To see that which is not a mark is not to fall into existence. To see that marks are non-marks is not to stagnate in non-existence.

When both existence and non-existence are simultaneously dispelled, one contemplates the Middle Truth. One who sees the Tathāgata sees the Tathāgata of the original nature of sentient beings; this is precisely the bodhicitta.
"If one sees that all marks are non-marks, then one sees the Tathāgata. The Householder Dharmakṣānti said:

"The Buddha feared that Subhūti, having become detached from these delusions of 'marks,' would seek elsewhere for a 'true' state of 'non-marks,' thereby falling into the views of the Two Vehicles. Therefore, the Buddha led him forward, teaching that within the very marks there is no mark."
Vasubandhu informed him: "The false is itself the true; existence is itself emptiness. Originally, there are no two distinct essences.
If one can perceive that all phenomena (*lakṣaṇa*) are, in their very substance, entirely empty of characteristics, then truth and falsehood are non-dual, and existence and emptiness are identical.

This is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), the vision of the Mahāyāna. As for the statement that 'all phenomena are non-phenomena,' it refers to the various phenomena of existence and non-existence."
Because their nature is fundamentally empty. Those who do not perceive emptiness as a fixed entity are neither attached to marks nor do they dwell in the absence of marks.
To see form and dwell in form is the common view of ordinary beings; to see emptiness and dwell in emptiness is the nihilistic view of the two vehicles.
Ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles follow along with various marks and fall into the extremes of existence and non-existence, seeing only one side.
If one sees that form is emptiness and emptiness is form, then there is neither existence nor non-existence, neither identity nor separation;
this is the right view of a bodhisattva. Because one attains the vision of the true mark of ultimate emptiness, it is said that one immediately sees the Tathāgata.
Huang Shangcai said: "To see that all marks are non-marks is to shatter marks; this is to manifest the nature.
Shattering marks is precisely the means by which the nature is manifested. As for the word 'see,' one must perceive it subtly; it is the true seeing that is without seeing."
Wang Lichang said: "This is the four-line verse of the School that Destroys Characteristics (Poxiangzong).
What the Sutra refers to as the 'four-line verse' must refer to this very one. The subsequent passage in the Sutra, 'If one sees me by means of form,' consists of these two lines:
'Seeing characteristics as not characteristics. The subsequent passage, 'Like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, and a shadow,' consists of these two lines: 'Whatever characteristics exist...'"
△ This section states that the Tathāgata’s manifested body is without marks. The fruit of a Bodhisattva is precisely the Tathāgata;
the *dharmatā* of the Tathāgata is like empty space. When considering his merits, they do not exceed manifesting a body and preaching the Dharma.
Apart from these two matters, there is no other such thing as a Tathāgata. Fearing that Subhūti might take marks to be the Buddha, the Buddha therefore first interrogates him.
Changshui says: "The thirty-two marks are reflections manifested upon the Great Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*).
Since they pertain to the category of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), they must be subject to the transformations of the four characteristics: arising, abiding, change, and cessation.
As for the Dharmakāya Tathāgata, in the past he did not come from non-existence to existence, and in the future he will not pass from existence to non-existence; he is without change."
"Different" cannot be refuted; it refers to the reason why [the unconditioned] differs from the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).

The Commentary on the Thesis states: "Having characteristics" refers to the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body); "without characteristics" refers to the *dharmakāya* (dharma body). The *dharmakāya* is the essence (*tattva*), while the *nirmāṇakāya* is its function (*vṛtti*).
One understands that function arises from essence; thus, it should be identical to the Dharma. For this reason, it is without marks. Therefore, the Treatise says:
"The marks spoken of by the Tathāgata are themselves no-marks. If one can thoroughly comprehend this meaning, then all marks of the mundane world—
There is nothing that is not the unconditioned Buddha-body of True Suchness (*tathatā*). A direct explanation states:
The Dharma-body does not abide in any marks; it is like empty space. Its essence is not possessed of marks, yet it does not reject them.
If, amidst all marks, one clearly perceives the fundamental nature as the mark of non-mark, this—without departing from the present thought—is precisely seeing the Tathāgata. This is certain.
Yiyun said: "The Dharma-body is also not without marks; it is precisely upon the marks of all phenomena that one perceives their non-markedness, and this is seeing the Tathāgata.
It is not that, apart from all phenomena, there exists some other distinct form or characteristic. Juefei said:
Regarding the phrase "all marks are non-marks," it does not mean that there is a separate "non-mark" existing apart from the marks themselves.
Therefore, the twenty-seven doubts are exhausted by the single word "mark. Severing these twenty-seven doubts is exhausted by the single word "shatter.
This not only shatters the mark of birth-and-death, but also shatters the mark of nirvana; it not only shatters the mark of affliction, but also...
It shatters the marks of bodhi, the mark of cause, the mark of fruit, the mark of existence, the mark of non-existence, and all marks of unity and difference;
there is nothing it does not shatter until even that which can be shattered is shattered, and the vision of original purity is revealed.

How could one remain in a state of attachment to marks? Below this are eight sections of inquiry and testing, three sections of summary exhortation, and five sections of comparative evaluation. This...
This is the first investigation.
○ Chapter Six: The Rarity of Right Faith.
In studying the Way, faith is the foundation. The Mahāyāna Dharma—non-abiding and signless—is the true orthodox teaching. Upon hearing this...
To accept this without doubt or fear constitutes right faith. Such persons are not easily found; therefore, it is called rare.
This reiterates that one should not dwell upon any marks (*lakṣaṇa*) in order to give rise to right faith. Juefei said:
"If one can believe that all marks are non-marks, then not only will there be no four marks, but there will be neither the mark of dharmas nor the mark of non-dharmas."
Thus, the Dharma-eye becomes clear and lucid; one is forever free from the delusions of worldly toil, universally manifesting all that is pure, and is non-dual with the Buddha.

Therefore it is said: "Right faith is rare. This section, together with the seven sections below, clarifies that what is not the Dharma is entirely a mere appearance, thereby revealing the true Dharma of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). It requires that people be fully detached [from appearances].
This is the purification of marks. In the Dharma-ending age, students of the Way face two kinds of obstacles: first, they perceive the Buddha through attachment to marks;

second, they practice by clinging to dharmas. Therefore, the five parts of the body are used to break down the mark of the person, and the six or seven parts are used to break down the mark of dharmas.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, are there any sentient beings who, upon hearing such spoken words and phrases—

referring specifically to the expressions of the third, fourth, and fifth sections concerning the practice of giving without dwelling and the vision of the Buddha without marks— [will attain understanding]?"
Do you give rise to true faith?
To speak of faith with one's mouth—faith is the source of the Way and the mother of all merit; it nurtures all roots of goodness.
Without faith, one cannot enter the Buddha-dharma. Yet, a person must have true knowledge and certain insight before they can truly believe.
How much more so when faith is said to be "real"—must one not necessarily fulfill the measure of that faith?
This is why Subhūti has these words of objection. Zeng Fengyi says: "This doubt arises from the practice of giving without dwelling, which follows from seeing the Buddha as having no marks.
Giving without dwelling is profound in its cause; seeing the Buddha as having no marks is profound in its fruit. Both cause and fruit..."

Profound! Where both person and phenomena are simultaneously extinguished, how could those of dull faculties in the final age believe and accept it? If they do not believe and accept it, would this not be a vain discourse?
The Buddha told Subhūti: "Do not speak thus. After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, during the final five hundred years, there will be those who uphold [this Dharma]..."
Those who cultivate merit through precepts, if they can give rise to faith in these words and passages, taking them as true, yet say such things,
they not only slight sentient beings and obstruct the faculty of faith in others, but furthermore become attached to these words and passages themselves.

Because one perceives the Dharma as a person, it is said: "Do not do so. Regarding the "latter five hundred years," this refers to the period after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, which is divided into five ages.
The first five hundred years is called the Age of Liberation; the next is called the Age of Meditative Concentration (*dhyāna*); both of these belong to the True Dharma (*saddharma*).

The third is called the Age of Much Learning; the fourth is called the Age of Stūpas and Temples; both of these belong to the Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpakadharma*). The fifth is called the Age of Strife; this constitutes the Final Dharma (*paścimadharma*), which is indeed heterodox.
Seeing this age of increase, those who take this as reality do not speak in vain, for there is a true principle here.
One must believe that these chapters and verses constitute the truth of ultimate reality. Do not say that there are no people of sincere faith today;

even though the world has become distant and the years have passed into oblivion, people still follow with such conviction. Huang Shangcai said: "Maintain the precepts and cultivate merit. [Through] precept and concentration..."
Faith is wisdom. As for "that which can give rise [to it]": once both precepts and meditative concentration are complete, wisdom arises spontaneously;
thus one illuminates the emptiness of all phenomena and perceives the reality of *prajñā*. Otherwise, this cannot be achieved. Regarding the cultivation of merit:

clothing and food constitute the merit of the body, while wisdom constitutes the merit of the nature. The merit of the body is summoned by means of giving and making offerings; the merit of the nature...

Regarding the karmic results of receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting [the scriptures], the *Śāstra* states: "Precept transcends the three miserable realms; concentration transcends the six heavens of the desire realm;
and wisdom transcends the triple world.
One should know that such a person has not planted roots of goodness under only one, two, three, four, or five Buddhas; they have already [planted them] under many.
They have planted various roots of goodness under immeasurable thousands of myriads of Buddhas.
As for the source of their genuine faith, one should know that such a person must not be looked down upon lightly;
this person has surely severed evil karma and planted roots of goodness at the same source and same root as all Buddhas.
Sheng’s Commentary: This person must have possessed profound roots of goodness and have planted much merit over many lifetimes, serving various Buddhas.
"Understanding the meaning" means that they have seen many Buddhas, heard the Dharma many times, and practiced extensively. "So" (所) refers to the place where these things occurred.

"Those who hear these chapters and phrases and give rise to pure faith for even a single thought-moment"—a single thought, a single mind, a single intention, unmixed with any other thoughts—this is called "pure faith. Lü Chang said:
The former is called "true faith," which means believing because one takes the Buddha’s words as true.

The latter is called "pure faith," which means believing that all marks are illusory and thus not giving rise to deluded thoughts; it is believing that the Tathāgata resides within one's own nature, yet not raising the mind to establish views.

Generally speaking, sentient beings are impure; hindered by both factual obstacles (*vighna*) and conceptual obstacles (*āvaraṇa*), their mental attention is not unified, and thus they are unable to believe.
This is what is called "single-minded pure faith" (*ekakṣaṇa-śraddhā*); it is the correct mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*) that is neither shifting nor distracted.
Subhūti, the Tathāgata fully knows and fully sees all these sentient beings who shall obtain such immeasurable merit.

This person is able to give rise to faith; their mind can then become conjoined with the marks of the Tathāgata. Through the Buddha’s wisdom and the Buddha’s eye, there is nothing of their mental states that is not known, and nothing of their actions that is not seen.
Although these sentient beings, in their present minds, have for a time attained the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), [the Tathāgata perceives them].
The future fruit will necessarily be perfectly accomplished and untainted; one shall obtain immeasurable, pure merit and virtue. As the commentary explains: Subhūti has already given rise to faith.
This is merely for the purpose of resolving the doubts of sentient beings. The word "thus" (*evam*) at the beginning of the chapter refers to seeing the Tathāgata.
Seeing the Tathāgata is indeed the sudden teaching (*tongjiao*); nevertheless, spiritual practice must necessarily rely upon cultivation and maintenance. Therefore...

Furthermore, it points out that upholding the precepts and cultivating merit—what is called "a single thought"—means traversing the myriad practices as if in a single thought; this speaks to the non-duality of faith.
"Pure faith" means the dual emptiness of both the grasping at a self (*ātman-grāha*) and the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*). This refers to what was previously called "seeing the Tathāgata."
This is what is meant by saying that the Tathāgata fully knows and fully sees all these sentient beings.
When sentient beings see the Buddha, the Buddha is within the hearts of those sentient beings; when the Buddha sees sentient beings, the sentient beings are within the heart of the Buddha.
In essence, this is simply the Bodhicitta reflecting equally upon one another.
Why is this? (To speak correctly: these sentient beings no longer possess the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, or the mark of a life-span;

[The Master] provides a detailed commentary. Furthermore, he asks: "What is the reason for obtaining merit? It is because within pure faith, emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is spontaneously perfected.

To realize *anātman* (non-self) is to know that both Buddhas and sentient beings each lack a self; thus, the four marks [of conditioned existence] do not arise. This is the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).

Since the four marks do not arise, all phenomena (*dharma*) have no basis upon which to be established. Therefore, one does not abide in the characteristics of phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*) and acts as follows...
There is existence. Not abiding in the characteristics of non-dharmas constitutes non-existence; this is the emptiness of dharmas (*dharma-śūnyatā*).

When both types of grasping are empty, one correctly attains the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, thereby accomplishing the foundation of pure faith. Dayuan said: "When the four marks are absent, there is the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*)."

There is no phenomenon; when phenomena are absent, they are empty of phenomena. There is no non-phenomenon; thus, emptiness itself is also empty. Once these three kinds of emptiness are realized, the mark of reality arises.
Because one possesses a pure mind free from marks, one receives pure merit free from marks. The Layman Ruru said:

He mentions "all sentient beings" three times, speaking with earnest and urgent repetition, truly wishing to awaken those who are dreaming.

those who grasp at marks falsely establish views and knowledge, and falsely give rise to birth and cessation. This is to grasp at the marks of phenomena.

it serves as the completing cause (*pariniṣpādaka-hetu*) for the *dharmakāya*, and it serves as the generative cause (*janaka-hetu*) for the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya*. Fearing that people might become attached to the characteristics of the sutra, the Buddha [thereupon...]
He swept it away with his words. Chengshi (盛釋) explained: "The Buddha-dharma is the principle of ultimate truth;
it is the Tathāgata’s perfect, awakened, wondrous mind. Hanshan said: "Prajñā is that which gives birth to the Buddha-dharma;
it is not itself the Buddha-dharma. Shengxian said: "Prajñā is fundamentally not the Buddha-dharma; this refers to the *prajñā* of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa-prajñā*)."
He said: "If one speaks of the *prajñā* of contemplation and the *prajñā* of words, these may indeed be called the Buddha-dharma. Qin Dayin remarked:
"The four fruits [of the śrāvaka path] in the following text should be explained directly and continuously as distinct stages. Why then is the mention of 'merit' inserted here?

It is because the central purport of this sutra is to negate both existence and non-existence; having just spoken of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), I feared people might fall into [the extreme of nihilism]."
"Boundless. Amidst this urgency, he suddenly makes a turn and speaks of "merit and the Buddha-dharma" to clarify that there is indeed a Buddha and a Dharma.
Yet, fearing that people might cling fixedly to the Buddha and the Dharma, thereby forming conceptual signs (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), he says "it is not so" to sweep them away.

Layer upon layer, it unfolds; it is the meaning of a single perfect sphere. ○ Chengshi explains: The preceding several sections on "non-abiding" and "subduing the mind" constitute the sublime practice of the *prajñā* of the true mark (*dharmatā*).
This is precisely seeing the Tathāgata, which is the true essence of the *prajñā* of the true mark.

That no dharma can be apprehended is the true fruit of the prajñā of the ultimate reality (bhūtalakṣaṇa-prajñā). That no dharma can be expounded is the wondrous teaching of the prajñā of the ultimate reality.
Hereafter, these expanded minor practices shall all be integrated into the Mahāyāna, so that the three vehicles may share a single liberation.
Chapter Nine: On the Single Characteristic and the Absence of Characteristics.
The four fruits appear to possess a single characteristic, yet in reality they do not exist.
This statement that all four fruits consist of unconditioned dharmas means that if one perceives there is a dharma to be attained or a path to be accomplished, this is precisely the conditioned.

It cannot be avoided that one still clings to signs (*nimitta*). Although the four fruits (*phala*) differ in their degrees of depth, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is one and the same; therefore it is said:

"one mark is no-mark. This ninth section and the tenth section below trace the points of realization and cultivation of all sages and worthies, showing that none of these can be grasped or described, for the realization of the Buddha-dharma is itself not the Buddha.

The meaning of the Dharma must be fully understood through the subtle and profound skillful hammering of the Tathāgata. Regarding the point where Subhūti attained deep and subtle realization, [the Buddha asked]:
"Subhūti, what do you think? Can a Srotāpanna (a person who has entered the stream; *srotāpanna* is a Sanskrit term translated into Chinese as 'entry into the stream') give rise to this thought?"

The phrase "the thought of attaining the fruit under [the Buddha's] finger" and the word "able" (néng) are not explained in any of the extant editions. It is suspected that these refer to the statement made at the time of realizing the fruit:
"Have I attained the fruit of srotāpanna?"

In the Buddha-dharma there is cause and effect. If one can cultivate the cause, one will immediately obtain the fruit. It is like planting peach seeds and obtaining peaches, or planting apricot seeds and obtaining apricots.
I am referring here to those who have attained the four fruits; I wonder whether they consider themselves to have obtained the fruit or not. (○) Commentary:
This follows from the previous statements that [the Dharma] cannot be grasped and cannot be spoken, serving as the third round of inquiry and examination. The preceding passage stated:

Unconditioned dharmas cannot be grasped. Fearing that the śrāvakas might each grasp at their own respective fruits, Subhūti—being one who has correctly attained the four fruits—asked on behalf of those who have attained the fruit: "Do I think, 'I have already attained the fruit'?
The Venerable One analyzed and discussed each point, stating the reality of what is attained, namely, that it is because there is no such thought. At the end, he further [addressed] himself...
"...is without thought and without practice. Please bear witness to this for me. Subhūti said, "No, World-Honored One.
