A Srotāpanna is called "one who has entered the stream," yet there is nothing into which they enter. (They have no mind of grasping or attachment. They do not enter form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or dharmas. This is...

He is called a *srotāpanna*, one who has "entered the stream. This means that having first entered its gate, he is able to perceive the stage of the Path and thus gains entry into the ranks of the noble ones (*ārya*).
To be "without entering" means not to cling to the characteristics of entering the stream. However, he has not yet been able to suddenly awaken to true emptiness; he merely...
Being able to leave behind coarse and heavy afflictions and not entering the realms of the six sense objects is called *srotāpanna*.
For this reason, this is the first fruit of the *śrāvaka*. One who awakens through the sound of the teaching is called a *śrāvaka* (voice-hearer).

Because they can go against the worldly stream, they enter the stream of the sages. This speaks of the first fruit being realized through the signless (*animitta*); having attained this fruit, one has already severed the views of the [four] truths.
Delusion. They have departed from birth in the four realms of existence, yet they are not yet able to abandon sensory objects.
○ Subhūti, what do you think? Can a Sakṛdāgāmin (in Chinese, "One Who Comes Once") form the thought:
"I have attained the fruit of a Sakṛdāgāmin"? ○ Subhūti replied: "No, World-Honored One. Why is this? The name 'Sakṛdāgāmin'..."
"One who comes and goes once," yet in reality there is no coming or going; this is called a *sakṛdāgāmin* (Once-returner).
"One who comes and goes once" means that after one visit to the heavens and one birth in the human realm, they immediately attain *nirvāṇa*.

The Sixth Patriarch said: "If the preceding thought gives rise to delusion, the succeeding thought immediately stops it; if the preceding thought has attachment, the succeeding thought immediately leaves it. This is what is meant by "seeing with the eyes."
Regarding these various objects, this mind undergoes only one arising and one ceasing; there is no second arising and ceasing. Therefore, it is said that it "comes and goes once.
However, having already realized true emptiness, it is ultimately able to transcend birth and death and does not undergo further cyclic existence.
In reality, there is no characteristic of coming and going. For this reason, he is named a Srotāpanna; this is the second fruit of the Śrāvaka.
This ranks one level higher than the stream-enterer (srotāpanna). This refers to the second fruit (sakṛdāgāmin) as realized through the signless (animitta).

A person who has attained this fruit has exhausted the first six grades of the nine grades of afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), yet the final three grades remain unsevered;

therefore, although they may ascend to the upper realms, they still return to the desire realm to take birth. Only when they are able to sever and exhaust the remaining afflictions will they no longer come and go.
“Subhūti, what do you think? Does an *anāgāmin*—the Chinese term for which means ‘one who does not return,’ also called ‘one who has emerged from desire’—ever have this thought:
‘I have attained the fruit of *anāgāmin*’? Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One. Why is that? An *anāgāmin* is so named because they do not return;
yet in reality there is no such thing as ‘not returning. It is for this reason that they are called an *anāgāmin*.”
Regarding those who do not return: they offer their gratitude in the human realm and are reborn directly in the heavens of the fourth dhyāna, never again returning to take birth in the desire realm.
In truth, there is no such thing as "not returning. Their fundamental nature is pure and luminous; it is true emptiness and devoid of self.

Seeing nothing that can be desired, and because the desire realm fundamentally does not exist, there is in fact no such thing as "not returning. This is called an Anāgāmin (Non-returner). For this reason—
Therefore, this third fruit of the śrāvaka still involves coming and going; it is one grade higher [than the second].

This clarifies that the three fruits are realized through the signless (animitta). Because the nine grades of afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm have been completely severed, one proceeds directly to the celestial palaces and does not return to the desire realm.

“Subhūti, what do you think? An Arhat—whose name in the language of China means ‘the Unborn’—is one for whom all outflows (*āsrava*) have been exhausted, who is no longer subject to afflictions, and who will never again undergo birth within the three realms.
They are also called ‘One Beyond Training’ (*aśaikṣa*), because they have reached the ultimate truth and there is no further Dharma to be learned. [End of] Collected Explanation: *A*...
An Arhat is one who is free from afflictions and does not undergo rebirth; they possess three meanings for which they should be venerated:

namely, that their afflictions of view and thought within the three realms are exhausted, that they do not receive a body in future lives, and that they should receive vast offerings from humans and devas.
One is able to think: "Have I attained the path of Arhatship?
The Arhat attains the principle of signlessness (*animitta*); both person and phenomena are empty.
Having already realized *nirvāṇa*, the path of the Śrāvaka reaches its fulfillment and ultimate limit. Therefore, it is not called a "fruit" but is termed a "path. The correct explanation states:
The first three sections speak of the fruit; like a flower bearing fruit, they carry the sense of accomplishment through diligent effort.
The path of the Arhat signifies that, having reached this point, one has attained thorough awakening, carrying the sense of realizing the principle through direct realization.
Subhūti said, “No, World-Honored One. Why is this? Because, in truth, there is no dharma that is called ‘Arhat.
World-Honored One, if an Arhat were to have the thought, ‘I have attained the path of an Arhat,’ he would thereby be attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span.”
Li Wenhui said: "To truly have no dharma means that there are no afflictions to be severed, no greed or anger to be abandoned, and that the mind is free from both adversity and favor.
When both object and subject are forgotten, there is not even a hair’s breadth of a dharma to be grasped;
this is what is called an Arhat. If one forms the thought, 'I have attained the path of an Arhat,' one is immediately attached to the four marks."
There is a vast distance between this and the stage of an Arhat. Why, then, is one called an Arhat? The Sūtra states: "In reality, there is no dharma;
the dust-like mind is completely purified, and there is no dharma to be learned. Only when one has reached the point where there is no dharma to learn does one attain the path of an Arhat.
If one forms the thought, "I have attained this path," this is no different from being attached to the four marks.

One is not even able to find leisure to subdue them; how could one possibly claim there is no Dharma to be learned? This clarifies that the four fruits of arhatship are realized through non-characteristic (animitta).
In these fruits, the afflictions of view and thought within the three realms are entirely exhausted. Those who have attained the four fruits all lack any mind of "attaining a fruit.
Thus, it is evident that the sages and worthies all rely on the unconditioned dharma (asaṃskṛta-dharma) and do not dwell at all in signs.
However, those of the four fruits of sainthood have merely realized their own single bodies and do not deliver sentient beings; in the Buddha’s gate, these are called the Hīnayāna.
World-Honored One, the Buddha has said that I have attained the Samādhi of Non-contention and am foremost among men;
I am the foremost Arhat free from desire.
"Contention" (*raṇa*) means strife. When the thought of worldly dust (*rajas*) desires to proceed and the thought of the Path desires to dispel it, they are like water and fire that cannot coexist;
these two thoughts contend with one another. When there is no contention, both principle and desire are forgotten, and not a single thought arises—this is *samādhi*.
The Commentary states: "No contention" means being free from the two obstacles of knowledge and affliction (*jñeyāvaraṇa* and *kleśāvaraṇa*). Being free from affliction, one does not cling.

There is a characteristic. When one is detached from [discursive] cognition, one does not cling to the signless (*animitta*). In a single thought-moment, nothing arises; all phenomena are without contention. Furthermore, the mind is without arising or ceasing, nor coming or going;
there is only the constant illumination of original enlightenment (*mūla-avabodha*). Therefore, it is called the Samādhi of Non-contention (*araṇā-samādhi*). The *Guǎnglù* states:

"Samādhi" is here translated as "right concentration" (*samyak-samādhi*), which refers to the mind being without arising or ceasing. It is also called "right reception" (*samyak-saṃprajanya*), referring to the mind...
It is the non-acceptance of any dharma. It is also called right view (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*), and it is also called right awakening (*samyag-bodhi*).

This refers to being far removed from the ninety-five kinds of false views. According to these four meanings, concentration (*samādhi*) should be taken as primary; for view is the vision that arises from concentration.

Awakening is also the awakening of meditative concentration; sensation is also the sensation of meditative concentration. Shengxian said: "This is precisely the inherently quiescent mind of awakening.
The scriptural passage stating that 'one does not grasp at marks' and is 'as-it-is and immovable' is a commentary on the correct samādhi of meditative concentration.
Regarding "among people," it refers to those among the disciples who have abandoned desire—that is, those who have completely severed the shadows of the afflictions of views and thought.
He does not give rise to a single thought of realization; this is precisely the true principle of neither attainment nor teaching.
World-Honored One, I do not harbor such a thought as: "I am a desire-free Arhat."
I, however, do not entertain such a thought as "I am an Arhat free from desire.
World-Honored One, if I were to think, "I have attained the path of Arhatship," then the World-Honored One would not say of me,
Subhūti, that I am one who delights in the practice of araṇya.
*Āraṇya* means "tranquility" in the language of China; it is also called "the state of having nothing. Yan Bing said:
"A practitioner of *āraṇya* refers to one who practices the path of non-self; this is the practice of purity. Outwardly, they do not perceive any dharma that is practiced."
Within, one does not perceive a mind that performs the practice; this is practicing while not regarding it as practice. As for "practitioner," consider it as one who cultivates the path.

[He thought: "If I were to maintain myself by means of the perception of detachment from desire, then the Buddha would not have designated me among his disciples as one who delights in the practice of araṇā."
Because Subhūti has in truth nothing upon which to act (and thus does not cling to the marks of action), he is named Subhūti,
the one who delights in the practice of araṇā.
"Truly there is no practice" means that the fundamental nature is empty and quiescent; although one responds to conditions and accords with stimuli, in reality there is no practice.
Because there is no mind seeking the path of Arhatship, one practices without regarding it as practice—this is called true practice.
Therefore, it is named the "practice of delighting in araṇya. This clarifies that the Pratyekabuddha realizes through the signless.

The *Jijie* (Collected Explanations) states: This section follows upon the fourth fruit, wherein Subhūti personally describes his own realization to testify to the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
At the point of the realization of the fourth fruit, there is no dharma that can be grasped; that which can be awakened to as the Buddha-dharma is precisely not the Buddha-dharma.
△ The preceding passage stated that the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) cannot be grasped and cannot be described;

thus, cultivation should take non-thought as its essence and non-attachment as its function. Fearing that the various bodhisattvas might seek the fruit of Buddhahood with such haste that the mind of "having something to attain" becomes difficult to abandon, the Buddha raises the four fruits to pose questions and resolve doubts, thereby demonstrating non-abiding.
This is the True Teaching (Shinjō). The Buddha said that the Dharma is not something to be grasped and that the Buddha is not something to be sought.

Fearing that those who hear this might find themselves without a basis for progress or retreat, [the Buddha] uses the four fruits of the śramaṇa to verify it in reverse. All [four fruits] arise from the distinctions within the unconditioned state of the worthy and noble ones.
When Subhūti speaks in detail of the [first] three fruits, he further provides testimony for himself; thus, there is no attachment whatsoever, and these are the four fruits.
All have no place of abiding; this sufficiently demonstrates that the Bodhi of the Tathāgata must, by its very nature, have no principle of abiding.
○ Xu Shiying said: The Buddha spoke of the four fruits of the path, each with its own hierarchy.

The first is described as "not entering into form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or dharmas," which shows that one should avoid the realms of desire, like a fruit newly born. The second is described as "once-returning."
The first is "treading upon the realm of desire so as not to return," like a fruit that is still green. The third is called "non-returning" (*anāgāmin*);

this is the discarding of desire as if it were cast away, like a fruit that has already ripened. The fourth is called "detachment from desire" (*vītarāga*); this is the state where there is no further desire to be eliminated, like a fruit that has already been gathered.

The Song dynasty Confucians claimed that Buddhism possesses "upward attainment" (*shàngdá*) but lacks "downward learning" (*xiàxué*). Observing this [text], one sees that it is precisely a point where downward learning leads to upward attainment.
Wang Zhenru said: "This is according to the gradual teaching (*jiànjiào*); as for supreme enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), it is not so."
To suddenly awaken to true emptiness is precisely to enter the stage of Buddhahood through this *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*.

What need is there, then, to speak of the four fruits of the śrāvaka path? Shengxian said: "To suddenly transcend to the stage of Buddhahood in this life must come from gradual cultivation in previous lives.
If one were an ordinary person on unconditioned ground (*śuddhabhūmi*), how could they achieve sudden awakening? Therefore, the Sūtra [uses] the Great..."

The Vehicle is the primary tenet, while the Two Vehicles are explained concurrently. This demonstrates that sudden enlightenment cannot do without gradual cultivation, yet gradual cultivation must not allow itself to terminate at the point of suddenness.
Song Zhengyu said: "If there were fruit, it would be unobtainable; if the Way could be accomplished, it too would be unobtainable.
To obtain through non-obtainment—this is perhaps close to the mark."

This is not an adornment consisting of external embellishment; rather, it is the adornment of the purity of the mind-ground. Therefore, it is called "adorned pure land.
This refers to how Buddhas and Bodhisattvas all take the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) as their... [foundation].
The intention is already complete. This Buddha also realizes it through the signless (*animitta*). ○ Juefei said: "The self-nature is originally pure;
there is no need for artificial adornment. Yet even adornment does not exist upon adornment; the pure mind is precisely that which serves as adornment.
○ This section is the proof and testimony regarding the bestowal of predictions (*vyākaraṇa*) by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. Adornment.

The earth cannot be grasped or described. [The Buddha] exhorted all bodhisattvas not to give rise to a mind of dwelling, employing a metaphor to clarify the greatness of the formless body, whereby Subhūti attained profound understanding.
The Buddha said to Subhūti, "What do you think? When the Tathāgata (Śākyamuni speaking of himself) was formerly with Dīpaṃkara Buddha, did he obtain any dharma?"
The previous statement that "the śrāvaka does not attain the fruit of mindfulness" refers specifically to the moment of realizing the fruit.
However, if one is practicing on the causal ground (hetu-bhūmi), where teacher and disciple engage in mutual transmission, there must necessarily be a point of accord and verification.
How could it be said, then, that there is no taking up [of the teaching]? This is why the Buddha questioned him regarding his own experiences during the causal stage: if you say there is...
"What was attained? What exactly was attained? If you say there was nothing attained, why did he receive a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*)?
The Buddha Dīpaṃkara—that is, Dīpaṃkara Buddha—was the teacher who gave the prediction to Śākyamuni Buddha.

At the time of the Buddha's birth, light issued forth from his eyes, ears, nose, and the hundred pores of his body, shining like the brightness of a lamp; therefore, he was named Dīpaṃkara ("Lamp-Lighter"). This question is entirely intended to...
"Empty—only the single character 'attainment'.
"No, World-Honored One. When the Tathāgata was with Dīpaṃkara Buddha, he truly attained nothing regarding the Dharma.
Dayuan said: "The Venerable One’s answer that there was truly nothing attained means that within his own fruition, there is truly no dharma whatsoever."
This is the principle. It is said that attaining Buddhahood arises from the awakening of the fundamental mind.

Although there are those who speak of the lamp and those who hear of Śākyamuni, language arises from conditions and lacks an inherent essence; it is not the Dharma realized through wisdom. On the day the Tathāgata [attained enlightenment],...
It is simply because one is personally free from discrimination that wisdom realizes its own non-differentiation.
When the wisdom of the mind merges with principle and the spirit encounters the object, how could there be anything grasped or explained? It is nothing more than sealing this very mind.
As it is said: "In the past, when I was with Dīpaṃkara Buddha, I had not yet become a Buddha; at that time, it seemed I could not help but rely [on him]."

Regarding the practice of the Dharma: it is difficult to say that there is no attainment within the Dharma. One does not realize that at the very moment the Tathāgata practices illusion, he is already free from the illusion of dharmas;
how could one wait until the realization of the fruit to perceive the emptiness of the aggregates?

This non-attainment regarding dharmas does not mean the exclusion of all things, but rather that there is no mark of dharma (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) and likewise no mark of non-dharma (*adharmalakṣaṇa*). The word "real" (*shi*) here corresponds to the word "real" in the preceding passage.
"It should be so. There is no attainment; this is originally the true mark (*dharmatā*), which does not belong to annihilation.
This was the fourth round of inquiry and verification. "Subhūti, what do you think? Does a bodhisattva adorn buddha-fields?"

The prediction of enlightenment (*bodhi-vyākaraṇa*) is indeed such that it cannot be grasped or described. When the Tathāgata was a bodhisattva, did he cultivate the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) and the myriad practices to adorn the Buddha-lands?
[The commentary states: To reveal the true land of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā-bhūmi*), one first raises the question regarding the land of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-bhūmi*).
Adorning the Buddha-lands refers to things such as golden grounds and jewel forests; it includes all acts of building monasteries and copying scriptures.

Practicing giving and making offerings is, in essence, adorning with marks of attachment. [The questioner] says: "Adorning the Buddha-lands" is spoken from the perspective of the objective realm (*viṣaya*).
[The Master] answers: This answer is also given from the perspective of the objective realm. To discuss the objective realm is precisely for the purpose of investigating the mind.

One sees that the mind is real while the objective realm is false and provisional. Since the objective realm originates from the mind and the realm manifests because of the mind, the Bodhisattva does not attend to the objective realm.
This concerns the mind. Shengxian said: "To practice cultivation and deliver sentient beings, one must rely upon a pure Buddha-land.
For the mind can indeed manifest objects, and objects can likewise encompass the mind.

This is why the Buddha, having first taught the primary principle of the Mind, further taught the secondary principle of the Pure Land to deliver sentient beings. The Buddha acted for the sake of deliverance...
Sentient beings manifest lands. Bodhisattvas cultivate the causes for manifesting lands in order to deliver sentient beings.

To cultivate the causes for manifesting lands means to give rise to a pure mind while concurrently practicing the six perfections and the myriad deeds. That the sutra does not explicitly mention them is because it cites the mind as encompassing all conduct.
"No, World-Honored One. Why is this? That which adorns the Buddha-lands is not truly adornment; it is merely called adornment.
When Bodhisattvas cultivate the six perfections and myriad practices to assist in propagating the Buddha’s transformation, it is not that they do not adorn the Buddha-lands; it is simply that..."
Taking external marks as adornments—such as the six perfections and the myriad practices—is entirely within the realm of unconditioned dharmas and pure conduct;

one never clings to the signs of a Buddha-land. To intentionally adorn a Buddha-land is to misunderstand its nature: a Buddha-land exists because of the Buddha, and when the Buddha passes away, the land through which he was delivered also ceases to exist.
Thus, such adornments are not substantially real; they are merely temporary, empty names called "adornments. (Extensive Explanation) Adornment.
"Adorning the Buddha-land" refers to the land of characteristics (*nimitta-bhūmi*). The *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states: "According as the mind is pure, so the Buddha-land is pure";
this refers to the land of nature (*svabhāva-bhūmi*). The Venerable One knows that the Buddha-land of self-nature is primordially complete and does not require artificial adornment.
Therefore, it is said that "it is not adornment"; the mind is eternally pure, an adornment through non-adornment. Furthermore, it is said that "this is called adornment";
in the state of the emptiness of nature, there is an indestructible mark, which is the adornment of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

In the following text, the Buddha demonstrates this by means of the adornment of the pure mind. This statement—that the adornment of the land is not to be grasped—is the fifth round of inquiry and examination.
One realizes that the fruit of Buddhahood is non-abiding; even the place where a Buddha dwells is a dwelling in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

(From the *Guanglu*). Regarding "adornment" (*zhuāngyán*): from the perspective of the objective realm, "adorn" (*zhuāng*) means upright decoration, and "adorn" (*yán*) means orderly refinement. From the perspective of the mind:
The true nature being undisturbed is called "Zhuang" (Serenity); the absence of deviant delusions is called "Yan" (Dignity). Regarding "Buddha-field" (*buddhakṣetra*):
in terms of its objective realm, it refers to the world of the Buddha; in terms of the mind, it points to the original ground of the mind.

It is called a "Buddha-field" because the Buddha-mind does not lose its original state and is able to perfect the ground of the mind—just as the Confucianists speak of the Way, which ultimately resides in the Sage. Among the Five Elements, it is Earth.
It dwells in the center and gives birth to the myriad things. The mind dwells in the central way and gives birth to the myriad dharmas; therefore, earth is used as a metaphor for the mind.
For this reason, Subhūti, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should give rise to a pure mind in this manner (this clarifies the intent of the question). Not...
"One should generate the mind by abiding in form; one should not generate the mind by abiding in sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or dharmas. One should generate the mind by abiding nowhere.
Subhūti was able to grasp the Buddha's intent, and the Buddha, following his words, spoke to him: "The Adornment of the Bodhisattva..."

"Adornment" does not consist in external embellishment; rather, it must be sought within the mind. The mind is fundamentally pure, yet it becomes impure when enticed by objects and transformed by them.
Once one realizes that in the Buddha-dharma there is nothing to be attained, and further realizes that adornment is non-adornment, [true adornment is achieved].

This is the pure mind that is without grasping or attachment. Bodhisattvas training in the Path should thus remain profoundly still and eternally empty without being defiled, and serenely settled in constant concentration without being confused. In this way they give rise to the pure mind.
They should not give rise to the mind by dwelling upon forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects. To dwell upon any one of these is to fall under the sway of the six sense-objects.
Bound by this, deluded thoughts arise in rapid succession, and one cannot achieve purity. One must know that the pure mind is wondrously perfect and all-pervasive;
it does not adhere to specific locations and fundamentally has no place of abiding. One should give rise to the mind within this state of non-abiding.
This is true adornment; this is true purity. [This] extensively explains how the World-Honored One uses the pure mind as adornment.
He solemnly demonstrates this; it constitutes the first round of exhortation. Previously, non-abiding in the six sense-objects was presented as signless giving (*animitta-dāna*);
here, non-abiding in form and so forth is presented as the pure mind and signless adornment (*animitta-vyūha*).
This concludes by returning to the salvation of sentient beings through non-arising, and abiding in non-abiding. Non-abiding to subdue the mind is the great purport of this entire sutra.
This mind is right wisdom; it is the true mind. Yet, when it dwells in attachment to objects, it remains hidden and does not manifest.
If the mind does not dwell [in objects], prajñā becomes clear and vivid. That which gives rise to this mind manifests the originally existent true mind;
it does not arise suddenly. ○ Ruru said: The previous mention of the Bodhisattva’s adornment was intended to indicate his meritorious practices.
The phrase "all bodhisattvas" refers to those who have received the entrustment and protection; they should give rise to such a pure mind.
This points to the aforementioned state of non-attainment and the teaching of non-adornment. What was previously called "giving rise to pure faith" is the awakening of a single thought-moment.
This pure mind is the entirety; the six perfections and myriad practices are all cultivated for its sake. This purity is the original ground, which is itself the ultimate ground.
What was previously called "giving without dwelling on form and so forth" is here expressed as "generating the mind without dwelling on form and so forth.
This shifts the focus from phenomena to the mind; thus, the term "not dwelling" is more subtle. Furthermore, this word "generate" (sheng) refers to the process of arising and ceasing.
"Arising. This arising of the mind is precisely arising through non-arising and non-ceasing; it is through non-arising that there is arising.

"Non-abiding" is utterly different from the "non-entry" of the first fruit (*srotāpanna*). Non-entry merely realizes the departure from desire; therefore, it takes non-coming and non-arising as purity.
Non-abiding, however, does not depart from form and so forth, yet is without form and so forth. Therefore it is said:

The Tathāgata said: "To give rise to the mind" means that the capacity to come and the capacity to produce are what constitute purity. Previously it was said, "One should practice giving without dwelling on anything";
here it is said, "One should give rise to the mind without dwelling on anything. Furthermore, one should practice giving without clinging to its marks.
That which is the state where purity is inexhaustible is precisely "arising. This is what is meant by the "descent of non-descent."

The subduing that is without anything to subdue—herein lies the mind-dharma of the thousand sages. This is why the Sixth Patriarch, upon hearing these words, attained sudden enlightenment into the Tathāgata.
These two sections clarify the Bodhisattva’s realization through non-characteristics (*animitta*). The Commentary states:

"The activities of a Bodhisattva do not lie outside of attaining the Dharma and adorning the lands. Regarding these two points: the preceding section spoke of attaining Bodhi as being without characteristics.
The next section speaks of the signlessness of delivering sentient beings. The phrase "it should be thus" below clarifies the intent of the question.
The phrase "no place of abiding" is the great purport of the entire sutra.
Subhūti, suppose there were a person whose body was like Sumeru, the king of mountains. What do you think? Is this body...
"Is it not great?
This is a flourishing explanation. This passage cites the body that receives the retribution of pleasure as the sixth instance of investigation and verification.

The thirty-two marks mentioned previously are manifestations of the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body). If it refers to the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body), these are produced by actual practice; its superior marks are difficult [to describe]."

[The Buddha] forgot. However, he wished to show that even if the physical marks (*rūpakāya*) were to remain stable—surpassing even Mount Sumeru in size—they would still be subject to spatial dimensions (*mātra*).
Desiring to grasp the true reality (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*), the World-Honored One relied upon a massive body to pose his inquiry. This was the correct interpretation of the intent of the question:

since the Buddha-dharma is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and without grasping (*anupādāna*), how could the *saṃbhogakāya* (retribution body) attained therein not involve grasping? Fearing such a doubt might arise, he established a metaphor to pose the question. [Brahmā...]
Regarding "Mount Sumeru," its Chinese translation is "Wondrously High" (Miaogao). It is the greatest among mountains, and is therefore called the "King of Mountains.
How could a human body possibly possess such magnitude? This is merely a figurative expression, similar to the description of the seven treasures filling the trichiliocosm.

Yan Bing said: "The retribution body is precisely the physical body. Although the physical body may be as vast as Mount Sumeru, King of Mountains, it is ultimately not great, because it is subject to arising and ceasing.
What the Buddha calls 'non-body' is simply my own pure fundamental mind."
This is the true Dharma-body. The Dharma-body pervades the Dharma-realm; this is called the "Great Body.
Subhūti said, "It is exceedingly great, World-Honored One. Why is this? The Buddha says it is 'not a body,' and thus it is called the Great Body."
[Subhūti] correctly understood and replied: "The body is like Sumeru, the king of mountains; it is truly great. [The Buddha said:
"If one speaks of a body in terms of physical form (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*), how could there be such greatness? That which the Buddha speaks of is not a body of physical form;

this is what is called the 'Great Body' (*mahākāya*). [Subhūti] further explained: "Subhūti has seen that retribution arises from the Dharma; retribution is itself the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). He is able to see it."

The body that is not a body; even the reward body (*saṃbhogakāya*) cannot be grasped. This is to clarify, in general, that the true mind of non-abiding pervades the entire dharma-realm and should not dwell upon the characteristics of physical form.
[This is from] the Extensive Record. This demonstrates that the reward body is free from the characteristics of the six sense objects.
The Dharma-body is free from the marks of mental objects; both mind and its objects are empty. This reveals that the Reward-body has no abiding object and the Dharma-body has no abiding mind.
This is an elucidation of the unity of the Dharma and Reward bodies. Song Zhengyu said:
"The Dharma-body fills the Dharma-realm and cannot be discussed in terms of large or small. Now, when the Buddha asks about Mount Sumeru, he is pointing to the Reward-body."
The reward body (*saṃbhogakāya*) serves as a metaphor; it can be discussed in terms of magnitude, which is why the answer states it is "very great.
Furthermore, fearing that people might cling to the reward body, he further states: "The Buddha says that what is not a body is called the Great Body.
This directly points to the *dharmakāya*. The commentary on the sutra states: "Not a body" refers to the *dharmakāya*, which is the true mind itself.

This is its nature. That which is not a body yet is called the "Great Body" refers to the non-abiding of the true mind, which is sufficient to encompass the great void and contain the sands of the worlds.
When one reaches this point, the meaning of non-abiding is fully exhausted.

If people do not seek it within purity, but instead seek something to be attained or something to be adorned, will they not, in doing so, conversely diminish their own mind? This is the Perfect Meaning.
The text says: "The Buddha reveals the true mind within non-abiding; Subhūti perceives the Great Body within that which is not a body.
When the dialogue reaches this point, one sees that both the body and the land are empty, and both mind and objects are transcended. Although he does not speak of merit, his merit is immeasurable.
The subsequent passage then proceeds to calculate and compare this merit. This section clarifies that the Buddha realizes [the truth] through the signless (*animitta*).
△ This section, together with the preceding one, both proceed from the characteristic of detachment (*viveka-lakṣaṇa*) to the point of non-appropriation (*an-upādāna*).

Furthermore, this is elaborated by means of the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) and the adornment of the land (*kṣetra-vyūha*). In the middle section, the intent of the question is clarified, and the single character "birth" (*janman*) is uttered.

It concludes by exhorting all bodhisattvas not to abide in the arising of the mind, but to give rise to it through a pure mind (*viśuddha-citta*), whereby the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) becomes perfected. This mind that constantly arises—

"Vertically deep and horizontally pervasive; without going or coming. By employing this analogy, he clarifies the greatness of the signless *dharmakāya*, and thus Ākāśagupta attained profound understanding.
It is not said that "the mind arises," but rather that "it gives rise to the mind. This mind is right wisdom (*samyagjñāna*);
it is the manifestation of the originally existent true mind (*tathatā-citta*). It arises within non-abiding and is not [an ordinary mental state].
He fell away from the view of extinction. When the Buddha posed the question regarding the "Great Body" (mahā-kāya), the Venerable One immediately realized the Great Body within the non-body;
he further perceived that both body and land are empty, and that the scope of the mind’s measure is vast and boundless. Master Lien said:

"The fact that 'mind' was mentioned above and 'body' is mentioned below does not mean that one is speaking of something external to the body. The character for 'body' (kāya) should be understood here as the character for 'mind' (citta)."
Look! The Tathāgata, wishing to broaden Subhūti’s mind, has merely asked this by means of the body of Sumeru, the king of mountains.
In this section of dialogue, although it speaks of non-attainment and the absence of adornment, when one reaches the state where the mind dwells nowhere, only then is this mind truly vast.
By relying on a great body to pose the question, this is again the Tathāgata...
This comes to reveal one principle for the sake of Subhūti’s awakening. Beginning with the *srotāpanna* and proceeding directly to the *bodhisattva*, the discourse advances layer by layer;
every point is a place where Subhūti demonstrates his skillful understanding. When it concerns those among the four fruits of the path, he answers according to the principles of the *Hīnayāna*.
When it concerns the *arhat*, he answers according to the principle of "non-contention" (*araṇa*). When it concerns the Buddha, he...
He answered with the principle of non-attainment (*anupalambha*). When Subhūti spoke of "bodhisattvas," he answered with the principle of non-adornment (*asaṃskāra*).
Thus, responding to each question as it arose, there is a passage in the interim where Subhūti himself speaks of the name of the Buddha;
this is Subhūti’s meaning of personal realization through his own body. Furthermore, there is the passage concerning the Buddha Dīpaṃkara; this is the Tathāgata’s [meaning].
The realization of Subhūti was embodied; every word corresponded precisely, without the slightest fragmentation.
This exchange of questions and answers should be taken as the true manifestation of the original ground of both men. Dàyuán said:

"If one does not know that what is 'not a body' is called the 'Great Body,' then all marks are non-marks, yet the whole person falls entirely into the mark of non-dharma. Where, then, is there any escape?"

This is the path of the body. If one does not know that the great body is itself no-body, then all worthies and sages will spend their entire lives falling upon the path of differentiation; on what day will they behold the manifestation of the whole body?

Only upon reaching this point does one realize that the three characters "wuwei-fa" (unconditioned dharma) are insufficient to name this sutra; thus, one cannot help but inquire as to the true name of this sutra.
...Indeed.
○ Chapter Eleven: The Superiority of the Merit of Non-action.
Non-action is the Dharma. The merit of upholding this sutra benefits both oneself and others; the merit of non-action surpasses [all other merits].

The Jewel Offering. ○ Juefei said: Previously, by explaining that the four fruits of the path involve no-thought and Śākyamuni has no attainment, he clarified that all worthies and sages are of this unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
Fearing that people might be unable to believe and uphold this, he has again compared and measured their merits.
Subhūti, suppose there were as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River. What do you think?
Would the grains of sand in all those Ganges Rivers be numerous?
The Ganges is the river of India in the western lands. It flows eastward from Lake Anavatapta and circles for forty *li*. Its sand is as fine as flour.
Because the Buddha frequently preached the Dharma there, it was taken as a metaphor;

this is because it is something familiar to his disciples, making it easy to understand. The number of grains of sand therein is immeasurable. The phrase "Ganges-like sands" is an inverted construction.
The Dharma is said to be as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Are the sands within all those Ganges rivers many?
This is also a metaphorical illustration; it merely expresses the ultimate limit of number to serve as a metaphor for the ultimate vastness of the world-systems.
Subhūti said, "Very many, World-Honored One. Even the Ganges Rivers alone are already countless, let alone their sands.
Suppose that for every grain of sand in the Ganges, there were as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand; and suppose all these rivers..."
Within each [of those rivers], there are likewise sands. The rivers themselves are already innumerable; how much more so the sands within them?

"Subhūti, I now tell you in truth: if there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who, with the seven treasures, filled as many trichiliocosm worlds as there are grains of sand in all those Ganges Rivers and used them for giving, the merit they would obtain—"
Not so. Previously, it was only said that one gives the treasures of a *trisāhasramahāsāhasralokadhātu*.

Here, the text increases this by saying "as many as the sands of the Ganges," which collectively demonstrates the extreme magnitude of such giving. The correct interpretation is that a comparison has already been made once before.

However, it has not yet been stated that the four fruits are mindless, that Śākyamuni has no attainment, that the Buddha-land is unadorned yet adorned, and that the Buddha-body is non-appropriated yet appropriated;

thus, these have not yet reached the ultimate limit of Prajñā. Now that this meaning is clarified and the principles of the Dharma are profound, we shall further take a vast amount of merit to compare with it, so that those who uphold and recite this may gain even greater understanding.
It is that which one tends toward.
Subhūti said: "Very much, World-Honored One.
For if one receives such merit through giving as this, how could there be any principle that it is not vast? It is simply that [Subhūti] did not know what the World-Honored One meant by...
Why is this so? The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, from within this sutra, were to receive, uphold, and even recite as little as a four-line verse for others, the merit of this would surpass the former merit."

To give gifts of the seven treasures is also a difficult feat; yet to uphold and expound [this teaching] is even more meritorious. Giving belongs generally to the realm of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*);

though its merit is great, it ultimately comes to an end. It is not like receiving and upholding the verses of this sutra and teaching them to others in turn, whereby all may enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Thus benefiting both oneself and others, one accomplishes the Unsurpassed Way and is liberated from saṃsāra.

It turns [the mind] back, forever transcending birth and death. This merit from the gift of Dharma remains constant throughout kalpas; therefore, it surpasses the giving of sand-grains along the Ganges.
Dayuan said: "The seven treasures are merely worldly treasures and are difficult to compare with the supreme, world-transcending treasure of the Buddha-Dharma.
All the sand within the Ganges River does not equal the Buddha-Dharma produced within this sutra."
As numerous as the sands of such Ganges Rivers may be, they do not equal the non-Buddha, non-Dharma,

and non-body unconditioned *dharmakāya* possessed by each individual within this sutra’s Buddha-dharma. Furthermore, the number of worlds contained within all the sands of those Ganges Rivers does not even approach the immeasurable and boundless Buddhas’ dharmas that arise from within that which is neither Buddha, nor Dharma, nor body.
Vast indeed is the difference. Through mere giving, one obtains only worldly blessings; through upholding [the precepts], one obtains the blessings of the nature (dharmatā).
Worldly blessings reach only oneself and, once exhausted, lead back to a fall. The blessings of the nature transform and benefit sentient beings universally and extensively.
How could these two possibly be compared?
△ This second comparison is one layer deeper than the comparison based on the eight divisions.

This is because up to the seventh division, it merely spoke of the attainment of the pure *dharmakāya*. At the eighth division, it compares [this scripture] by means of merit (*puṇya*), stating that all the Buddha-dharma emerges from this sūtra.
From the eighth division downward, it enumerates both *śrāvakas* and *bodhisattvas*, all of whom [arise] from...
Within the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharmas, many distinctions manifest; ultimately, they all return to the unconditioned.
Thereafter, [the text] exhorts all bodhisattvas not to abide in the arising of the mind, using the metaphor of assuming a "great body" to verify this.
Thus, the entire essence and great function within the pure *dharmakāya* appear simultaneously. This is the comparison of merits.
Therefore, with every step, one goes deeper. The Layman Ruru said: "Since this is a 'Great Body,' what measure can its merit have?
Thus, by upholding and reciting [this teaching], one can obtain supreme merit. However, by selecting the external to represent the internal, it is called the 'nature of merit';
by taking the fundamental internal to manifest the external, it is called the 'Great Body. These are not two separate meanings. How then is this merit [to be understood]?"

Its virtue surpasses previous merit. For while the preceding discourse on the Dharma was indeed profoundly subtle and wondrous, it still contained the gradations of distinctions between the worthy and the sages.
This [present teaching], however, brings the four fruits of arhatship and the bodhisattvas together in a single return to non-attainment; the Great and Small vehicles are blended as one.

Through the revolving perfection of the sutra’s meaning, it reveals the extraordinary excellence of upholding and expounding it. As for the nature of mind thus explained, there is no difference in depth between its earlier and later parts.

It is profound. ○ Furthermore, it is said: from the phrase "Since the time of the Srotāpanna, one can form this thought" up to this point, the greatness of the signless (animitta) is revealed through the Great Body.
To summarize its meaning: the Tathāgata’s pure Dharma-body is originally without any dharma that can be attained.
If one cannot uphold all dharma-gates, it is not yet sufficient to be called "Great. Now, by means of...
The Buddha’s non-attainment sweeps away the non-attainment of the four fruits of the śrāvaka path; this sufficiently draws the Hīnayāna into the Mahāyāna.
By means of the Bodhisattva’s non-attainment, one seals the Buddha’s non-attainment, which is sufficient to transform the Mahāyāna into the Supreme Vehicle (Anuttarayāna).
As the Wheel of Dharma is turned, it transforms base iron into gold. A single body is pure, and many bodies are pure; this is called the "Great Body" (*mahākāya*). Its...
The merit [accruing from this] is beyond all calculation; how, then, could one doubt that the one who upholds and expounds it shall obtain such blessings?
Thus, the excellence of the signless (*animitta*) is made perfectly clear. Song Zhengyu remarked:

"In the preceding section, it was stated that what is not adornment is called adornment, and what is not the body is called the body. Fearing that people might negate cause and effect, he now restates the superiority of the merit."
Either one uses non-existence to dispel existence, or one uses existence to dispel non-existence; this is using existence to dispel non-existence.
This continues until there is no longer even "non-existence" to be dispelled, whereupon one may approximate the state of non-action (wuwei).
Chapter Twelve: Honoring the True Teaching.
The Buddha’s teaching is truly great; those who receive and uphold it are revered by both devas and humans. To express the utmost respect for the true teaching, this sutra is titled accordingly.
The true teaching is the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), established by the Buddha through the dharma of bodhi.
These teachings are all principles that exhaust human nature and reach the destiny of life; they are grand, correct, and heterodox-free discourses.
If people can honor and revere them, they will clarify the mind, perceive the nature, and realize ultimate emptiness, thereby upholding the orthodox teaching.
Devas and humans alike gave rise to reverence. ○ Dayuan said:
This section clarifies why the merit of this sutra is so superior, thereby fulfilling the meaning of the eleven preceding sections. First, it clarifies that the location is worthy of veneration.

Second, it clarifies that the person [who teaches] is worthy of honor; third, it clarifies that the place where the Buddha resides is [sacred]. These together explain the reasons why this merit is superior.
Furthermore, Subhūti, wherever this sutra is spoken, even as little as a single four-line verse, you should know that this place is [a site of supreme merit].
All those in the world—gods, humans, and asuras—should all make offerings to it as they would to a stupa or temple of the Buddha;
how much more so for anyone who is able to fully receive, uphold, read, and recite it?
The Layman Ruru said: "Regarding the previous two statements on attaining merit, both 'upholding' and 'explaining to others' were mentioned together.
I fear that practitioners might merely pursue the literal words and labor in vain for superior merit, while failing to contemplate and cultivate the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
If one cannot achieve realization for oneself, how can one benefit others? Thus he spoke.
The emphasis is placed on receiving and upholding [the teaching] to demonstrate the foundation of preaching the Dharma. The subsequent passage, "How does one expound it for others?
precisely accords with this meaning. Huang Shangcai said: "Expounding according to [the capacity]" corresponds to the latter phrase, "being able to respond exhaustively.
The four characters "expounding according to" (suishuo) must be read as a single, continuous breath and may not be separated. Whether it be half a volume, a single chapter, or even...

"At least as much as a four-line verse" refers to the meaning of the scriptural passage cited. Chen Xiong states that it is "spoken in accordance with sentient beings," thus taking the character *suí* (隨) to refer to those who hear the Dharma.
Wang Rixiu states that it is "in accordance with wherever one may be," thus taking the character *suí* to refer to the location;
however, this conflates the character *chù* (處) from the subsequent phrase, and both interpretations conflict with the word "exhaustively" (*jìn*).
The two characters "néng" (capable) do not correspond to one another. The *Shu* (Commentary) states: "That which is capable according to what is taught" refers to the Prajñā of a single section;

"that which is capable in its entirety" refers to the Prajñā of the whole body [of the teaching]. "Worldly devas, humans, and asuras" refers to the celestial realm, the human realm, and the realm of Māra.
A "stūpa" is that which enshrines the Buddha’s śarīra; a "temple" is that which establishes images of the Buddha. Thus it is said.
This sutra must be explained strictly according to the principle of purity and non-abiding. To preach the Dharma with the fundamentally pure mind is itself the Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata.
For those who show reverence to it, how is this any different from a stupa or temple?
If the place where the sutra is preached is to be treated with such respect, how much more so for those who do not merely follow its words, but are able to fully receive, uphold, read, and recite it?
Subhūti, you should know that such a person accomplishes the most supreme and foremost, rare and marvelous Dharma.
As the Layman Ruru said: "The reason this sutra is esteemed for being upheld and expounded is that this sutra constitutes the most supreme and foremost, rare and marvelous Dharma.
It does not hinder one from following and reciting even a single verse or stanza when guiding others. If...
One must certainly strive to achieve personal accomplishment and be able to fully receive and uphold [the teachings].
The dharma accomplished by one who is thus fully capable is the most supreme, foremost, and rare dharma. How could this not evoke even greater reverence from devas and humans?

"Receiving" (*śruta*) means to comprehend the meaning; it is the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*). "Retaining" (*dhāraṇa*) means to take [the teaching] to heart and not lose it; it is the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*). To face the original text is called "reading" (*pāṭha*);

to recite apart from the original text is called "recitation" (*svādhyāya*); this is the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*). Regarding the sequence of these three wisdoms, one first reads and recites, and subsequently receives and retains.
When it is said here that one should "receive, retain, read, and recite," it implies that if one merely reads and recites without receiving and retaining, the benefit realized will still be shallow.

Once one has received and maintained [this teaching] and recites it, the essence grasped therein becomes profound. The cultivation and maintenance of the myriad practices are all subsumed within these four characters;
therefore, one is able to achieve the foremost [attainment]. As for the phrase "exhaustively able," it means that there is nothing that does not enter into the profound wisdom of the Vajra.
To uphold this is not to seek one's livelihood through words and phrases;
it is the most supreme, foremost, and rare Dharma—namely, the aforementioned Dharma of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Perfectly Equal and Perfect Enlightenment is the foremost.
"Foremost" is its essence; "most supreme" means unsurpassed; "foremost" is its characteristic; and it is "rare."
This is the primary function. Therefore, the subsequent text summarizes only the first [point], encompassing the unsurpassed and rare quality.
It does not say "accomplishment of merit" but rather "accomplishment of the Dharma," because the one who receives and maintains it accomplishes wholesome dharmas to benefit sentient beings;
they do not merely seek their own liberation through merit alone, but must also achieve the accomplishment of the Dharma. However...
This refers to the subsequent accomplishment of merit; therefore, the following passage speaks of "accomplishing merit.
Wherever this scripture resides, it is as if the Buddha himself were present, as well as his honored disciples.
This is the correct interpretation. It is not merely that recitation can move the divine; wherever this scripture resides, it is as if the Buddha is present there.
One need not seek him elsewhere. Where the scripture is, the Buddha is; and the great disciples are likewise there.
Thus, the Three Jewels dwell together. Song Zhenyu said: "Ruò" (若) here means "and" or "also," indicating that—
The Buddha and his disciples were both present. The Layman Ruru said: "The two characters 'ruo' (若) are not empty words;
they are the term for achieving the foremost state. They express deep faith within the mind. This is because his wisdom merges with the principle (*li*);
wherever the scriptures are located, he perceives them as if the Buddha were there—this is the 'seeing the Tathāgata' mentioned in the preceding passage."
One takes refuge and upholds [the teachings], regarding oneself as a disciple of the Mahāyāna who is no different from Mañjuśrī and the other great bodhisattvas;
this is what is meant by "shouldering the burden of the Tathāgata" mentioned below. Otherwise, there are many in the degenerate age who treat the scriptures as mere dregs.
If one were to tell a commoner while holding them: "The scriptures contain the Buddha and his disciples."
Would one not consider this to be迂誕 (extravagant and absurd)? Vajrabodhi’s Jewel-Sphere says: "Where do the scriptures reside? They reside precisely within this mind.

If one is able to fully uphold and recite them, such that one can recite this scripture from one's own mind, understand its meaning from one's own mind, and realize the principle of non-attachment and signlessness from one's own mind, then with every thought one should be diligent and constantly cultivate the Buddha."
Practice. This very mind is the Buddha; therefore, it is said that there is a Buddha therein. One is thus called a "Son of the Buddha" (Buddhaputra); therefore, one is called a "disciple.

These three phrases praise the practitioner for whose mind the state of constant purity is attained, who realizes the wondrous nature of True Suchness (Tathatā), and who benefits both self and others.
Their merit surpasses that of giving alms as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. It is fitting that they be honored by devas, humans, and asuras.
Thus it is.
△ The preceding statement that merit gained through non-action is superior is because the Dharma of this sutra is supreme.

Although this sutra may consist of only a few phrases or verses, if one explains it for others, it can immediately shatter the greed, anger, and ignorance of sentient beings and lead them to nirvana. Therefore—
Devas, humans, spirits, and ghosts will all offer worship and show reverence; how much more so for one who is able to fully receive, uphold, read, and recite it?
This is the most supreme and foremost, most rare Dharma. Such a person will certainly be able to achieve success and will be even more revered by devas and humans.
All Buddhas emerge from this sutra; therefore, wherever this sutra resides, that place is itself a Buddha.
Wherever [the teacher] resides is precisely where the disciples of Dharmapāla reside; thus, wherever this sutra is, it is there that the True Teaching resides.
It does not exist merely because it is being expounded, nor does it cease to exist when it is not being expounded. It exists when someone recites it, and it does not exist when no one recites it.
This is why it continues the past and opens the way for the future, transmitting the Dharma and delivering sentient beings. — Changshui.

Regarding the six *pāramitās*, each is a resolve that is free from marks (*lakṣaṇa*), undertaken for the benefit of sentient beings.
This section is a general division that does not go beyond the three dharmas of principle, practice, and fruit.

Having already demonstrated the principle of the true mark (*dharmatā*) so as to cause people to believe and understand it, it further clarifies non-abiding practice so as to cause people to cultivate it, and reveals non-attainment...
The response enables people to realize and enter [the truth]. These three points have already been clarified, and the formal exposition is concluded.
Therefore, from here down to the sixteenth section, the text merely reveals the supreme merits and exhorts others to propagate [this teaching].
At that time, Subhūti, having heard this sutra being preached, deeply understood its meaning and intent; weeping with tears of sorrow, he addressed the Buddha, saying:

"O Great Perfect One! Śūnyatā-utpanna (Subhūti) knows that the merit resulting from giving up one's life is not equal to that of upholding and preaching [this sutra]; his mind has awakened to the Truth."
Regarding the meaning and intent of emptiness and signlessness, he lamented that his awakening had come so late; thus, moved by this extreme emotion, his tears fell.
Previously, Śūnyatā-janman (Subhūti) had applied his mind to the level of the true mark (*dharmatā*), but had not yet opened his eyes toward the state where all marks are non-existent.

Therefore, his attachment to dharmas had not yet been forgotten. Only after the Tathāgata pointed out that the name of the sutra is *Prajñāpāramitā* did he finally pierce through to the Diamond Eye (*vajranetra*).
At this moment, one finally realizes that the true mark (*dharmatā*) is itself the absence of marks; that the four marks of sentient beings are themselves the absence of marks.

When the sentiments of ordinary and sage are exhausted, and both person and phenomena are forgotten, all marks are transcended. Within the present environment and its inhabitants, the sense organs and their objects—none are other than the realm of the Buddha.
This is what is called "profoundly understanding the meaning and intent. "Meaning" refers to the significance within names; the *Sūtra* [uses] *prajñā*...
If one speaks in terms of its name, Prajñā takes the deconstruction of marks (*lakṣaṇa*) as its primary function; not abiding in marks is precisely the meaning of this sutra.
The ultimate point of arrival for this meaning is its "destination" (*gati*). Not abiding in marks gives rise to the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), which is the destination within the meaning.
After emptiness gave rise to understanding, I rejoiced at having heard it and grieved that it was so late; furthermore, I felt compassion.
The sentient beings of that time, as well as those of the future, were deaf and blind to this Dharma; they wept with tears flowing together because they did not realize it.
How rare, World-Honored One! That the Buddha has preached such a profound sutra as this. Through this, I have obtained the eye of wisdom that I had not possessed since ancient times.
"Never before have we heard such a sutra as this. Dayuan said:
"The previous praise of its rarity was spoken from the perspective of saving sentient beings; this praise of its rarity is spoken from the perspective of the place where the Dharma is taught.
The former is shallow and the latter is deep. When the Buddha speaks such a profound scripture as this, it is not merely that persons are empty," and so forth.
Furthermore, phenomena are empty, and the characteristics of the wisdom of prajñā are likewise empty. Previously, having attained the eye of wisdom, he merely stilled attachment to the self;
now, hearing this sutra, he has also emptied attachment to phenomena. Marveling at its rarity, he sought to initiate instruction in order to manifest it for the sake of future generations.
As the *Ruru* says: "The two instances of the character 'to hear' (*wen*) must be examined with care. This corresponds to the character 'to hear' in the preceding phrase 'willingly desires to hear.

Śāriputra himself describes the scope of what he has heard; he does not simply say that he "profoundly understands the meaning and purport," but first says, "I have heard this sutra being preached.
It is precisely through hearing that one is able to understand.
World-Honored One, if there should be another person who hears this sutra and, with pure faith, gives rise to the mark of reality,
you should know that such a person accomplishes the foremost and most rare merit.

Dayuan said: "Śāriputra personally declares his own realization, yet he still fears that there may be śrāvakas of the Lesser Vehicle in the assembly who, upon hearing this, might not necessarily believe it.

Therefore, he says: 'If there should be anyone who hears this sutra and believes that outside of this there is no other dharma, and that herein no marks of dharmas can be apprehended—then both attachment to persons and attachment to dharmas are abandoned.'"
When both the emptiness of persons and the emptiness of phenomena are revealed together, one perceives the true nature and characteristics.

This arises precisely from within this signlessness, just as the emptiness of a mirror enables it to reflect. This which is thus heard constitutes the purity of the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).

This which is faith constitutes the purity of the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*). This which is the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) constitutes the purity of the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).

The entirety of True Suchness (*tathatā*) is the reality (*dharmatā*) that has not yet arisen. Even if one cultivates meritorious virtues, they do not transcend the functioning of conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and out-flowing (*sāsrava*) phenomena;

these are all merely illusory appearances arising from defiled conditions. Once the reality has arisen, the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) inherently possesses nature-born merits as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, which are spontaneously perfected in every place;
these are all the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Therefore, it is said to be "rare. Transformation...
Regarding the statement that "merit is called accomplishment": when accomplishment is achieved and fruition is perfected, merit is no longer worth mentioning. Master Padmasambhava said:

"The two characters 'true reality' (bhūtatathatā) are the Tathāgata’s actual ground of practice. If one has not yet practiced from the standpoint of true reality and instead speaks vaguely of empty phenomena, one will fall into mere quiescence;
how then could [enlightenment] arise? Therefore, he spoke of 'true reality' so that people might proceed from this."
The characteristics of emptiness truly arise from the ground; this is what is cultivated from hereon. Chen Xiong said:
"Within the nature is contained the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata; this is called the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

Now, when one awakens to principle and reaches the realization of the true mark, I know that the Dharma-body is accomplished, and no merit surpasses this. Therefore, it is called 'the foremost rarity. Li Teng.
Fang said: "Faith" means to have faith in the four marks such as non-self and to practice the conduct of non-abiding in marks.
"Purity" refers to the mind of the twofold emptiness of person and phenomena, which does not abide in marks. "True Reality" (dharmatā) is...
This is precisely the pure *dharmakāya*: neither existent nor non-existent, neither arising nor ceasing, suchness (*tathatā*) that is immovable.
As for the "giving rise to the true mark" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), it is because the human mind is fundamentally pure by nature; yet, due to dwelling upon signs (*nimitta*), delusion arises.
Because one does not dwell in marks, the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) arises. It is spoken of as the "true mark" only by way of contrast with the false and illusory;
because the false and illusory are extinguished, it is said that the true mark arises. Since reality means that marks return to the markless, how could there be any arising?
Thus, regarding the arising of emptiness, the text below shifts its phrasing and says: "That which is the true mark is precisely the absence of marks."
"World-Honored One, this true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is itself the absence of marks; therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of it by the name 'true mark.
Furthermore, fearing that people might hear the name "true mark" and consequently give rise to the conceptualization of a true mark, Xukongsheng quickly shifts his phrasing to sweep it away:
"This so-called true mark means that the ultimate essence is entirely empty, such that neither of the two extremes is established, nor is there a middle way."
It is unconditioned, like the vast void; it has no form or characteristics that can be grasped, and is therefore said to be "the absence of characteristics. [Commentary on the *Saṃyuktāgama*]:
The true characteristic (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is the original nature of emptiness and purity; there is not even the slightest dharma for which a characteristic can be sought.
If you cling to seeking awakening through the scriptures, you will cast aside your own true scripture; ultimately, this is not real.

Furthermore, the Tathāgata regards non-characteristics as the true characteristic and regards having characteristics as illusory characteristics; he speaks only of the true characteristic as being without characteristics.
This does not mean that the true mark (dharmatā) is non-existent; do not misunderstand this.
Furthermore, since it is called the "true mark" and yet called "non-mark," and since it is called "non-mark" and yet called the "true mark," it is like empty space:
though one cannot find it by searching throughout the ten directions, it is nonetheless not the case that empty space does not exist.
“World-Honored One, for me to now hear such a sutra as this, and to believe, understand, accept, and uphold it, is not difficult. But if, in a future age,
