As it is said: "When Xingkong first had the good fortune to hear this for himself, he immediately regarded those who can hear it as superior;
furthermore, he looked toward the sentient beings of the future five-hundred-year period and spoke of them as 'foremost' once, and again as 'foremost.

His earnestness was identical to that of the Buddha when he exhorted those who obtain blessings to uphold and recite [this teaching]. This is because he truly knew how to receive, uphold, and read [it]."

Recite it; this can accomplish the foremost Dharma. Furthermore, fearing that sentient beings might mistakenly believe that the practice of upholding, reciting, and chanting depends entirely upon the words and phrases, such that they fail to give rise to their own roots of goodness, [the text] first speaks of faith for the sake of purification.
Next, the term "faith and understanding" (*śraddhā-adhimukti*) is mentioned to demonstrate the foundation for receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting [the teachings].
This Venerable One deeply believed that the Dharma was supreme; having already enlightened the great assembly gathered there, he further desired to transmit it to future ages.

"Hearing" refers to the wisdom of hearing (*śruta-mayī-prajñā*); "faith and understanding" refers to the wisdom of reflection (*cintā-mayī-prajñā*); "receiving and upholding" refers to the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*). Furthermore, within "faith," four meanings are contained. First:

First, believe that the myriad dharmas do not exist apart from the one mind. Second, believe that this sutra is certainly able to open the spiritual nature and bring about liberation from birth and death.
Third, believe that all sentient beings each possess the one mind and the three kinds of prajñā. Fourth, believe that within daily life, the essence of the mind is empty and quiescent;
this is precisely the power of upholding the Great Dharma. Therefore, it is said to be "the foremost rarity. The subsequent text further investigates this rarity.
Because they possess it.
Why is this? Such a person has no mark of self, no mark of person, no mark of sentient being, and no mark of life-span.
How is its rarity to be seen? Precisely because the meaning of this sutra is profoundly deep; it is not merely a matter of upholding the words and letters.

This may be called "faith-understanding" (śraddhā-adhimukti). It is simply that the four marks are all absent; thus one is able to awaken to the wondrous meaning of Prajñā, and to believe, understand, accept, and uphold it.
This is the emptiness of persons (pudgala-śūnyatā).
Why is this? The mark of a self is itself no-mark; the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, and the mark of a life-span are themselves no-marks.
Furthermore, it should be known that as for why this person is able to uphold this sutra while remaining free from these four marks, it is because...
His faith was pure and clear. He realized that the five aggregates are originally empty and quiescent.
The mark of self is precisely no-mark; self and other are fundamentally beyond all relativity. The mark of person is precisely no-mark; the myriad phenomena are sealed by the single Dharma.
Sentient beings are precisely not sentient beings; billions of kalpas do not transcend a single kṣaṇa. The mark of a life-span is precisely no-life-span. Having thus awakened—
The principle that all marks are non-marks means that the four marks need not be laboriously severed or extinguished, for they are entirely empty in their very substance.
This is the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*).
Why is this? Because to be free from all marks is precisely what is called "all Buddhas."
Furthermore, how do we know that the four marks are non-marks? It is simply because they are said to be "markless. Even those of the Two Vehicles can attain this;

however, they only succeed in realizing the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). Once one knows that marks are themselves non-marks, then phenomena are fundamentally without existence. When the characteristics of phenomena are empty, even the view of emptiness is forgotten.
Thus, one purely awakens to the three kinds of emptiness, harmonizes with the true principle, and the numinous nature manifests, enabling the realization of the pure Dharma.
This is the body. Herein, even the view of emptiness is forgotten. As it is said: "To see that all marks are no-marks is to see the Tathāgata.
At the end, it was asked how one sees this; the answer was that all Buddhas emerge from this sutra. At the end, it was asked how they emerge;
the answer was that now, having reached the point of understanding and realization, one establishes the definitive meaning by saying: "It is apart from oneness..."
To sever all marks is precisely what is called the Buddhas. Such is the seeing; such is the emergence. The subtlety lies in being free from words. The ordinary is opposed to the mundane;
the non-existent is opposed to the existent. To be free is to simultaneously cast off both existence and non-existence, so that neither right nor wrong can be established.
There is no falsehood and no truth—only the profound, pervasive, and perfect enlightenment. Therefore, the Buddha spoke again to seal this realization.

The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is, so it is. If there should be anyone who, upon hearing this sutra, is not startled, not terrified, and does not fear, you should know that such a person is most rare."
Subhūti has given rise to faith in the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Having forgotten both self and dharmas, he has reached the point where all marks are exhausted; this is what is called a Buddha.
Every word of his perceives the Truth (*satya*), and he profoundly accords with the intent of the Tathāgata. Therefore, [the Buddha] confirms him with the seal "Thus, thus.
Not only is it rare for him to have faith, understanding, and to uphold [this teaching], but even upon hearing this sutra, he is not startled by the excessiveness of its words, nor does he feel fear.
The loftiness of that Way does not fear the difficulty of its practice; such a person is also rare indeed. To investigate the reason for this, it is said:
"The Buddha feared that Subhūti might cling to the view of being foremost and thus still not be free from signs;

therefore, as soon as he granted his seal of approval, he immediately urged him to advance further on the tip of the staff, thereby stripping away what he had occupied. This was because Subhūti possessed a profound understanding."
One weeps with sorrow. Sorrow arises from joy; joy arises from astonishment. Astonishment gives rise to fear and dread as their mutual causes;
thus, there is ultimately a primary characteristic present. Therefore, this is taught to demonstrate it.

To reach the profound state of being without astonishment, fear, or dread requires that one first attain faith, understanding, and upholding [the teaching]. "Astonishment" means to be startled; "fear" means to be apprehensive.

Furthermore, "fear" (*wei*) refers to hesitation. "Startle" (*jing*) is the opposite of "love" (*ai*); "terror" (*bu*) is the opposite of "joy" (*le*); and "apprehension" (*wei*) is the opposite of "keenness" (*rui*).

If a person can bring their wisdom into accord with principle, such that they do not give rise to thoughts of love, do not form conceptions of joy, and are entirely devoid of keen striving, then one may apply this name [to them].
Why is this? Subhūti, that which the Tathāgata calls the foremost pāramitā is not, in fact, a foremost pāramitā;
it is merely designated as the foremost pāramitā.
Since Śāriputra was already able to understand this deeply, the Tathāgata required him to practice the six *pāramitās* in earnest.
Therefore, what follows below demonstrates them through the six *pāramitās*. Dayuan said:

"Among the six *pāramitās*, *prajñā* is the primary cause of the *dharmakāya*, while the other five *pāramitās* serve as auxiliary conditions. The *dharmakāya* is the greatest and most unsurpassed; it is only..."

Because Prajñā can accomplish the Dharmakāya, it is called "the foremost. The previous statement that "Prajñā is itself not Prajñā" was made in reference to the single Pāramitā of Prajñā; it means that it has no inherent nature of its own.
This "foremost" being "not foremost" is said in contrast to the other five Pāramitās, indicating that the six perfections are collectively one and the same.

If the myriad practices are equally perfected as the foremost, it is because they arise from the lower patience (*kṣānti*) and giving (*dāna*), with the intention of being detached from all marks (*nimitta*).
As it is said in the *Ruru*: "That which is not the foremost is the pure mind;
that which is named the foremost is the principle of perfect realization. The *Yuanzhi* says: "That which Subhūti calls 'rare' is..."
One who is able to see the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is what the Buddha calls "rare":

namely, one who, when the true mark manifests before them, is neither startled, nor terrified, nor afraid. For the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā* penetrates the five perfections and is the foremost *pāramitā*.
Yet, that which is called "foremost" is that which, despite this, remains without alarm or fear; this is what constitutes being "first. There is.
To be terrified is not the characteristic of a pure mind. How, then, could it be considered the most rare and marvelous?
Subhūti, the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā) taught by the Tathāgata is not a perfection of patience; it is called the "perfection of patience" [only] as a designation.
This phrase does not appear in the Qin translation or in ancient manuscripts. Regarding the term "tathatā-tathatā" (suchness-suchness):

the preceding passage stated that it is "not the prajñāpāramitā" and "not the foremost pāramitā," because there was still concern that sentient beings might not yet have attained thorough penetration of the five perfections.

Therefore, I have once again brought forth patience (*kṣānti*) to demonstrate it. Morality (*śīla*), diligence (*vīrya*), meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and wisdom (*prajñā*) are all cultivated within the mind.
Generosity (*dāna*) and patience, however, manifest in what ought to be done. When a bodhisattva benefits sentient beings, they are precisely examining the mind regarding what ought to be done;
thus, the sutras state that generosity and patience encompass the remaining perfections. It is precious to initiate this cultivation.

Because it involves the ability to relinquish, one cultivates through the means of giving (*dāna*). Because the attainment of the fruit is more noble than the ability to forget, one gathers the fruit through patience (*kṣānti*).
Dayuan said: "Among the six perfections, none is as difficult to remain free from signs as the single perfection of patience.
To be reviled and harmed by others is called 'humiliation' (*ru*); to be able to accept this with composure is called 'patience' (*ren*). This is practiced after the realization of the nature."
Cultivating wisdom through meditative concentration is the most critical juncture. Therefore, a Bodhisattva should practice the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
However, if one perceives that there is an insult to be endured, then one is truly unable to endure it. This patience originally arises from *prajñā* (wisdom).
In the fundamental mind, which is tranquil and unmoving, one does not perceive externally any sign of an insulting object, nor internally...

Seeing that there is a mind capable of endurance, one realizes that within the essence of *prajñā*, there is fundamentally no self and no person; who, then, could be the one who endures, and toward whom could there be endurance?

Why is this so? Subhūti, as when I was formerly dismembered by King Kali (the first proof), at that time I had no perception of a self, no perception of a person, no perception of a sentient being, and no perception of a life-span.
To investigate why that which is "endurance" is not truly "endurance," one must verify it by means of the deeds he himself performed.
[Commentary: Endurance does indeed possess these characteristics; why, then, is it said to be "not endurance"? It is solely because he was able to remain free from the four marks (*catur-nimitta*).
The Tathāgata cites his own experience to clarify this: *Kāli* (in Chinese, *Jí'è*, meaning "extremely evil"). Long ago, for the sake of... [the Tathāgata].
Having realized the first stage (*bhūmi*), he dwelt in the mountains practicing the Way. The king, accompanied by his palace women, went out hunting; becoming weary, he fell asleep.

The others entered the mountains to pay homage to the immortal. When the king woke up, he was greatly enraged and entered the mountains to search for him. He asked the immortal whether he had attained the fruit of realization.

He replied, "I have not yet attained it. He asked again, "By what do you take as your precept? He replied, "I take patience as my precept. The king cut off his ears, yet his countenance did not change.
Again, he had his nose severed and his hands lopped off. His ministers strove to remonstrate with him, but he would not listen. The Four Heavenly Kings rained down sand and stones.
The king was struck with fear and repented; the seer’s body returned to its former state. Thereafter, the king placed his faith in him.
He received the prediction.

Why is this? If, when my body was being dismembered limb by limb in the past, there had been in me any notion of a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span, then resentment would have arisen (which conversely demonstrates that it was not patience).
There are four characteristics. When there is perception, one sees humiliation; with humiliation, there is resentment; with resentment, there is endurance; and with endurance, there is abiding.
To abide in endurance is not to be without endurance. The Tathāgata cherished his own ascetic practices to transform the greed and anger of others.
If there is malice or resentment, then the one who is being mutilated and the one who inflicts harm share the same ignorance.
This would not be compassion; how then could one transform and guide others? ○ Chengyun says: The previous passage spoke of the foremost *pāramitā*;
here, moreover, among the six *pāramitās*, the single quality of patience (*kṣānti*) is cited to demonstrate that even body and life are without abiding.
It is said that this is not patience; it is patience without the notion of patience. As I have realized once: even this endurance of extreme suffering is not patience.

It is devoid of the four marks (*catur-lakṣaṇa*). This precisely clarifies that it is not patience. This being devoid of the four marks when delivering sentient beings and being devoid of the four marks when upholding the sutra mutually illuminate one another.
Thus, while its name is "patience," its essence is entirely *prajñā*, just like that of a Bodhisattva.
He practiced austerities and went directly to the source, yet did not produce the fruit of suffering.
Subhūti, furthermore, recall that in the past, for five hundred lifetimes, he was a rishi of patience (another proof); during all those lifetimes...
There is no mark of a self, no mark of a person, no mark of a sentient being, and no mark of a life-span.
Furthermore, this practice of patience was not limited to such an occasion with King Kali alone;
even before encountering King Kali, he had practiced the path of patience as a patient seer for five hundred past lifetimes.
Having transcended the four marks, one dwells in the world without the burden of the four marks. Throughout kalpas, one can spontaneously awaken to true emptiness.
When speaking of the Buddha’s cultivation, it does not pertain to merely one lifetime or one single deed. Thus we know that patience is the foremost priority in studying the Way;
its primary requirement is to destroy the mind of anger, whereby one may then depart from the four marks. The four marks ultimately converge into...
The mark of self (*ātman*). Regarding giving and patience, the knot of the mark of self is extremely firm; therefore, it is stated repeatedly that patience is signless (*animitta*).
Furthermore, it is stated below that giving is non-abiding (*apratiṣṭhita*). This is nothing other than showing the bodhisattva the meaning of non-self (*anātman*).
Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva should set out for anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi having abandoned all marks. (These five characters govern the following text in general.)

The Tathāgata said: "The above detailed explanation of the departure from marks is established as a standard for practice; this is spoken with reference to those who have resolved their minds [on enlightenment].
The Buddha’s intention is that those who hear this sūtra are very far removed from the Buddha, yet they can remain free from alarm and fear regarding various marks.
Even the Seer of Endurance had not yet attained Buddhahood, yet he was already free from the four marks such as 'self. You must not..."
This refers to being free from all marks (*lakṣaṇa*). This is the ultimate attainment of all Buddhas, and it is for this reason that Bodhisattvas should resolve their minds [upon enlightenment].
The Sūtra states that Bodhisattvas are devoid of the four marks; it likewise states that sentient beings are devoid of the four marks.

To say that sentient beings have neither the mark of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) nor the mark of non-phenomena (*adharmalakṣaṇa*) is to say that the Tathāgata is neither a phenomenon nor a non-phenomenon. It speaks of being detached from the one...
"All characteristics" refers to the Buddhas. Thus, it is said that one should give rise to the bodhicitta by departing from all characteristics;

this is the fundamentally equal limit (*koṭi*) wherein it is determined that sentient beings are Buddhas. Before [the teaching on] emptiness arose, he asked how to abide and subdue [the mind], yet he did not ask how to give rise to the mind.
The Buddha, however, showed him the giving rise to the mind by departing from characteristics—what is called the original ground of the causal stage.

To clarify water, one must reach its source; to nourish a tree, one must reach its root. To recognize the attainment of the mind that is free from signs (*animitta*), one need not seek elsewhere for abiding or cessation.

(This section constitutes the essential summary for transcending signs. One should not give rise to the mind by abiding in form (*rūpa*); one should not give rise to the mind by abiding in sound, odor, taste, touch, or mental phenomena (*dharma*). One should give rise to the mind that is non-abiding.
[Commentary on the intent of the question: If the mind has a dwelling place, it is precisely a non-dwelling.
As it is said: "To resolve the mind by departing from signs means that the mind thus resolved is a mind that dwells nowhere."

When there is arising, there is birth. Therefore, one should not give rise to the mind by dwelling on forms; one should not give rise to the mind by dwelling on sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or dharmas.
It is appropriate to give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere. The two phrases regarding "not dwelling on forms" have already been seen above;
here they are restated to clarify that one should not give rise to the mind with a point of attachment, and that this is what one should not do.

There is a mind that dwells; this subtle nuance differs slightly from what was said previously. The earlier statement, "One should give rise to the mind while having nothing to dwell upon," might lead people to perceive two distinct layers:
a mind that does not dwell, and furthermore, a mind that is produced. This would result in a departure from purity. Therefore, it is stated directly:
"give rise to a mind that has nothing to dwell upon. This means to give rise to this very mind which is fundamentally without any place of dwelling.
The mind need not be generated by dwelling nowhere. What was previously stated—that one should not dwell on appearances and that one should dwell as instructed—is fundamentally one in meaning.
The principle of this unity is elucidated here by the statement: "If the mind dwells anywhere, it is non-dwelling.
Dayuan said: "To be free from the four marks of self, person, sentient being, and life, one must first be free from..."
The six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) and the four marks of self and person (*ātma-pudgala-catur-lakṣaṇa*) arise from dwelling in and clinging to the six sense objects.
"One should not dwell on form and so forth" is an admonition against practicing while giving rise to a mind attached to the arising of marks (*nimitta*).

"One should practice with no place of dwelling" is an exhortation to practice while remaining free from the arising of marks. "If the mind has a dwelling, it is precisely non-dwelling" means that [dwelling] upon form is [in truth] non-dwelling.
...and so forth. That is to say, one does not abide in awakening. Between entering this and exiting that, at the slightest interval, one must be careful.
Therefore, the Buddha said: "A bodhisattva’s mind should not abide in form when practicing giving.
Subhūti, for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, a bodhisattva should practice giving in this manner. (The word "for the sake of" [故] is absent from various editions.)

Shengyun says: "One should not abide in form while practicing giving. Furthermore, this follows the principle of not abiding when generating the mind of awakening, concluding by returning to the fundamental intent of being free from marks (*nimitta*).

This character "form" (*rūpa*) should be understood simply as the character "mark. As Ruru said: "This character 'form' includes within it sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental phenomena (*dharmas*).
Previously, it was stated that one practices giving without abiding in marks; now, it is stated again that one does not abide...
When the mind arises in relation to form and so forth, this refers to the mind not dwelling upon form and so forth; that is, giving while not dwelling on form.
This integrates the two meanings from the preceding text. The preceding text explained in detail the departure from all marks until reaching the state where nothing is not empty.
Fearing that emptiness might give rise to attachment, [the Buddha] then used his own realization of non-arising as the very essence of the Buddha’s...
Being detached from all marks, he sets aside all sentient beings; therefore, he calls out urgently to demonstrate this.
"Bestowal" refers to the gift of the Dharma. "To deliver sentient beings" means to benefit them.
Fearing that practitioners might mistake the absence of deliverance for nihilistic emptiness, the Buddha uses the two characters "benefit" to point toward the ultimate reality.
It must surely benefit others' merit and virtue, and increase others' wisdom; only when its function is truly realized does one achieve nirvana.
This is the measure of the Bodhisattva’s great vows and the foundation for encouraging cultivation. The preceding passage’s departure from all marks was intended for this very purpose.
Because sentient beings dwell in attachment to the sense organs and their objects, he extensively carries out transformation and guidance. If...
Regarding the giver: they first possess a mind of attachment. How, then, can one transform that attached mind? It is for this reason that one must resolutely practice such giving;
only then will one’s own nature attain the merit of pure non-action, and sentient beings likewise receive the benefit of pure non-action.
The Tathāgata has said that all marks are, in fact, no-marks; he has also said that all sentient beings are, in fact, no-sentient-beings.
Dayuan said: "Have you not heard the words of the Tathāgata, who taught that one should practice giving while remaining detached from marks? The Tathāgata...
It is taught that all marks arise from causes and conditions and are entirely provisional combinations;
thus, a mark is itself no-mark. All sentient beings are without exception children of the Buddha: when deluded they are sentient beings, but upon awakening they are no longer sentient beings;
birth is itself no-birth. Now, since a mark is already no-mark, what form or characteristic could there be for one to dwell upon when practicing generosity? Since sentient beings...
It is not a sentient being. How could a dāna characterized by marks benefit it? [Commentary on the Collection:

Furthermore, this explains the *dharmatā*—the nature of phenomena—in which both the ordinary being (*sattva*) and the Buddha share a common source, and which is originally quiescent and extinguished, because there is nothing to be dwelt upon in either appearance or marks.
[Correct Explanation: All marks are the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*); that is, they are non-marks. This reveals the Dharma.
"Emptiness. All sentient beings are the realm of persons; they are, in fact, not [substantial] sentient beings. This reveals the emptiness of the person (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).
Yet, these two characteristics—person and phenomena—are fundamentally empty and non-existent. Sentient beings do not know this and falsely cling to them as being existent.

That which the Tathāgata speaks is intended to cause them to realize this and thereby abandon such clinging. ○ The *Jingguan* (Mirror of the Sutra) states: "This section concludes the preceding and initiates the subsequent. The Tathāgata..."
The two phrases "all marks" [refer to] the preceding point that a bodhisattva should be detached from all marks; they serve to conclude the meaning that all such marks are not marks.

The two phrases "all sentient beings" [refer to] the fact that, following the detailed explanation above regarding the benefit of sentient beings, there is a concern that people might again give rise to the notion of a "sentient being";
therefore, the word "all" (衆) is raised once more to clarify this thoroughly, concluding the previous discussion on parinirvāṇa.
"Immeasurable sentient beings"—in truth, there is no intention of their being extinguished. "All marks are non-marks" means that all marks do not belong to the original nature;
one departs from them. Since they are originally absent in the original nature, they are called "non-marks.
One should not dwell upon them, for fundamentally there is nothing upon which to dwell. "All sentient beings are non-sentient beings" means that each clarifies their own original nature.
The nature that is free from all marks is precisely the Buddhas.
Subhūti, the Tathāgata speaks what is true, speaks what is real, speaks according to reality, speaks without deception, and speaks without deviation.
Subhūti, as for the Dharma attained by the Tathāgata, this Dharma is neither real nor unreal. (This clarifies the intent of the question.)

The Buddha feared that people might fail to accord with the principle of formlessness, or that they might harbor doubts, thinking that as the Buddha’s words progress, they become increasingly profound.
Therefore, he used five statements to strengthen people's faith: these words are true, without falsehood or delusion;

these words are suchness (tathatā), acceding with the principle of True Suchness (bhūtatathatā); they are not deceptive words, nor are they words of change or anomaly; they all speak of non-existence.
To ascend to Bodhi is for people to awaken to the Buddha-dharma. Ruru said: "The Dharma spoken by the Tathāgata is the very Dharma attained by the Tathāgata.
Previously it was said that one should not grasp at dharmas; why then speak of attaining the Dharma?
It is because that which is not one's own is grasping, while returning to what belongs to oneself is attainment. This mind is empty and void.
Profoundly empty. All dharmas arise from this. To grasp at them is to lose the source of their emptiness; when the mind is lost, the dharmas are lost.
Without grasping, one returns to my original ground of purity; when the mind is attained, the dharmas are attained.

This term "dharma" (fa) should be seen as distinct from minor dharmas. Previously, I spoke of "empty space" and "emptiness" (xu wang), fearing that if one clings to these, they will become an obstruction.

Regarding reality, one speaks of generating true faith, saying that this is reality. Fearing that attachment to this might again obstruct the understanding of the empty, one further says, together with emptiness, that it is "neither real nor unreal. This is what is called the Dharma-gate of Non-duality. Dayuan said:
"This is precisely the Tathāgatagarbha which is both empty and not empty. Because it is not [merely] real, the six perfections are practiced concurrently, and..."
The mind does not abide in existence; because it is not non-existent, it is free from all marks (*lakṣaṇa*). Yet, phenomena have never fallen into non-existence.
When concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) proceed in equal measure, and stillness and response are unified, this is precisely the wondrous realm of Bodhi.
This is what the Buddha attained; this is what he taught. Li said: "This Dharma is this very mind. That which is without reality is the mind."

The essence is empty and quiescent; that which is not void does not exist. Its wondrous function has no fixed direction. Chengyun said: "Dharma" refers to the unconditioned Dharma of True Suchness (*tathatā*).

Since the essence of Dharma is empty and quiescent, and no characteristics can be apprehended, it is said to be "without reality. Yet, non-characteristic is itself characteristic; because there is the substance of true emptiness, it is said to be "not void.
One must not cling to existence by means of words, nor must one cling to non-existence by departing from words.

This is precisely non-abiding. Master Padmasambhava said: "The two characters 'emptiness' (xu) and 'reality' (shi), when spoken of together, possess profound flavor. From within emptiness, one contemplates the actual reality;
from within reality, one contemplates the principle of emptiness. When emptiness and reality manifest in relation to one another, they constitute the wondrous Dharma of the Tathāgata."
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva dwells with a mind fixed on phenomena while practicing giving, it is like a person entering darkness who sees nothing at all.
If a bodhisattva practices giving— referring here specifically to the gift of Dharma— with a mind that does not dwell on phenomena, it is like a person with eyes who,
when the sun shines brightly, sees all manner of forms.
The Commentary says: "The Dharma of the Tathāgata is neither false nor real; it exists for the purpose of benefiting sentient beings.
If so, when a Bodhisattva benefits others through the practice of giving, can they abide in that dharma?

As for "dharma," it refers to all dharmas—both mundane and supramundane—that transform sentient beings. The preceding text repeatedly speaks of being detached from all marks (*lakṣaṇa*). From [this point]...
"Benefit and merit are fulfilled. From the passage "The Bodhisattva acts for the benefit of all beings" onwards, the text elaborates upon the practice of benefiting others.
It further states: "Darkness refers to the absence of wisdom; light refers to the presence of wisdom. Light and darkness are opposites; they are correlative phenomena (*pratipakṣa*).
When wisdom arises, the absence of wisdom ceases; when light arises, darkness ceases. [The] *Jíjiè* (Compendium of Explanations) notes: "The sun is able to dispel darkness."
As wisdom destroys delusion, so the eye can see emptiness; as wisdom realizes principle, these two metaphors merge into a single wisdom.
(O) This is the third section, a summary exhortation. Above, it was stated that this Dharma is neither real nor false;
having already seen that there is nothing in the Dharma to grasp, he now demonstrates the gain and loss of abiding in non-abiding. The body’s lack of abiding arises from...
Because the mind has no abiding, one investigates its source and speaks of it in terms of the mind. To abide is to cling to signs and be obstructed by afflictions;
therefore, it is said that one enters darkness. To have no abiding is for both self and others to be forgotten, so that the light of wisdom shines alone.
Therefore it is said: "various forms.

Subhūti, in a future age, if there are sons of good family or daughters of good family who are able to receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra—[this reference to upholding the sutra serves as the transition to the following section]—then the Tathāgata, by means of the Buddha’s wisdom, will fully know these persons and fully see these persons, all of them.
One attains the accomplishment of immeasurable and boundless merit.
This Dharma of non-abiding is fully explained as being capable of anything—delivering oneself and delivering others—despite existing within this degenerate age.
There are those who uphold and practice [this teaching]; they all abide within the wisdom of the Tathāgata, and he knows and sees them all.

Furthermore, the *Jiegu jing* (Sutra on the Return to the Source) is superior. The commentary on the sutra states that the character "能" (*néng*, "to be able") governs what follows, as both [sections] speak of not abiding in dharmas, which constitutes being a Tathāgata;
and because they equally possess *prajñā*, it is immeasurable and boundless. This is because it is not merely...
He awakens to his own nature and likewise awakens to the nature of others; he does not awaken merely for a single moment, but awakens throughout ten million ages.
He takes the benefit of sentient beings as his merit and the nurturing of bodhi as his virtue.
Pervading the entire dharma-realm without fixed direction, it remains ever-present throughout ten thousand kalpas. How could its accomplishment have any limits or boundaries? Long.

Shuiyun said: "The attainment of True Suchness (tathatā) arises from the purity of the mind; the purity of the mind arises from non-abiding in phenomena; non-abiding in phenomena arises from possessing wisdom;
and possessing wisdom arises from hearing this sutra. One should know that this sutra possesses supreme merit; therefore, it must be praised in order to demonstrate it to those of the future."
△ Above, the efficacy of upholding this sutra has been explained in detail; the sutra is titled *Prajñā*. *Prajñā* takes the deconstruction of marks (*lakṣaṇa*) as its primary function.
By not dwelling upon marks, one gives rise to the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). The Venerable One personally recounts his realization and understanding, praising those who believe in the sutra.
The true mark is the departure from all marks; its merit is rare and extraordinary. It is because of this principle of departing from marks that the Buddha [expounds this teaching].
To express this in its ultimate sense: taking patience and giving as examples to illustrate the rest, the teaching shows that practice arises from understanding.
Within each of the six *pāramitās*, one should generate the mind of awakening by detaching from all signs (*nimitta*) for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.

This single path is reiterated and clarified again and again, inferring that because all signs are non-existent, there is nothing upon which to dwell; thus, it enables the practitioner to know the proper object of their endeavor. And...
"Neither real nor unreal"—this encapsulates the essential purport of this sutra. Furthermore, it borrows the metaphor of entering a dark place with a light to illustrate the superiority of the sutra;
thus, one truly knows that the dharmas of the mind have no abiding place. How could the Tathāgata’s teaching possibly be erroneous?
Those who receive, uphold, read, and recite it, if they can suddenly awaken to their own mind as empty tranquility without abiding, will not concern themselves with the marks of form.
Seeking to bring benefit to the entirety of the *sāhasra-lokadhātu*, one proceeds from nature (*prakṛti*) toward cultivation (*bhāvanā*); this is the true nature of merit.

From the initial arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) until this point, there is nothing that is not subdued, and nothing that is not *bodhi*. From the fifth section onward, up to this section, it is titled "The Cessation of All Buddhas.
This is, in its entirety, the seeing of the Buddha through the departure from signs (*nimitta*). From this section onward, it arises in such and such a manner.
This concludes the sixteenth section, collectively titled "The Correspondence of Practice and Understanding.
○ Section Ten-Five: "The Merit of Upholding the Sūtra.
The merit of upholding this sūtra is difficult to measure. ○ This section correctly explains the excellence of the merit of upholding the sūtra.

The preceding chapter uses the four lines beginning with "By means of the Buddha’s wisdom" as its main framework. The subsequent sections each follow from the preceding one, culminating in the inconceivable.
Regarding the instruction to explain it for others: the former statement says that sacrificing one's life is not equal to upholding this sutra;
to speak briefly, the latter statement says that the meaning of the sutra is profound and subtle, beyond the capacity of those with inferior faculties to bear.

"Ho. This correctly explains the reason for the superiority of merit. Regarding the passage "In every place," it says that wherever there is a whole-body relic of the Buddha, people should show it reverence.
Juefei said: "One who sacrifices their body in giving cannot yet perceive their true nature."

The retribution of karmic results is finite. However, the Mahāyāna sūtras teach that by directly perceiving one's nature and explaining it for the sake of the multitude, one immediately becomes a bearer of the Buddha-dharma;
this is because such merit resides within one's own inherent nature.
Subhūti, if there were good sons or good daughters who, during the first part of the day, gave as many bodies in charity as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River;
and during the middle part of the day, again gave as many bodies in charity as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River;

and during the latter part of the day, likewise gave as many bodies in charity as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River—this extensively explains the meaning of upholding this sutra—and if they were to give their bodies in charity in this manner for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of kalpas. If...

Furthermore, if there are those who, upon hearing this sutra, believe with a mind as pure as described before and do not oppose it—as previously stated, they are not startled, terrified, or afraid—their merit shall surpass that of the former.
How much more so for those who copy, uphold, read, recite, and explain it to others (as later stated: "to undertake this Dharma and circulate this sutra").

In the former case, although one upholds the Dharma according to the law, the merit is not supreme because it still arises from cultivating the realization of nature, rather than arising from nature itself to cultivate.
Now, however, the mind does not dwell upon dharmas, yet one fully upholds the entire sutra; thus, boundless merits are all accomplished.
This is the inconceivable path-dharma of the Mahāyāna. Therefore, [the Buddha] called out to Subhūti and said:
He informed him: "The first day," "the middle day," and "the final day" refer to a single day, meaning the three periods of morning, midday, and evening.
"Ganges sands" expresses their great number; "immeasurable kalpas" expresses their great duration; both are metaphors. One should simply sacrifice one's body and life.

If one cannot see one's nature, one still remains subject to the causes of outflowing karma. However, upon hearing this sutra and gaining faith, one suddenly sees one’s own nature and practices with single-minded resolve, never again regressing.
Such a person attains the merit of Prajñā, which far surpasses the merit of giving one's life;
how much more so when they can further explain it to others, leading all people to practice by arising from their own nature—its boundless [merit] is beyond compare.
"Are these merits conceivable? Are they measurable? Chen Xiong said:

"The Buddha feared that people of the world would cling to the teaching of the Tathāgata’s patience and merely practice the giving of the body, thereby providing not the slightest benefit to one's own nature or the nature of others.
Therefore, he spoke of it in thirteen sections; having reached this point, he speaks again, repeatedly saving [beings]."
Regarding its loss: [the following section] then deduces the reasons why its merit is superior.
Subhūti, to state it briefly, this sutra possesses inconceivable, immeasurable, and boundless merit.
The excellence of a person’s merit arises from the excellence of the sutra; yet the excellence of this sutra is beyond the capacity of praise to exhaust.
To state it in brief: the essence of this Prajñā is vast and devoid of names or characteristics; its merits are likewise vast and devoid of names or characteristics.
It cannot be conceived by the mind, nor can it be discussed by the mouth, nor can it be contained within any vessel.
The measure of this Dharma cannot be fathomed by its boundaries; therefore, the Tathāgata did not lightly preach it for others.
It was preached solely for those of great capacity who have resolved to attain Bodhicitta, who follow the Bodhisattva vehicle, and who pursue the Supreme Vehicle.
This sutra is the Prajñāpāramitā of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) as elucidated within its words. As it is said, "The essential is the core."
To respond to capacities does not preclude the employment of provisional means; returning to the source lies in the manifestation of the ultimate reality.

That which is called the Sudden Teaching elucidates non-duality and non-triplicity; words and thought are utterly transcended. This is the essence of the sutra. It is inconceivable, and therefore cannot be measured.
Whether it be the giving of wealth, the giving of one’s body, or contemplation over many kalpas, none can compare to it; thus, its merit is boundless.
The Tathāgata speaks for those who have set out upon the Mahāyāna; he speaks for those who have set out upon the Supreme Vehicle (Agrayāna).
"Mahāyāna" refers to the Bodhisattvayāna. "Supreme Vehicle" refers to the Buddhayāna.
The Śrāvaka understands only birth and death and does not deliver sentient beings; thus it is called the Hīnayāna, like the smaller types of vehicles that can only carry oneself.
The Pratyekabuddha benefits half of others and half of themselves; because those saved are not many, this is called the Middle Vehicle (*madhyayāna*).
The Bodhisattva is able to save all sentient beings; this is the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*). The Buddha is able to save both sentient beings and Bodhisattvas simultaneously;

this is the Supreme Vehicle (*anuttarayāna*). Beyond this, there is no further vehicle. "To set forth" (*fa*) refers to the act of initiating and arousing—meaning to arouse and initiate [the mind of enlightenment].
This vehicle (*yāna*) is for the purpose of delivering sentient beings. Master Padmasambhava said: "Vehicle" refers to a carriage; it takes the sense of traveling a great distance.
Although there are distinctions of great and small, superior, middling, and inferior, as a vehicle they are one and the same.

A vehicle has wheels so that it may be turned and put into motion; therefore, the Dharma is called the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*). To possess the Dharma yet be unable to circulate it is like having...

To "mount" [the vehicle] yet not use it to travel far is what is meant by the term "Mahāyāna" (Great Vehicle); this takes its meaning from the sense of turning the Wheel of Dharma so that it may penetrate everywhere.
As it is said: "To set forth the Mahāyāna and the Supreme Vehicle is precisely to set forth the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
A Bodhisattva is one who has already set forth as a person of the Supreme Vehicle, O son of good family.
A virtuous woman is one who is able to set forth the Supreme Vehicle; sentient beings are those who have not yet set forth the Supreme Vehicle.
Yet, those who have not yet set forth the Supreme Vehicle are in truth those capable of setting it forth.

The Tathāgata has entrusted this to the Bodhisattvas to speak for those who have already set forth the Supreme Vehicle, to speak specifically for those capable of setting forth the Supreme Vehicle, and for those who are able to set it forth.
It is said for those who have already set out on the Supreme Vehicle; it is also said for those who have not yet set out on the Supreme Vehicle.
Therefore, the following text explains this extensively for all people. The Tathāgata knows and sees these people completely.
If there are those who can receive, uphold, read, recite, and extensively explain this for others, the Tathāgata fully knows these people and fully sees these people;
they shall all achieve immeasurable, incomparable, boundless, and inconceivable merit.
As it is said: "To receive, uphold, read, and recite [the teachings] is for one's own benefit; to explain them extensively to others is for the benefit of others.

One's own benefit is the root of benefiting others, and benefiting others is the actualization of one's own benefit. Only when self and other are non-dual does one possess the mind-measure of the Supreme Vehicle (Agryayāna).
To explain them extensively to others is precisely because one desires to cause others to receive and uphold them just as one has done oneself. This is indeed [the practice of] non-..."
One attains the accomplishment of merit by means of the marks of self, person, and so forth, through the salvation of sentient beings.

As for the statement that the Tathāgata "knows all and sees all," it is because the mind of this person who extensively preaches for others is identical to the Tathāgata’s mind in generating the aspiration to preach the Supreme Vehicle;
they are equal and universal in this regard. According to the meaning of the sutra, this must proceed from the essence (*tattva*).
Because its function is pervasive, it is itself inconceivable, extending to the incalculable, the immeasurable, and the boundless.

Speaking in terms of human accomplishment, since the essence is manifested through its function, it is itself immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless, ultimately returning to the inconceivable; thus, all four [perfections] are fully accomplished.
Regarding the phrase [“...with merit”], it corresponds to the first accomplished merit mentioned in the preceding text.
Regarding the two phrases below, “[such a person as this]...,” which speak of the Dharma, they correspond to the supreme Dharma accomplished in the preceding text.
Such persons as these shall indeed bear the burden of the Tathāgata’s *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Why is this? Subhūti, those who delight in inferior dharmas—being attached to the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, and the view of a life-span (to clarify this further by stating the opposite)—will be unable to hear, receive, read, recite, or explain this sūtra for others.
Ruru said: "The *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of the Tathāgata is what is called the Mahāyāna Dharma, the supreme Dharma.
Why do you not say that he has attained *bodhi* for himself, but instead say that he 'shoulders the *bodhi* of the Tathāgata'?"
The Buddha feared that Śūnyatā-prabhava might mistake his realization of *bodhi* for a personal attainment of a virtuous fruit.
Therefore, he showed that *bodhi* fundamentally originates from the Tathāgata, thereby demonstrating the core principle of the transmission of the True Dharma.

That the Tathāgata’s protective mindfulness and entrustment are solely for the sake of seeking one who can shoulder this burden—the meaning of "shouldering" arises from the character for "vehicle" (*yāna*). Yet, this vehicle is that which carries one to the state of Buddhahood.

The Dharma-realm. To shoulder and carry forth the Buddha’s Dharma-realm upon one's own person, becoming one upon whom all Buddhas rely—until all beings are saved and Buddhahood is attained, there shall be no day of resting the shoulders.
How could those who delight in inferior dharmas ever reach such a state? The three phrases concerning "delighting in inferior dharmas" provide a reverse explanation of the Supreme Vehicle.
Thus one is able to be signless (*animitta*). To be signless and yet to be able to receive, uphold, explain, and expound [the Dharma] is the perfection of merit.

What was previously called the "mark of self" (*ātman-lakṣaṇa*) is here called the "view of self" (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*); this is an even more acute source of affliction. That human beings transmigrate through the cycle of birth and death is due to the existence of deluded views.
Where there is viewing, there is grasping; where there is grasping, there is attachment; where there is attachment, signs are formed. Therefore, deluded views are further termed "delusion."
The root of signs consists of four kinds of views; by these, one cannot perceive various forms.
Subhūti, wherever this sutra may be found, it should be venerated by all the world, including devas, humans, and asuras.
You should know that such a place is itself a stupa; everyone should pay homage, prostrate, and circumambulate it with reverence.
One should scatter various flowers and incense upon that place.
The merit contained within this sutra is inconceivable. How could one treat with contempt the place where this sutra resides?
Within this sutra, the entire bodies of all Buddhas are present; wherever it is circulated, that very place is the eternal abiding of the Dharmakāya. Therefore, for all...

Wherever this sutra resides, there is a Buddha. Therefore, all devas, humans, and asuras ought to pay inner reverence and offer outer worship at that place, scattering various precious flowers and exquisite incenses throughout it.
To revere that place is to revere the Dharma. If even the location where the Dharma resides is worthy of reverence, then...
How much more so for those who uphold the Dharma! Therefore, one who maintains and expounds it with faith is able to shoulder the burden of Bodhi;
compared to this, even giving away one's body as an offering throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas would not suffice. [The preceding section] spoke of stupas and temples.
This refers to the place where the sutras are expounded; this is the place where the sutras exist. Each has its own distinction, and collectively they are called the "Excellence of the Sutras.

The previous mention of the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) was explained in terms of the six objects (*viṣaya*), which is still coarse. This present mention of the four views (*dṛṣṭi*) is explained in terms of the six faculties (*indriya*), which is somewhat more subtle.
△ This fourth comparison concludes with the teaching of its superiority. If one possesses faith and does not oppose it, one immediately attains merit and virtue;
how much more so for those who circulate this sutra and undertake this Dharma, thereby enabling people to see their true nature?
However, a great Dharma requires a great capacity; therefore, it is revered and honored as the Mahāyāna, the Supreme Vehicle.
For the Buddha takes it as his own responsibility to deliver sentient beings through the preaching of the Dharma, bearing this great burden upon his person.
If such a person can awaken the human heart, benefiting both self and others, and cause the Dharma to abide for a long time, then they directly shoulder the great burden of the Tathāgata.
This is not something that those of the Hīnayāna can rival. Wherever this sutra is present, it is as if the Buddha himself is there;

among the devas and humans of the triple world, there are none who do not pay homage to it. How much more so for one who can thus receive and uphold it, and thus expound it extensively—how could the merit thereof have any limit?
This section speaks twice of merit: the former refers to the inherent power within the sutra itself.
"Virtue" (*guṇa*). The subsequent statement refers to the merits accomplished by a person. Zongtong says: "To receive, uphold, read, and recite [the teachings] is the practice for one's own benefit;
to explain them extensively for others is the practice for the benefit of others. By practicing both benefits simultaneously, one can ensure that the lineage of the Buddhas is not severed;
therefore, it is called 'shouldering the burden. One who practices the bodhisattva path transforms those below through great compassion and [benefits others] through great wisdom."

Seeking the supreme goal, one should practice with great vows in union. Upon the shoulders of diligence, remaining unstuck from moment to moment, one must ensure that oneself and others are liberated together;
only then shall one lay down this burden.
Chapter Sixteen: The Section on Purifying Karmic Obstructions.
Purifying the mind through upholding [this sutra] can eliminate karmic obstructions. To elaborate, the merit of upholding this sutra is inconceivable.
Juefei said: "The first sixteen sections point to form as emptiness; the latter sixteen sections point to..."

Emptiness is form. The former [section] refutes attachment to the self; the latter refutes attachment to phenomena. If one does not understand the meaning of the sutra, this constitutes being entangled in karmic obstructions.
If one can purify the mind and uphold the sutra, one will directly perceive one's nature; not only will karma be extinguished, but one shall attain right enlightenment.
How could this be comparable to making offerings to the Buddhas? This is a general statement that the merit is inconceivable.
The first section speaks of the inconceivability of the extinction of offenses; the second section speaks of the inconceivability of the realization of the fruit;
and the final section summarizes the inconceivability. These two phrases of the sūtra’s meaning constitute the conclusion within the conclusion.
Furthermore, Subhūti, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family receives, maintains, reads, and recites this sutra, yet is treated with contempt by others,
it is because of the karmic seeds of offenses committed in their previous lives that they ought to have fallen into the evil realms.
The three evil paths are those of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals; they are the sufferings of the three realms of misery (*tricāṭu*). "Previous lives" refers to past births.
Some say that having committed evil in the past and now turning toward goodness in the present is merely changing one's circumstances within this world;
this is also considered an ancillary reference to previous lives. The Sixth Patriarch said: "Speaking in terms of principle, 'previous lives' refers to the deluded thoughts of the past."
"Mind. "The present life. This refers to the mind that awakens in the subsequent moment; this is the method for practicing cultivation.
It should not be used as an exegetical commentary on the scriptural text. People who do not contemplate its essence merely speak of these four characters in terms of abstract principle.
Because they are now treated with contempt by the people of this world, their sinful karmic obstructions from previous lives will be immediately extinguished,
and they shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Regarding the merit of upholding this sutra, one is already revered by devas and humans; yet, if one is instead treated with contempt by worldly people, this must be the result of karma from previous lives.
Such a person should have fallen into the evil realms, but having merely encountered contempt, their heavy punishment has been lightened to a mild reprimand.
According to the meaning of this section of the sutra, it is specifically taught for those who cultivate wholesome dharmas yet receive an evil retribution; [the author] fears that...
Because those who do not understand their past karma may retreat from the mind of enlightenment, [the Buddha] therefore reveals to them as well that they can attain Bodhi.
Master Padmasambhava said: "This further opens a gateway for self-renewal for those of the Lesser Vehicle. As Ruru said:
"One who would have fallen into the evil realms now merely suffers contempt from others; this is the power of upholding this sutra. By means of this present...
The single phrase, "Because worldly people treat me with contempt," contains great merit and practice in patience.
Only when one can feel compassion for others does one no longer perceive their contempt; it is precisely through this practice that I manifest my mind of guidance and salvation.
Completely forgetting the mark of self, one benefits others with such thorough dedication; only then is one a person capable of bearing the burden.

Not only does this mean not hiding filth or accepting impurity, but it also means not seeking retribution for those who act without the Way. Therefore, by entering the gate of merit, the transgressions and karmic offenses of previous lives are extinguished;
by entering the gate of wisdom, one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Subhūti, I recall that in the past, immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas—
asaṃkhyeya being the Chinese term for "innumerable," and kalpa meaning "eon" or "world-age"— ago.
"Before the Buddha Dīpaṃkara" means prior to encountering the Buddha Dīpaṃkara; during that time,
he met eight hundred and forty thousand million nayutas of Buddhas.
*Nayuta* is the Chinese term for ten million times ten million. *Zhi* means "to encounter.
He encountered them all and made offerings and served them, none passing by in vain.
He offered them incense, flowers, banners, lamps, silk canopies, clothing, food, and other such items, and furthermore, with his own body...
He served them as an attendant at their side, never passing by a single Buddha in vain.

Furthermore, if there should be someone in the future final age who is able to receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, the merit they obtain would not equal even one-hundredth part of the merit from my own offerings to all those Buddhas;
nor one-thousandth, nor ten-thousandth, nor one-hundred-thousandth, nor one-billionth, nor even by calculation...
It cannot be reached by calculation or analogy.
Guṇadatta said: "The merit of making offerings to the Buddha does not lead to the realization of reality; however, by upholding this Dharma-gate, one quickly attains such realization.
World-Honored One, it was only after making offerings to countless Buddhas and passing through countless kalpas that [the Buddha] attained Buddhahood; yet now, by merely upholding this sutra..."
One attains Bodhi, surpassing the vast number of eons required for a Tathāgata; therefore, it is called "swift realization.

The previous mention of attaining Bodhi was spoken for those with heavy karmic offenses, as they shall be able to become Buddhas in a future life through this sutra’s power to extinguish sins and their diligent practice;
this present statement of "swift realization of Bodhi" is spoken for those without offenses, who, through this sutra, awaken to faith and thereby transcend directly.
This is the stage of the Tathāgata. The Tathatā says: The Buddha again deprecates himself in order to manifest the merit of upholding [this teaching].
One who makes offerings serves immeasurable Buddhas; one who does not know how to uphold it carries the burden of a single Tathāgata.
This statement that making offerings does not equal upholding is not because the Buddha is inferior to people of the末 (mo) age.
"Receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting," which includes "explaining them to others," were previously all compared in terms of *puṇya* (merit).

Here, however, it speaks of *guṇa* (virtue) rather than *puṇya*. This is because the fruit of *puṇya* resides within one's own person, whereas the preservation and salvation brought about by *guṇa* extends to other beings.
Since a Bodhisattva undertakes cultivation for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, they take this preservation and salvation as their primary aim.
As for the karmic fruit, Subhūti, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra during the final age at the end of time,
the merit they would thereby obtain— if I were to describe it in its entirety (meaning to exhaustively describe it), some who hear it might have their minds become deranged or fall into doubt.
