This means that because it is free from the marks of mental objects, free from the marks of verbal expression, and free from the marks of names and designations, its retribution is like the fruit of bodhi;
it cannot be sought through the mind, names, words, or speech. People of inferior faculties may not necessarily be able to penetrate the meaning of signlessness;
how then could they know that its merit is so immense? For this reason, on the contrary—
Doubts arise. When the Buddha speaks thus, it is precisely because he hopes for firm faith from those who find it difficult to believe.
Therefore, he concludes by stating that one should understand the meaning of the sutra as follows: "The various marks are not marks; they are the substance of empty space."
When sentient beings hear these words, they give rise to true faith and pure faith; their upholding of the merit is the effect of genuine practice.
Why is it that in the final age, upon hearing such teachings, some become deranged, harbor doubts, and do not believe?
To see the signless is to see the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). When one is free from signs, the mind is sealed [in realization]. To speak exhaustively of the merits is itself to be attached to signs.
To be attached to marks is to delude the mind; such frantic confusion and doubt are signs of impurity within the heart.

This is why the Buddha taught people that they should truly cultivate merit, yet not allow the mind to be distracted by or obsessed with merit. To realize the Dharma-body and attain Bodhi constitutes the fruit;
to realize the two bodies of retribution and response and obtain blessings and virtue constitutes the reward. The meaning of the sutra is inconceivable.
[Discourse on] the deliberation. Therefore, the retribution of the fruit is likewise inconceivable. This reveals that the Mahāyāna does not seek retribution as its goal.
△ This is the fifth comparison. Previously it was said that upholding the sutra gains merit; here it is said that one may also extinguish transgressions.
Even for those with past karma, this may be granted to those of superior capacity. In total, it is seen that there is no person and no ground [where this does not apply]; it is most supreme.
It is only the sutra. Furthermore, he again cites his own past causes to compare them with the superiority of the sutra:

"Though one were to make offerings to many Buddhas, it would not suffice to equal even a ten-thousandth part of this. This is the ultimate comparison and the pinnacle of measure; beyond this, both praise and comparison cease entirely.
Therefore, it is concluded with the phrase "inconceivable. [Note: Sin and merit have always been relative. To speak of merit while omitting sin means this doubt will not be resolved.
Furthermore, the nature of sin is fundamentally empty; if one can merely receive and uphold [the teaching], giving rise to a pure mind, karmic obstructions will naturally find no place to settle.
One will directly perceive one's nature, and not only will sin be extinguished, but one shall attain the Unconditioned.
[This concludes] the ascent to Bodhi. From "To state it briefly" up to this point, the supreme excellence of the signless (animitta) within the Mahāyāna, the most supreme vehicle, has been clarified.

All the merits of receiving and upholding [this teaching] arise from the sutra. If a person can give rise to the resolve for enlightenment while remaining detached from signs, [they shall attain these merits].
To uphold and extensively expound this [teaching] is more vastly different from those who delight in inferior dharmas than the distance between heaven and earth.

To accomplish such merit, to shoulder the burden of the Tathāgata, to extinguish sinful karma, and to attain perfect enlightenment—how could these be measured by the offerings made to the various Buddhas?
This is because, in total, the meaning of the sutra cannot be grasped through mere appearances; therefore, its karmic retribution likewise cannot be fathomed through appearances.
The excellence of the signless is manifest.

(Above is the total count) There are eight stages of investigation: first, seeing the Tathāgata by means of his physical marks (*pañcavastuka*); second, the Tathāgata attaining the Dharma and preaching it (*saptavastuka*);
third, realizing and preaching the four fruits [of the śrāvaka path] (*navavastuka*); fourth, receiving the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*); fifth, adorning the land; sixth, the great... [text fragment].
Body. (Ten parts each) Seven Tathāgatas have preached the Dharma. Eight [parts] of the atoms of the trichiliocosm. (Thirteen parts each).
There are three successive exhortations: first, one should thus give rise to a pure mind; one should give rise to that mind by dwelling nowhere.
Second, one should depart from all marks and resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; one should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere.
Third, by introducing the metaphor of illuminating a dark place, it is shown that one should dwell in non-dwelling.
The gains and losses (each consisting of fourteen parts). Five comparisons:
first, the gift of jewels throughout a great trichiliocosm (eight parts); second, the gift of jewels throughout worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges (eleven parts);
third, the gift of body and life throughout worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges (thirteen parts); fourth, three times a day for one day with the [sands of the] Ganges...
The gift of one's own body and life, such as [the offering of] sand and so forth (Fifteen Sections); the merit of making the fivefold offerings to all Buddhas (Sixteen Sections).
Up to this point, there is nothing further to be compared or discussed; the merit of the signless (*animitta*) is superior. The meaning [of this section] is thus exhausted.
Subsequent comparisons are all intended for other purposes, serving merely to sever doubts; they do not specifically treat the superiority of this sūtra.
The above constitutes the first half of the volume, which discusses the Dharma of Prajñā. The following constitutes the second half of the volume, which clarifies the true reality of Prajñā:
the selflessness of dharmas (*dharmanairātmya*).
The Great Master Yunqi said: "The meaning of this sutra is free from the marks of mental objects and free from the marks of verbal expression;

therefore, to direct the mind toward it is already a deviation, and to stir a thought is already an error. Even if one were to seal the mouth and forget words, one would still remain stuck in the state of indeterminate *prajñā*.
To speak of the mutual forgetting of person and dharma is still not yet the inconceivable point. Thus spoke Śūnyatā-jāti.
Furthermore, they do not understand that it does not reach this point. Therefore, the subsequent text asks again about the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*).
This precisely proceeds from the inconceivable. *The Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Volume One.
In the second fascicle of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Dayuan states:
"The first half of the text requires that one leave behind signs (*nimitta*) to see the Buddha; the second half requires that one penetrate the selflessness (*anātman*) of all phenomena.
If one does not leave behind signs to see the Buddha, one cannot penetrate the selflessness of phenomena. If one does not penetrate [this], [one cannot realize it].
One realizes that all phenomena are without self, yet one cannot personally realize a Buddha who is devoid of marks. Juefei said:
"The first half of the volume purely discusses *prajñā*; the second half clarifies the non-self of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*). This is the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) of true *prajñā*.
Supreme Perfect Enlightenment is the designation for the fulfillment of the fruit of conditions and the total exhaustion of one's original nature."
This is precisely the *gotra* (spiritual lineage) inherent within each person.

The *prajñā-dharma* (wisdom-dharma) is nothing other than the self-contained awakening and illumination within that *gotra*, reflecting back upon one's own inherent *gotra*; there is no separate dharma.

Therefore, by giving rise to one’s own mind from within the *gotra*, there is no "self" of a mind that seeks dharmas. By attaining one’s own *dharmatā* (the true nature of phenomena) from within the *gotra*, [one realizes this].
There is no self that receives the prediction of enlightenment through the attainment of dharmas. There is no self of unadorned non-action who cultivates wondrous conduct upon the lineage (gotra).

When one penetrates the dharma of non-self, the mind is empty across the three periods of time; this is the non-existence of a self-mind. When the Dharma-realm universally transforms, there is no self-merit.
Being detached from form and detached from marks, there is no self of form and marks. This is not something to be spoken of.
It is not attained; there is no self that attains it. To practice goodness with a pure mind is the non-self of action.

To transform others where there is nothing to transform is the non-self of deliverance. Form and sound are not the self; annihilation is not the self; there is no self of either permanence or cessation.
Knowing that all phenomena are without self, one attains the stage of patience (*kṣānti*). Thus, within the Dharmakāya and the Dharmadhātu, there is ultimately no self;
the nature of singular, luminous emptiness is revealed. Reaching this point, the myriad dharmas are as they are (*tathatā*);

all delusions are subdued without being forcibly suppressed, and the true mind abides without abiding. The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, which is the very nature of selfhood, cannot be fully expounded even through extensive explanation. Hereafter—

This constitutes the general purport of the first half of the fascicle. Regarding the *Jijie* (Collected Explanations): the former discourse concerns the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*), while the latter concerns the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*).

What is termed the "selflessness of persons" refers to the severing of the afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi-heya-kleśa*); what is termed the "selflessness of phenomena" refers to the severing of the afflictions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya-kleśa*).
In Subhūti’s initial inquiry, there was a predominance of the intent to subdue the innate grasping at a self (*sahaja-ātma-grāha*); as for his subsequent inquiry...

The primary intent is to subdue the innate grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*). Regarding the two types of grasping—those at the self (*ātman*) and those at phenomena—the term "innate" (*sahaja*) is used because they arise simultaneously with birth.
This is the correct interpretation. Śūnyatā-saṃbhava again raised the previous question according to principle, and the Buddha answered as before.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "there is truly no dharma that gives rise to the mind," if one sees that even the mind that gives rise [to awakening] is non-existent as a dharma, how much less could there be a dharma for subduing the mind or abiding in the mind? Subhūti’s mind seeking the Dharma has not yet been transformed;
this is because his subtle attachment to my Dharma has not been forgotten. The Buddhas directly excise this from its very root, saying: "In truth, there is nothing."

There is a dharma: my subtle attachment to dharmas has been completely eradicated without remainder. From this point until the twenty-fifth section, it is collectively titled "Forgetting Dharmas and Realizing Suchness."
Chapter Seventeen: Ultimate Non-Self. Directly and immediately ultimate:
fundamentally, there is no essence of self. This section reiterates the principle previously explained to clarify non-self.
That "non-self" is precisely the absence of the four marks [of existence]. To speak simply of "non-self" is because all four marks are caused by the self.
They arise from the marks; therefore, where there is no self, there are no four marks. There are two meanings to ultimate non-self:
the first is the natural essence (*svabhāva*), and the second is the conditioned phenomenon (*dharma*). The Sūtra relies upon the natural essence to demonstrate to people the conditioned phenomenon.
This is similar to the meaning of "manifesting as sincerity" in the *Zhongyong*. Juefei said: "The myriad..."
All phenomena are empty. There is no self that gives rise to the aspiration for enlightenment; there is no self that descends and abides;

there is no self that delivers sentient beings, bestows predictions of enlightenment, or manifests adornments. If one can penetrate this, only then will one see that all phenomena are without self, and perceive the view of self as primordially pure.
Dayuan said: "This section should be viewed in three parts; in reality, there is nothing [to be grasped]."
From the passage "The Dharma gives rise to bodhicitta" onwards, it is stated that a bodhisattva’s arousal of the mind must be free from signs (*animitta*).

Tracing this back to the original source of the arousal of bodhicitta, there is fundamentally no dharma. This refers to the "Great Body" attained at the stage of the Buddha Natural Lamp (*Svayambhū-pradīpa*);
that is, the Tathāgata attains bodhi through the non-existence of dharmas. This clarifies that the bodhisattva arouses bodhicitta by means of the non-existence of dharmas.

"Furthermore, the Bodhisattva is also like this," and so forth. This states that the Bodhisattva’s deliverance of sentient beings is without self, just as the Buddha’s attainment of Bodhi is without dharmas.
This serves to clarify the meaning that, in reality, there are no sentient beings who attain extinction.
It is solely because one gives rise to Bodhi without dharmas that one delivers sentient beings without self; these are all part of a single, interconnected process.

At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, how should a son of good family or a daughter of good family who has resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* abide? How should they subdue their mind?"
Shengxi (盛釋) explains: Although this Venerable One’s repeated request uses the same wording as his previous inquiry, the meaning is actually different.

How so? He asks how one should abide in order to achieve subjugation (*damana*). Therefore, the latter fascicle extensively answers the subjugation of the mind, because right view regarding abiding is precisely what constitutes the subjugation of the mind.
Dayuan (大圓) says: When Śūnyatā-utpanna (Subhūti) heard the name of the sutra, he should have distanced himself from all [conceptualizations].
If one realizes that both person and phenomena are empty, this is already clear. Yet, reaching this point, one again gives rise to doubt:
"Since one has already detached from signs, how can the mind be aroused? If I wish to detach from this very arousal of bodhicitta as well," [how should I proceed?]
In that case, this mind would have no point of attachment whatsoever. When a bodhisattva practices the six perfections, where could they abide?
Furthermore, even the dharmas by which awakening is generated would be abandoned; thus, there would be no handle for bodhi at all when practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva.
There are many points that are difficult to subdue; how, then, is this mind to be brought under control? For this reason, the previous question is restated.
The Layman Ruru said: "This is identical in meaning to the initial question, though the phrasing differs.
Its intent is that one who has resolved upon Bodhicitta is without grasping, without dwelling, and without attainment, remaining free from all marks until reaching the inconceivable."
When one seeks the single mind, it cannot be found. Who is it that dwells? Who is it that subdues? Where does that dharma reside?
This is to forcibly seek a dharma within the absence of dharma; it gives rise to a new source of doubt rather than reiterating the previous request.
At the time of the initial question, only the arousal of the aspiration was manifested, while dwelling and subduing were not yet understood; therefore, the method of practice was shown.
It is appropriate. When asked again, one fears that the signs of dwelling in quiescence will obscure the mind capable of awakening;
therefore, all such states are swept away together. The previous answer was a response to what was asked; this answer is a negation of what was asked.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "Good sons and good daughters who have resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi should give rise to this thought."

The phrasing of this sentence does not stop here; it runs directly through the following three sentences. These "good sons" and so forth should be understood as referring to those within the stages of a Bodhisattva.
As it is said: "The previous statement that 'one gives rise to a pure mind' and 'gives rise to a mind that dwells nowhere' is sufficient to manifest the wondrous state of the mind.
However, one must fear that if one clings to even a single mark of purity, that itself is impurity."
To be attached to the mark of "dwelling nowhere" is itself to dwell; therefore, one must dissolve both extremes and speak of "giving rise to such a mind.
This non-differentiation is called "Suchness" (tathatā), and this non-contradiction is called "is-ness" (asti). It is the "is-ness" of the true reality (dharmatā).
When it is said that one "gives rise to the mind of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi," it does not necessarily mean seeking how to dwell or how to subdue.
I submit that one should simply give rise to this thought:
"I ought to bring all sentient beings to parinirvāṇa;
to bring all sentient beings to parinirvāṇa is precisely what a Buddha must do."

"Having brought all sentient beings to parinirvāṇa, not a single sentient being has actually been brought to parinirvāṇa" (this speaks to the meaning of *pudgala-nairātmya*, the selflessness of persons).
These three preceding phrases all refer to this very mind. The Buddha said:
"Regarding sentient beings, I merely cause the various classes of beings to save themselves; there is no dharma that can save, nor is there any being to be saved. This is purity.
The fundamental reality of the true realm and the true mind does not cling to even a hair’s breadth of signs or conceptualization;
therefore, it is said that "in truth, there are none to be liberated. As for the term *tathatā* (suchness): the previous statement, "I shall cause all to attain liberation," reveals his power;

this present statement, "I ought to liberate them," points to his vow. The previous statement, "liberating immeasurable and boundless sentient beings," indicates the vastness of its scale; this present statement...

Having brought sentient beings to extinction (nirvāṇa), its divine merit is such that it was previously stated that "in reality, there are no sentient beings who have been extinguished," which universally demonstrates equality;
here it is said that "not a single sentient being has been extinguished," which subtly expresses the state of total oblivion. Altogether, these are one and the same meaning.
Why is this? Subhūti, if a bodhisattva possesses the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, or the mark of a life-span, they are not a bodhisattva.
To explain further: if one has the thought of "I" saving sentient beings, that is the mark of a self; if there is a sentient being for whom I [act], that is the mark of a person.
The thought of those to be saved is itself the mark of a person (*pudgala-nimitta*). When the marks of self and other multiply, it is the mark of sentient beings (*sattva-nimitta*).
To constantly maintain such thoughts while seeking *nirvāṇa* is the mark of a long-lived being (*jīvaka-nimitta*). One must ensure that these four subtle attachments are completely eradicated;
only then is one truly able to subdue the mind. The previous section concerned the objects of salvation; this concerns the subject who saves.
The mind and its objects are both discarded; how then could dharmas be established? Therefore, it is said below that "in reality there are no dharmas.

Dayuan says: What preceded was the refutation of delusion to reveal wisdom; the delusions refuted were the coarse attachments to the four marks, such as self and person, which belong to Bodhisattvas who have not yet awakened to Prajñā. What follows here is the forgetting of delusion to reveal the principle, refuting...
The subtle grasping at the four marks, such as self and person, belongs to those bodhisattvas who have already realized prajñā after having demolished [the view of self].
As it says in the *Ruru*: "These four marks differ from those mentioned above. The four marks in the preceding passage are the marks of dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*); these four marks..."
This is a mark of non-dharma. The aforementioned mark of self is the mark of parinirvāṇa; this mark of self is the mark of no parinirvāṇa.
Why is this? Subhūti, in reality there is no dharma that sets out for anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Seizing the mind" (this refers to the meaning of the selflessness of phenomena) is described as suchness.
It is said: "The Bodhisattva’s mind is none other than the originally pure ground of awakening of sentient beings.
The nature of awakening is constantly arising; because it is constantly arising, mindfulness can be brought forth. If there were any dharma, it would not be pure. Why? Because...
He gave rise to a pure mind. Śāriputra set aside the question of generating the mind and asked about abiding and descending.
The World-Honored One, in turn, set aside abiding and descending to clarify the generation of the mind. This is not merely clarifying the cause; it is clarifying the fruit within the cause itself.
If the ground is not clarified, all myriad practices will be erroneous. To know that the Bodhicitta is without-dharma and yet generate it, is precisely to know Bodhi.
It cannot be obtained through ordinary means; rather, the entire *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* is subsumed within the four characters "giving rise to such a mind.

If one awakens to the character "giving rise" (*sheng*), one can thereby realize the unarisen (*anutpāda*). Dayuan said: "In the sūtra, the single character 'I' (*aham*) is set forth as the primary focus, stating only:
'I should bring all sentient beings to parinirvāṇa,' without further mentioning giving. From this we know..."

His meritorious practice is already perfected; there remains only the view of "birth" and "Buddha" that has not yet been extinguished. This refers precisely to the subtle attachment to the four marks.
The passage "I should enter parinirvāṇa, yet in reality there is none [to be saved]" clearly demonstrates, in accordance with the truth, the absence of an object to be saved.
The passage "If there were marks such as self or person, one would not be a bodhisattva" conversely demonstrates the absence of a person capable of saving. In reality, there is none...

The "Dharma-awakening mind" (dharmacittotpāda) generally reveals the Dharma that is devoid of subject and object. This is precisely the dwelling of non-dwelling, the descent of non-descent, and the self of non-self;
it is the mind that a bodhisattva ought to generate. If one perceives externally that which is to be saved, [one has not yet realized this].
If there is an internal subject capable of transcending, and the subject and object remain distinct and clear, this deviates from the Way of Non-abiding;
it is not the kind of mind that a Bodhisattva should give rise to. How could this be consistent with equality and non-abiding, within which not a single dharma can be apprehended?
And would one create obstacles for oneself? The subsequent text repeatedly and earnestly emphasizes only the three characters "no dharma" (wǔ yǒu fǎ).
This section places particular weight on this single phrase: if one who has resolved their mind [for enlightenment] perceives a dharma, it is precisely the view of self (ātman-dṛṣṭi).
Subhūti, what do you think? Did the Tathāgata, while in the presence of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, obtain any dharma called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
This Buddha, by means of the fruit of enlightenment he himself realized, bears witness to the bodhicitta generated by that bodhisattva;
therefore, he raises the example of Dīpaṃkara Buddha to inquire about it, thereby clarifying that among phenomena there is no phenomenon.
"No, World-Honored One. As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, there is no dharma by which the Buddha attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* under the Buddha Dīpaṃkara."
The meaning spoken by the Buddha is precisely what was stated above: that, in reality, there is no dharma that gives rise to the bodhicitta.

Since there is originally no dharma that gives rise to the mind, how could there later be a dharma that attains the fruit? Therefore, one directly perceives that there is truly nothing to be attained;
this is the correct realization of the Tathāgata’s attainment of the Dharma. This is attained within one's own mind, not bestowed by a teacher.
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is, Subhūti. In truth, there is no dharma that the Tathāgata has attained as 'anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi'."
His words deeply accord with the Buddha’s mind; thus he is praised as "it is so, it is so. When practice arises entirely from the nature, there is no dharma that is brought forth;
how then could there be any dharma that is attained? Being without anything to lack and without anything to be able to do, one spontaneously manifests perfect enlightenment.
Subhūti, if there were any dharma that the Tathāgata had attained as anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi,
then Dīpaṃkara would not have bestowed upon me this prediction: "In a future age, you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni."
The Buddha said: "If there were anything to be attained, then internally there would be a mind capable of attaining, and externally there would be an object to be attained.
As long as the mind and its objects have not been extinguished, this constitutes the existence of dharmas; such a state is utterly contrary to the quiescent, signless Bodhi.
How, then, could Dīpaṃkara have conferred a prediction upon me? The *Jinguan* (Mirror of the Canon) states: "The Buddha feared that people would mistake dharmas for reality."
One recognizes Dīpaṃkara Buddha as the Buddha; one recognizes the Tathāgata as the Buddha, yet fails to recognize that one’s own nature is the Buddha.
Therefore, he asks this question to bring it forth. If one must wait for some external dharma before attaining bodhi, then one’s original nature would not be the Buddha.
In truth, there is no dharma by which one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
For this reason, Dīpaṃkara Buddha bestowed upon me a prediction, saying: "In a future age, you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni."
Because there is nothing to be attained, the wondrous fruit realized is in fact the Dharma-gate inherently possessed within the nature-ground;

thus, one receives the prediction that in a future life one shall become a Buddha. People may doubt that enlightenment cannot be attained through the absence of dharmas, yet how could they know that the Buddha precisely attains it by means of the absence of dharmas?
The following section investigates the reason why it is attained through the absence of dharmas.
"Zhengyi" (Righteousness) is the Sanskrit *Śākya*, which here means "Capable Benevolence" (*Nengren*). This refers to the nature of the mind being pure and complete, encompassing all things.
"Muni" is translated as "Silent Stillness" (*Jimo*). This refers to the essence of the mind being fundamentally quiescent, such that movement and stillness do not alter it.
Silent stillness is its substance, which is *Tathatā* (Suchness); capable benevolence is its function, which is *Āgata* (Coming). Thus, Śākya is explained first, followed by Muni.
This means that the function is subsumed to return to the essence. "First as it was, and later as it comes" means that the function arises from the essence.
In total, this is a single true nature (*tathatā*). When the title is added, he is Śākyamuni; in general terms, he is called the Tathāgata and also the Buddha.
As for "Buddha," it means self-awakening, awakening others, and the fulfillment of awakening. At that time...
Regarding all phenomena and in all their aspects, he has awakened himself and awakened sentient beings;
thus, he abides neither in nirvana nor in samsara. All that he practices is nothing other than the conduct of the Sage’s tranquility and silence.
It is simply that when practice is perfected and the fruit is fulfilled, he manifests thousands of billions of transformation bodies for the sake of future generations.
This supreme and wondrously luminous title neither increased during the time of Śākyamuni, nor did it decrease during his time with Dīpaṃkara Buddha.

If one erroneously divides the stages of cultivation between this life and future lives, claiming that even for a Tathāgata to become a Buddha is merely a matter of waiting, then one might argue that diligent practice need not be vigorous. How, then, could such a person instruct sentient beings?
Therefore, until the attainment of the wondrous fruit of Bodhi, even when Kāśyapa became a Buddha, he likewise waited for a future birth to realize the true mark of Bodhi.
The attainment of Buddhahood by all sentient beings is explained through one reversal and one conformity established on the spot; this clearly elucidates the definitive meaning.
Why is this so? Because "Tathāgata" is the meaning of the suchness of all phenomena.
When the Tathāgata attains bodhi, there is in truth no dharma whatsoever. Why is this?

It is because that which constitutes the Tathāgata as the Tathāgata is precisely the meaning of all dharmas being such as they are in their own nature. Apart from dharmas, there is no separate tathatā;
apart from tathatā, there is no separate dharma. Dharmas are themselves the Buddha, and the Buddha is himself the dharmas. (Extensive Explanation)

[Subhūti] said: "True nature is the fundamental essence of the self; all phenomena are established from without. If one knows only that True Suchness (*tathatā*) is the essence of phenomena, then one knows that phenomena are not obtained from without.
Ruru said: "In the preceding passage, Subhūti directly realized the non-existence of phenomena, and the World-Honored One repeatedly spoke of the non-existence of phenomena.
The two minds have already reached a mutual seal of understanding. [The Buddha] feared that sentient beings..."
Having recognized that no phenomena exist as a basis for nihilism, he now further elucidates the reason for this and points out the essence of the Tathāgata.
To speak of the "Tathāgata" is to refer to the meaning of the *tathatā* (suchness) of all phenomena. That which is by nature immutable is called "Tathā" (Thus).
"All dharmas" refers to all mundane and supramundane phenomena. The meaning of "the suchness of all dharmas" (*dharmatathatā*) is precisely the arising of this mind.
When the mind undergoes change or alteration, it does not arise; when true suchness (*tathatā*) is unchanging, it is that which gives rise [to the mind].
True suchness can give rise to all dharmas, and it also relies upon all dharmas to arise—what is called, for example, earth nurturing sprouts. —Hanhua (憨)
The Mountain Master said: "Subhūti does not understand that the true essence of the Dharma-body does not belong to cause and effect;
he clings to the fixed notion that the Tathāgata is something that can be cultivated or attained. The Buddha then pointedly showed him: 'Why do you say there is nothing to be attained?
For the Tathāgata is not a designation for physical form; he is simply the meaning of the suchness (tathatā) of all dharmas.'"

If someone were to say, "The Tathāgata has attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi," and that the meaning of all dharmas being suchness (tathatā) implies that in reality there is no dharma at all— then if one says the Tathāgata has an attainment,
how could that be the true meaning of the Tathāgata? This is a determination made by borrowing the words of others.

Subhūti, in truth there is no dharma by which the Buddha has attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. (The above concludes the refutation of doubt regarding the Buddha; next follows the refutation of doubt regarding the Dharma.
Subhūti, that *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* attained by the Tathāgata is therein neither real nor unreal.
For this reason, the Tathāgata says that all dharmas are the Buddha-dharma. Subhūti, as for what is called "all..."
"Dharma" refers to the fact that it is not any dharma; for this reason, it is called "all dharmas.
To explain this extensively: herein lies the mind of the pure Dharma. The mind is fundamentally empty and still, devoid of even a single thing.

Bodhi is utterly without form or characteristic; therefore, it is said to have no reality. That which is the emptiness of form and characteristics is precisely the locus of true nature and reality. This is...
It is bodhi; therefore, it is said to be "not false. Since it is said to be neither real nor false, all phenomena are bodhi;
thus, it is said that "all dharmas are Buddha-dharmas. One must not seek bodhi apart from all phenomena. Nevertheless, all phenomena are not ultimately real;
people merely rely upon them as a provisional means for practice. Therefore, it is said: "Dharmas are themselves non-dharmas."
Regarding the Dharma: one must not grasp at the existence of bodhi within all dharmas. Li Chang said:

"The aforementioned 'non-existence of dharmas' does not mean a blank void or nihilistic annihilation. True Suchness is profound and tranquil; it does not establish a single dharma, yet all dharmas are suchness;
it does not abandon a single dharma. To say that 'all dharmas are not all dharmas' is because within them there is no reality."
Regarding the statement that "all dharmas are the Buddha-dharma," this is because there is nothing false therein. As it is said in the *Tathatā-sūtra*:

"The preceding passage spoke of generating such a mind, yet it did not specify where 'such' (evam) resides. It is specifically for this reason that the two characters 'is' (shi) and 'middle' (zhong) are singled out.
'Is' (shi) is precisely the 'is' of 'thus' (evam). 'Middle' (zhong) refers to the Middle Way. Whenever there is existence, there is [the middle]."

Emptiness. Where there is emptiness, there is also reality. Through their mutual opposition, they establish one another as negations: reality becomes emptiness, and emptiness becomes reality. It is through emotional attachment that stagnation arises.
Only through the Middle Way are characteristics abandoned and opposition severed; both existence and non-existence are simultaneously dispelled.
Thus, there is no substantial reality that obstructs, nor is there a barren emptiness of non-existence. As the preceding text states: "neither real nor unreal..."
"Empty" is spoken in terms of phenomena (*dharma*); "neither real nor empty" is spoken in terms of the mind. Phenomena arise from the bodhicitta.
That which is "not empty" takes skillful means (*upāya*) as bodhi; therefore, the Tathāgata says that all dharmas are Buddha-dharmas—this refers to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
That which is "not real" takes true nature (*tathatā*) as bodhi; therefore, regarding all that is spoken...
That which is the Dharma is not all dharmas; this is the Truth of Emptiness (*śūnyatā-satya*). That which is without reality is also without falsehood;

because true wisdom constitutes Bodhi, it is therefore called "all dharmas. This is the Middle Truth (*madhyama-satya*). Because these two are present, the word "middle" (*madhya*) is explained here in close succession.
What was previously called "the dharmas of the Buddhas" is here termed "all dharmas," further including the dharmas of the five vehicles. Thus, O Buddha...
Bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, humans, devas, and all phenomena are all Buddha-dharma; the holy and the ordinary are equal, for the provisional and the ultimate converge.
What was previously stated as "Buddha-dharma is not Buddha-dharma" is here expressed as "all dharmas are not all dharmas.
This does not merely refer to the Buddha-dharma being non-dharma; it means that all ordinary dharmas likewise arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions.

It is born without fabrication and without reception; therefore it is called "all dharmas. These are neither dharmas nor non-dharmas, yet they are both dharmas and non-dharmas, all being one within the Bodhi-Dharmadhātu—namely, the meaning of the "suchness" (tathatā) of all dharmas.
Combining the preceding and following sections, the initial statement that "one should have no dwelling-place in dharmas" serves as the basis for cultivation, thereby fulfilling the first [point].

How rare is this Dharma! Fearing that people might pursue illusions and lose sight of the truth, it states that one should neither grasp at phenomena nor grasp at non-phenomena, thereby shattering both attachments so that nothing is grasped.

Fearing that people might perceive this as a state of indeterminate nothingness, it further clarifies the subtle point by stating that there is no attainment regarding phenomena and that, in reality, no phenomenon exists.
Yet, if it were to stop merely at saying "no phenomenon exists," it would fear being perceived as...

[The disciples] stood there, unable to follow. Therefore, taking the Dharma attained by the Tathāgata and the meaning of the "suchness" (tathatā) of all dharmas as the target for their pursuit and realization, he initially spoke only of the "Dharma of the Tathāgata.

Fearing that such a lofty proclamation might leave the listeners bewildered, he then broadened the path of benefit by stating that "all dharmas are the Buddha-dharma," and that "not-all-dharmas are named 'all-dharmas. When his teaching reached this point, it was as follows:
The maṇi jewel manifests colors according to its surroundings; it is like the common rice of a household, which may be eaten according to one's capacity.
When the Buddha Natural Lamp arrived here, he said that the ground of the Tathāgata is empty and possesses nothing at all.
"Subhūti, it is as if there were a person with a large body.
Before he had finished speaking, the Correct Meaning [of the commentary] states: "A large body is not real; this is a metaphor for how dharmas are not real.
A person has a large body, yet how can they avoid having birth and extinction? How could they be considered a truly real 'large' one? This follows the preceding by establishing a metaphor.
This serves as an introduction to the following passage. Chengxian says: "For example, a person's body is large and tall.

This clearly uses the physical body (*rūpakāya*) as a metaphor for the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). The meaning of this section is that the unreality of the physical body is used as a metaphor for the fundamental nature of all phenomena (*dharmas*).

Although it is said that [the Dharma-body] is great, the intention does not lie in its magnitude. While the phrasing resembles the section on Sumeru, King of Mountains, the meaning is actually different from what precedes it;
for the Reward Body (saṃbhogakāya) clarifies the Dharma-body by borrowing the analogy of the Mountain King. Therefore, the subsequent treatise explains that it is neither great nor not great.

Within the act of sweeping away traces, there is an underlying intent to trace back to the source. This uses the physical body (*rūpakāya*) as a metaphor for the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), explicitly stating the character "human" (*puruṣa*).

What follows merely discusses reality and unreality to reveal that the Dharma-body is without marks; it possesses only the intent of sweeping away traces, lacking the intent of tracing back to the source.
Dayuan says: These words concern the essential nature of the true Buddha and the true Dharma, used to reveal the non-existence of a Buddha.
The subtle principle of the Dharma has not yet been fully explained.
Subhūti said to the World-Honored One: "When the Tathāgata speaks of a person’s body being large, it is precisely because it is not a large body;
it is merely designated as a 'large body.'"
Yuanzhi said: "All dharmas pervade the entire realm of sand-grains; how are they not identical to the Great Reward Body?
Yet, it is not that 'non-dharma' is named 'dharma,' just as it is not that 'non-body' is named 'Great Body. Kongsheng did not wait for the Buddha to finish his explanation but spoke directly.
Shengxian remarked: "To say 'non-body' is named 'Great Body' is simply to speak directly from the human body downward."
It is not necessary to integrate this into the *dharmakāya*, yet the meaning of the *dharmakāya* is clarified within these words. The Correct Meaning (*Zhengyi*) states:

"To know that the great body is no-body is to know that all phenomena are non-phenomena. Ruru says: "The previous statement, 'The Buddha said it is no-body,' refers to the absence of the characteristics of a body;
this statement, 'it is not a great body,' refers to the absence of the characteristics of a great body. The metaphor is the same."
The meaning is different. This "Great Body" (mahākāya) should be applied directly to all phenomena (*sarvadharma*);
only then will it not be a mere general statement. If all phenomena are the Buddha-dharma, then all worlds are the Buddha-body.
If all phenomena are not [merely] all phenomena, then the Great Body of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is precisely not a Great Body. That which is not a Great Body is all...
The Buddha-world is like a flower in the sky. Yet, the sky is the unmoving essence; therefore, it is called the "Great Body.
In the sutra, the term "Great Body" is mentioned twice: once to praise non-attainment and once to praise attainment.
Non-attainment and attainment are the two eyes of this sutra; thus, in the following passage, Subhūti [speaks] in terms of attainment...
To be without attainment is to elucidate the meaning of their harmony. This refers to the fact that on the stage of the Tathāgata’s fruition, there is emptiness and nothing whatsoever.
Subhūti, it is the same for a bodhisattva: if one were to say, "I shall bring immeasurable sentient beings to parinirvāṇa," then one would not be called a bodhisattva.

Regarding the statement that "the Bodhisattva delivers sentient beings," there is no self [in those beings]. This is also like the Buddha’s attainment of *bodhi*, which likewise has no phenomena (*dharma*).
To speak according to the preceding meaning, making such a statement refers specifically to the deliverance (*parinirvāṇa*) of sentient beings. Dayuan said:

"Since the fruit of realization is non-existent, how could the cultivation of the cause be allowed to exist in isolation? Thus, the Bodhisattva’s arousal of the thought of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) should also be understood in this way."
Such is the characteristic of the non-arising of dharmas. If one thinks to oneself, "I shall attain parinirvāṇa," then one is identifying with the dharma of saving sentient beings;
one is likewise identifying with the dharma of attaining bodhi. Thus, one cannot be called a Bodhisattva. The Correct Meaning says:
"The name 'Bodhisattva' means one who awakens sentient beings. That it is unreal is also like this. Indeed, [it is] true...
In their fundamental nature, there are originally no sentient beings; it is only because of karmic conditions that they manifest forms.

If one speaks of these three phrases, one first uses the inverse statement to clarify them. Why are there four phrases? It is precisely to explain their meaning correctly. The subsequent section on "adornments of Buddha-lands" follows this same pattern.
Why is this? Subhūti, there is truly no dharma that can be called a "bodhisattva.
The Buddha further inquires why they are not so named: it is precisely because a bodhisattva receives their name through purity.
In reality, there is no dharma that can be grasped or realized by a person, yet it is by means of this that one delivers others. [Commentary on the Collection: Internal Wisdom.
"Emptiness and stillness; all dharmas do not arise—this is called a Bodhisattva. The Correct Meaning (*Zhengyi*) states:

"A Bodhisattva relies precisely upon the practice of the Buddha-dharma to deliver sentient beings. To say that 'in reality there are no dharmas' means that within true nature (*tathatā*), these dharmas are not perceived.
Since there are no dharmas, what further could be said? That which the Buddha taught was only the teaching of the absence of the four [extremes]."
This is to clarify that true emptiness is signless (*animitta*).
Therefore, the Buddha taught that all phenomena (*dharma*) are without self (*anātman*), without a person (*pudgala*), without a sentient being (*sattva*), and without a life-principle (*jīva*).

Furthermore, this explains the meaning of the aforementioned statement that "in reality, there is no dharma whatsoever. All dharmas spoken by the Buddha do not exceed what is adapted to the capacities of beings.
He accords with and guides sentient beings so that they may awaken to their original nature. The self, the person, the sentient being, and the life-span—these have never existed from the beginning.
All dharmas are fundamentally devoid of the four marks; how can one cling to the mark of a single sentient being and say, "I shall deliver sentient beings"?
Ruru said: "The Tathāgata has no dharma by which he attains Bodhi. It is only because..."
The "suchness" (*tathatā*) of all phenomena is their true meaning. The Buddha is thus; the Bodhisattva is also thus. This single suchness is without a second suchness.
This character "thus" (*ru*) corresponds to the arising of the "thus-mind. The two instances of the character "thus" should be viewed as the "thus" of the Tathāgata.

The subsequent text speaks of "suchness-as-suchness" (*tathātathatā*), which also means being "thus" in accordance with True Suchness (*bhūtatathatā*). In the sutras, it is sometimes referred to simply as "thus" (*tathā*).
Regarding the term "coming" (āgata), some say it refers to Bodhisattvas; these appear interchangeably and erroneously, each having its own subject and object.

When speaking of the teaching of the Dharma, the Tathāgata is the subject and those who extensively expound and proclaim it are the objects, for all extensive exposition and proclamation are rooted in the Tathāgata’s protective mindfulness and entrustment. When speaking of practice, the Bodhisattva is the subject, and the Tathāgata...
This serves as a guest-commentary. This sutra specifically addresses the bodhisattva’s generation of the mind of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*), using the Tathāgata as the standard of measurement.

Previously, it was stated that generating such a mind involves no mark of phenomena (*dharma-nimitta*); this was explained by noting that to have a mark of self (*ātman-nimitta*) is not the way of a bodhisattva.
Here, it is stated that if one says, "I shall bring about parinirvāṇa," this is to have a mark of self; this is explained by means of reality (*tattva*).

There is no dharma called "bodhisattva. To explain the reason for this: attachment to a self (*ātman-grāha*) is precisely attachment to dharmas (*dharma-grāha*), and attachment to dharmas is precisely attachment to a self.
Therefore it is said: "If the mind grasps at dharmas or grasps at non-dharmas, one is then attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span.
A bodhisattva truly has no dharma; that is, they truly have no self. It is like sentient beings who give rise to faith—they are without a self.
This characteristic is itself the absence of the characteristic of phenomena and the absence of the characteristic of non-phenomena.

To say, "I shall bring sentient beings to extinction," is no different from the previous statement, "I should bring all sentient beings to extinction. However, to speak in such a way is not to give rise to the true mind;
therefore, one is not called a Bodhisattva.
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva were to say, "I shall adorn the Buddha-fields," he would not be called a bodhisattva.
It is not only that dharmas lack marks and cannot be perceived; for indeed, seeking the fruit of Buddhahood above and transforming sentient beings below are both the duties of a bodhisattva.
Since one seeks the fruit of Buddhahood, one ought to adorn the Buddha-fields. However, even the adorning of fields is not a substantial dharma.
If a bodhisattva says of himself, "I shall adorn the Buddha-field with the seven treasures and five colors," this is attachment to marks;
such a person is not called a bodhisattva. According to the correct principle, this "Buddha-field" refers to the Buddha’s *kṣetra* (realm).
As the Tathāgata explains below, adorning the Buddha-field actually refers to the Buddha’s mind-realm (*citta-kṣetra*). The tenth section states that the bodhisattva adorns...
Regarding "adorned Buddha-lands": this is because one observes that worldly people devote themselves exclusively to external ornamentation and adornment;

therefore, it is clarified that the Bodhisattva does not abide in such things. This section states that the Bodhisattva does not, through the adornment of the Buddha-land, regard himself as possessing capability.
Therefore, only the adornment of signlessness is shown. Why is this?
When the Tathāgata speaks of adorning Buddha-lands, it is not actually an adornment; it is merely designated as "adornment."
Why is it not called "Bodhisattva"? That which the Tathāgata speaks of as the adornment of Buddha-lands is not an adornment through grasping at signs according to worldly truth;
rather, it is the adorning of the mind’s land. The land of the mind is signless and fundamentally pure. How could there be adornment?
It is unstained by the six sense objects, and concentration and wisdom are ever-present. Within that which is not adornment, there lies wondrous adornment. This is so.
This is what is called "adornment. As it is said: "This further clarifies, through the absence of adornment, that there is no sign of saving sentient beings.

To adorn the Buddha-land means to benefit all sentient beings through all dharmas, operating with both compassion and wisdom in tandem, and manifesting both merit and insight, thereby accomplishing the pure land of enjoyment. It is not the adornment of a [physical] Buddha-land.
"Earth" means to cultivate all dharmas while being without the marks of any dharma, and to benefit all sentient beings while being without the marks of any sentient being.
Previously, one was called a "bodhisattva" through the adornment of the bodhisattva;
here, it is simply said that "I shall adorn," yet this is not yet named a bodhisattva. Previously, the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) served as the adornment; here, [it is...]
"All dharmas serve as adornments. Previously, it was established through "non-adornment" that there is nothing to be attained; here, it is clarified through "non-adornment" that there is no self.
The phrasing is identical, yet the meaning differs. The *Shengshi* (Extensive Commentary) states: "Adorning the land is for the purpose of saving sentient beings.
From the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), one clarifies the teachings of Dharma and body to discipline sentient beings; thus, one should adorn the Buddha-land."
According to the Truth of Ultimate Reality (*paramārtha-satya*), the Buddha-field is fundamentally empty; since cultivation is entirely contained within its nature, it is said to be "not this.

According to the Truth of the Middle Way (*madhyama-satya*), nature and cultivation are non-dual; therefore, it is said to be "named as such. One does not perceive the person who adorns, nor does one perceive the land that is adorned; this is the adornment of the mind-land.
Furthermore, when one internally does not perceive a self and externally does not perceive phenomena, only then is there the "non-existence of dharmas" (*dharma-abhāva*).
It can be attained. Taken together, there is birth that can be saved and lands that can be adorned; both of these involve the notion of a self.
Yet, saving is actually no saving, and adorning is actually non-adornment; both arise from the absence of self. Therefore, he concludes with the principle of penetrating the dharma of non-self.
This speaks of the Bodhisattva’s saving of beings as being empty and non-existent.
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva penetrates the dharma of non-self, the Tathāgata calls him by the name of a true bodhisattva.
One who gives rise to the thought of delivering sentient beings and clings to marks of adornment cannot be called a bodhisattva. Ultimately, how can he be named?
It is one who is able to penetrate the dharma of non-self. This summarizes the meaning of the aforementioned fact that no dharma exists:
the arousal of the mind, the attainment of the fruit, and the bestowal of the prediction—all are non-dharmas; even the saving of sentient beings and the adorning of the lands—all are non-dharmas.
This is the dharma of non-self within the emptiness of the four marks of the Prajñā. One who penetrates this dharma is pure and fundamental, and without...

There is no self of persons and no self of phenomena; one abides in that which is neither real nor unreal. When one’s practice of profound *prajñā* is thus, one is rightly named a bodhisattva—this faith is not deceptive.
If even a bodhisattva cannot be grasped as having a self or phenomena, how much less could a Tathāgata have any phenomenon by which he attains *bodhi*?
Yet, it is all the more evident that there is no phenomenon by which the mind of enlightenment is generated.
Thus it is said: "The meaning of thorough penetration lies entirely in clarifying all dharmas. For all dharmas are devoid of self;
one can thereby penetrate from this dharma to that dharma, each and every one without obstruction.

Having thus washed away the false imaginings of ordinary beings and further melted away the partial emptiness of the two vehicles, one is able to shoulder the burden of the Tathāgata and benefit [sentient beings]."

"Sentient beings [perceive] dharmas; 'dharmaless-self' (dharmānātman) means that there are no dharmas. To penetrate this without obstruction is precisely the mind capable of arising, which is not bound by dharmas.
Dayuan said: "Speaking from the perspective of the dharma-body being inherently present, it is called 'dharmaless-self.
Speaking from the perspective of the Bodhisattva’s wisdom-realization, it is called 'selfless-dharma. [This is distinct from the realization of] Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas."
If one merely knows non-self but cannot integrate this into all phenomena, one can only save oneself and cannot save others;

such a person is a "name-only bodhisattva. If one practices toward all phenomena yet cannot know that all dharmas are originally without self, then the characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa) still persist, and one ultimately remains within the provisional vehicle. If a bodhisattva, regarding each and every dharma...

Penetrating to the very source of non-self, one perceives that within the six perfections and myriad practices, neither subject nor object is established; this is called "thoroughly penetrating the dharma of non-self.
Throughout the day one adorns the buddha-lands, yet there is never any adornment; throughout the day one delivers sentient beings, yet from the beginning there is no one delivered.
There is no hindrance of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), nor is there any hindrance to knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Human attachment is empty, and as for dharmas—
Since even grasping is empty, the Tathāgata himself would have conferred the prediction of his attainment of Buddhahood and declared him to be a true Bodhisattva.

△ Regarding the resolution of doubts: it is said that the initial inquiry concerning "abiding" and "descending" in the sutra is addressed to Bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds toward Great Enlightenment.

At the initial stage of generating the mind to deliver sentient beings, one clings to various signs and practices according to the five aggregates (*skandha*), while practicing giving by grasping at the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*).
The bodhi thus sought has a physical body that can be seen and a Buddha-field that can be adorned;

therefore, the Buddha repeatedly refutes these notions until all phenomenal marks are transcended, whereupon one accords with the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) of Prajñāpāramitā. This is the former [stage].
This is the intention of the first half of the fascicle. At this point, the question regarding "abiding" and "descending" is addressed; it refers to a Bodhisattva who has already awakened to Prajñā.

Although the wisdom capable of realization has not yet been forgotten and the dualistic view of sentient beings and Buddhas has not yet been extinguished, subtle traces of the two types of grasping still persist.
Thus, it remains as if there were still a single dharma existing within me; therefore, it is said that "there is truly no dharma" means that "there is truly no self.
The Tathāgata has no dharma to be attained, and the Bodhisattva likewise has no dharma to be attained.
Therefore, one takes non-crossing as crossing and non-adornment as adornment. Zongtong says: "To deliver sentient beings is great compassion; to adorn the Buddha-lands is [great compassion]."

These are matters within the domain of great wisdom and the internal affairs of all Bodhisattvas. However, should one harbor even a single thought of deliberate effort, one is no longer a Bodhisattva.
One who thoroughly penetrates the dharma of non-self not only departs from the self of persons (*pudgala-ātman*), but also departs from the self of dharmas (*dharma-ātman*).
Not only can such a person’s wisdom believe in this dharma of non-self, but there is also no person who possesses that wisdom. Therefore, they spend their entire days delivering sentient beings.
He has never saved sentient beings; he adorns them all day long, yet he has never adorned them. This is true formlessness; this is true non-abiding. Caoxi said:
"This passage of the sutra, from 'repeatedly requesting instruction' to 'thoroughly penetrating selflessness,' is explained as a single continuous sequence.
Vasubandhu divides it into four doubts: first, formlessness; second, lack of cause; third..."
There is no Buddha-dharma; there is not even a single dharma of a Bodhisattva. All things ultimately return to non-self (*anātman*); this is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).

In the initial response concerning abiding and descending, one was still at the stage of destroying deluded attachments to reveal true wisdom. What was destroyed were the coarse attachments to the four marks (*catur-lakṣaṇa*); what was revealed was the correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*) of Bodhi.
Arriving here, the response is given once more regarding abiding and descending, which lies in destroying deluded attachment so that wisdom is forgotten. What is destroyed...
The "four marks" refer to subtle attachments; that which is forgotten is the arousal of the bodhicitta. If even bodhi does not exist, how can there be the four marks?
If wisdom is not established, from where could deluded emotion arise? Therefore, the arousal of bodhicitta refers to what was said previously;
the non-arousal of bodhicitta refers to what was said subsequently. When the mind is devoid of that [conceptual] mind, then there is no affliction to be subdued. This is called the True.
"Descending. There is no dwelling that can be dwelt upon; this is called true dwelling. The Layman Ruru said:

"From the phrase 'arousing the mind of Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi' up to this point, all [the preceding discourse] serves to negate the questions regarding how one should dwell and how one should subdue.
When speaking of 'arousing the mind,' one need not ask how one dwells or how one subdues; rather, one should instead ask how one arouses it."
Furthermore, at the very inception of generating the bodhicitta, if there is no longer any notion of a self (*ātman*), how could there be any notion of dharmas?
If one generates the mind without [clinging to] dharmas, how could there be any attainment through dharmas? Therefore, it is sufficient that the mind itself be generated;
why must one further seek how to abide or how to subdue?
Explanation of the Essential Meaning: The commentary briefly states that from this point downward, the text is divided into four chapters.

These constitute the Tathāgata’s primary response for subduing [opponents] through the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), wherein the practice of abiding is contained. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* says: "All phenomena are non-existent."
Thus it is so. Within these seventeen sections, the two chapters on "opening and closing" constitute "non-existence.
The subsequent four chapters—on seeing and wisdom, the three karmas, saving sentient beings, and coming and going—constitute "thus it is so."

Chapter 18: On the Contemplation of the Single Essence The Buddha possesses the five eyes, yet their substance is not substantially existent; it is only the eternally abiding true mind, empty, luminous, and unclouded.

Although the eyes are divided into five, their illumination is unified within the single mind. This is what is meant by "the myriad dharmas returning to the One"; there is no further divergent contemplation.

“Do you have the Dharma-eye? “Yes, World-Honored One. The Tathāgata has the Dharma-eye. “Subhūti, what do you think?
Does the Tathāgata have the Buddha-eye? “Yes, World-Honored One. The Tathāgata has the Buddha-eye.”
Master Chengshi explains: The preceding passage stated that one who does not perceive any phenomena is called a bodhisattva. Yet, within this non-perception, there is inherently true seeing;
therefore, it is verified by means of the Buddha’s five eyes. These five eyes are fully present within a single mind.
Its essence is fundamentally one, yet its functions are five; it abides neither in the one nor in the five.
Only the Buddha possesses this. Dayuan said: "The Buddha asked about the five eyes, and all replied that they exist.
This is because they know that within true emptiness, actual vision arises spontaneously, without the slightest obscuration. Chen Xiong said: "The Avataṃsaka Sūtra states:"
The fleshly eye sees all forms; the divine eye sees the minds of all sentient beings;
the wisdom eye sees the faculties and spheres of all sentient beings; the Dharma eye sees the true mark of all phenomena as they are.

The Buddha-eye (*buddhacakṣus*). Because it perceives the ten powers (*daśabala*) of the Tathāgata, it is what is referred to in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* as the "pure five eyes" (*pañcacakṣuḥ pariśuddha*).
Yan Bing said: "To perceive through the contemplation of illusory odors is the fleshly eye (*māṃsacakṣus*); to universally illuminate the great trichiliocosm is the heavenly eye (*divyacakṣus*)."
The constant illumination of the lamp of wisdom constitutes the *prajñā-cakṣus* (eye of wisdom). Thoroughly understanding that all phenomena are empty constitutes the *dharma-cakṣus* (Dharma-eye).

The constant awakening of the original nature constitutes the *buddha-cakṣus* (Buddha-eye). These terms refer solely to the self-nature of the Tathāgata’s fundamental substance (*svabhāva*). According to this, the fleshly eye sees what is near but not what is distant;
it sees within obstructions but not beyond them. The celestial eye can see beyond obstructions. As for the eye of wisdom, by means of its faculty...

Fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) illuminates the principle of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) and attains the insight of true emptiness. The Dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣus*), by means of discerning wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇa-jñāna*), penetrates the principle of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and clarifies all phenomena.
As for the Buddha-eye (*buddha-cakṣus*): "Buddha" carries the meaning of awakening; with subtle afflictions forever exhausted, it is perfectly luminous and universally illuminating.
It takes the wisdom of the samādhi of perfect enlightenment as its essence and non-effortful wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*) as its nature.
Shenxian said: "The eye has the meaning of gazing and illuminating. As for the five eyes, it is not that there are actually five eyes; they are designated as 'eyes' based on what is seen.
In terms of form, they are the physical eyes; in terms of principle, they are the apertures of the mind. Such is the state of *tathatā*."
It is said: "That which penetrates all is the cultivation of the Bodhisattva; that which encompasses the myriad phenomena is the Tathāgata-garbha.

Since all dharmas are the Buddha-dharma, the vehicle of humans, the vehicle of devas, the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, and the vehicle of the Bodhisattvas—none are not subsumed within the Buddha-vehicle.
The Dharma-body pervades all places; the eye is its particular manifestation of perfection."
This is but one among them. The essence of wisdom can perceive emptiness and perceive form; it can perceive that which is neither empty nor form;
it can perceive that which is both empty and form. Because it universally illumines the entire dharma-realm, it is metaphorically designated as the "eye"—this is precisely what is called *prajñā*.
Only when this essence of great radiance exists does one first become a Tathāgata.
The body; thus, the eye of the Way is fully encompassed by the Dharma-body, just as the perfection of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā) fully encompasses the six perfections.
The preceding passage speaks of "seeing the Tathāgata," "seeing various forms," and "the Tathāgata knowing and seeing all"—none of these refer to seeing by means of the faculty of the physical eye.
This is because the capacity of the listener lies in the ability to hear; therefore, for those of sharp faculties, [the teaching is intended].

The ear-faculty (*śrotra-āyatana*) is the fundamental principle for those who manifest through transformation; it is predicated upon the capacity for seeing. Therefore, the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) regards the gift of the eye as paramount.
Yet, because sentient beings give rise to the illusory cataracts of their own accord due to dualistic attachments to emptiness and existence, they are unable to use this eye to illuminate that eye.
Consequently, they are unable to reach that vehicle by means of this vehicle; though they recognize their own doctrine with extreme clarity, they ultimately lack the eye of wisdom.
Therefore, the World-Honored One reveals it to them by means of the five unimpeded eyes.

(This section follows upon the previous by showing that through seeing purity, one realizes the purity of wisdom. "Subhūti, what do you think? Regarding all the grains of sand in the Ganges River—does the Buddha say they are sand?
"So it is, World-Honored One; the Tathāgata says they are sand. "Subhūti, what do you think?
If there were as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand in a single Ganges River, and then the number of grains of sand in all those Ganges Rivers—"
"Are the Buddha-worlds thus numerous? "Very many, World-Honored One.
Previously, the Ganges was mentioned as a metaphor for giving; here, the Ganges is mentioned as a metaphor for world-systems. The intended meaning in each case is distinct.
As for "Buddha-worlds," wherever there is a world-system, there must necessarily be a Buddha to teach and transform it; therefore, they are all...
This is called a Buddha-world. Such worlds are exceedingly numerous, and the sentient beings within them are even more so;
therefore, he first asks about these many worlds. "It is so" is the phrase used to accept [the premise].
The Buddha told Subhūti: "In all those lands, the Tathāgata fully knows the various kinds of minds of all sentient beings.
This analogy has five layers: first, he uses the Ganges River to count its sands; second, he takes each grain of sand as a river.
1. Counting the rivers; 2. Counting the sands within those rivers; 3. Counting the realms based on those sands; 4. Counting all sentient beings within those realms; 5.
Counting the minds of those sentient beings—their births and deaths in myriad forms—as numerous as these sands. As it is said: "Suchness (Tathatā) is thus."
The minds of sentient beings are inverted minds. "Of various kinds" refers to the sense that their states cannot be enumerated in detail.
This encompasses the three periods of past, present, and future. Because the Tathāgata is perfected in wisdom and conduct, he is able to know others.
His knowledge is not a mere observation of emptiness; rather, because of his intimate concern rooted in the realization of the same essence, he acts out of compassion.
This constitutes true wisdom, while simultaneously performing the work of delivering others from distress.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata has taught that all minds are "not-minds"; it is for this reason that they are called "minds."
The Tathāgata has taught that the various minds of sentient beings all manifest as reflections of the six sense-objects;
they are all the deluded minds of the inverted consciousness-spirit (*vijñāna*), not the true, eternally abiding fundamental mind. These are merely empty names for "mind. Yan Bing said:
"When the Tathāgata speaks of various minds, in reality no mind can be apprehended; therefore he says they are 'not-mind,' yet they are given names by force of convention."
It says: "The mind. According to this, it is called the "phrase of the mind. All versions interpret this as pointing directly to the true mind (*zhēn-xīn*).
The Correct Meaning (*Zhèng-yì*) states that although the meaning of these words seems profound and subtle, they do not harmonize with the context of the preceding and following passages.
Both [versions] treat them as "not the mind" (*fēi-xīn*). These two phrases, "this is called the mind," should simply be read straight through without explicitly identifying the true mind. Below...
The third section clarifies that the mind cannot be apprehended; it specifically elucidates these two phrases.
As for what constitutes the true mind, it has likewise never been explicitly revealed. Why is this so?

What is the distinction? It is said: the initial statement [of the Buddha] speaks of transcending birth by being free from a self; the eleventh doubt asks, "If there is one who can transcend, it must be a self";
the fourteenth doubt asks, "If there is no self, who is it that transcends? This doubt [realizes] that within the equal Dharma-realm, there is no correspondence with the act of transcending birth.
These four meanings are clearly distinguished; the elucidation of the one who has no transcender is both detailed and exhaustive.
Section Twenty-Six: The Dharma-body is Without Characteristics.

The pure Dharma-body does not belong to the realm of appearances. This section further states that the Tathāgata cannot be seen by means of characteristics, thereby completely sweeping away all previous conceptualizations of dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). From this point onward, the teaching is directed toward the bodhisattvas.
One must penetrate the dharma of non-self. However, to penetrate the dharma of non-self, one must first select and dismantle the view of self.
To penetrate the dharma of non-self, it is essential to achieve total integration; only when total integration is achieved can one shatter all marks.
Therefore, the three phrases—"that which is," "is not," and "is called"—are spoken simultaneously. Hereafter, they are all...
Instructing others to discern and shatter "existence," one must distinguish the view of self clearly. Only when it is clearly distinguished can all views be shattered.
The twenty-sixth [view], the view of characteristics of the Tathāgata, is the view of existence and is called a false path.
The twenty-seventh, the view of characteristics being incomplete, is the view of non-existence and is called annihilationism. Thus it is said later.
This Tathāgata comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; therefore, he is named "Tathāgata. Thus, the views of existence and non-existence are completely shattered.

Furthermore, fearing that people might give rise to a view of duality—between the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) that appears to come and go, and the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) that neither comes nor goes—he uses the analogy of a single mote of dust within a world-system to illustrate their unity.

The characteristics are clarified by analogy. To speak of that which is not an object as an "object," that which is not a realm as a "realm," and that which is not a composite as a "composite"—by this, the views of unity and difference are completely shattered. When all views are utterly destroyed, the view of self vanishes;
naturally, there is no person, no sentient being, and no life-span possessor. Only when one knows seeing as non-seeing does [true insight arise].
This is the Tathāgata’s right view. He commands those who have resolved their minds to know, see, and believe in this manner;
thereafter, the four marks will not arise. The three phrases are spoken together: "the mark of dharmas," "not the mark of dharmas," and "named the mark of dharmas.
This truly enables one to penetrate the dharma of non-self. In relation to the entire sutra, this refers to the section prior to the twenty-fifth division.

This is the *prajñāpāramitā* taught through the secret method of destroying marks (*lakṣaṇa*). From the twenty-sixth division onward, it is the *prajñāpāramitā* taught openly by destroying views (*dṛṣṭi*).
In contrast to the latter half of the sutra, that which precedes the twenty-fifth division is for those of profound understanding.
By stating "that which is not" and "this name" in a continuous sequence, each [aspect of] the non-self of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) is perfectly fulfilled.
This is the matter of the initial awakening (ādikṣānti-bodhi) merging with the fundamental awakening (mūla-bodhi). It is what is called the profound discourse on entering into principle.
From the twenty-sixth section onward, it is also taught for the sake of beginners; it is explained by analytically distinguishing that which is "about to be" from that which "is not.
That all instances of the view of self (ātma-dṛṣṭi) are completely shattered is the matter of the initial awakening arising from non-awakening (a-bodhi).
This is what is called the establishment of the gateway, the protective mindfulness, and the entrustment; it is ultimate and complete.
Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be perceived by means of the thirty-two marks?

The preceding statement that "the perfection of all marks is itself non-perfection; it is called perfection" implies that the primary and secondary marks (lakṣaṇānuvyañjana) are fundamentally inseparable from the Dharma-body (dharmakāya).
One who contemplates the Buddha perceives the marks and signs of the Dharma-body; through this, one may perhaps awaken to the markless Dharma-body.
There is a distinction between "contemplating" (guan) and "seeing" (jian): "seeing" takes the marks as being the Buddha, whereas "contemplating" compares the marks [to the reality].
"Contemplation": that is to say, can one contemplate the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata within the marks of the response-body?
Subhūti replied: "So it is, so it is. One contemplates the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks."
"One cannot see the Tathāgata by means of marks. Śūnyatā-utpanna (Kongsheng) has repeatedly answered this with great thoroughness; why now do you instead answer in such a way?
It is because "contemplating" is not the same as "seeing. To "see" is to take marks as the Buddha. To contemplate the Buddha by means of marks—this is what you mean.
Thus, although the marks (lakṣaṇa) are not themselves the Buddha, these marks and signs originally manifest from within the markless (animitta).
Therefore, by means of these marks, one may contemplate the subtlety of the markless; this is certainly not impossible.
Moreover, whereas Subhūti previously understood only the pure Dharma-body as "that which is not," he now understands that "that which is not" and "the name" are unified.
If it were the fulfillment of the Dharmakāya, then this answer given by Subhūti would not be incorrect; it correctly identifies the point of another's progress.
However, it was not the intention behind the Buddha’s question. Had a beginner heard this, they would inevitably fall into a wrong path.
Therefore, the Buddha immediately used the difficulty regarding the Cakravartin to cut off [Subhūti’s] argument.
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "If one were to view the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks, then a Wheel-Turning Sage King would be the Tathāgata.

This extensively explains that if one grasps at and clings to the response-body (nirmāṇakāya), one does not penetrate the essence of the Dharma. The World-Honored One feared that [beings] would cling to signs.

[The Buddha] saw that there were still subtle afflictions (*anuśaya*) not yet eliminated; therefore, he challenged [the interlocutor] with the analogy of the Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*). He said:

"Though their physical appearances may be identical, the basis upon which those appearances depend is actually different. One must judge the derivative from the fundamental; one cannot judge the fundamental by means of the derivative.
The Wheel-Turning King refers to the Four Heavenly Kings (*cāturmahārājika*). Like the turning of a wheel, they govern the four continents and oversee the good and evil of the human realm.
One who, by virtue of karmic retribution and merit, also possesses the thirty-two marks—is such a person then the Tathāgata?
This passage directly demonstrates the selfless Dharma-body as the ultimate conclusion of this entire sutra.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, as I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, one should not perceive the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks.
At that moment, the Venerable One attained realization; he understood that a Wheel-Turning King cannot be regarded as the Tathāgata, and thus he came to know the Tathāgata.
One cannot know [the Tathāgata] by means of comparing him to signs; thus, he concludes the proof by means of the "inapplicability of signs.
The World-Honored One ended with a verse. Commentary: Subhūti originally had no false views; a single turn of the wheel made him enlightened.
His subsequent response regarding "inapplicability" was due to the challenge posed by the Cakravartin King; it was the Buddha who turned the questioning back upon him regarding external signs.
Thus, having clearly perceived that the Dharmakāya is without self, one must not seek the Buddha within [phenomenal] marks.

In the Sūtra, there are four instances where it is stated that the Buddha cannot be seen through marks (the first, seventh, seventeenth, and this present case). First, it clarifies the doubt regarding the cause in relation to the fruit;
next, it clarifies that the realization of the fruit is free from marks; and subsequently, it explains how the real manifests as the provisional. This [passage] clarifies...
Seeking through the conventional and seeking through the ultimate have distinct meanings.
