This nature is fundamentally empty and does not grasp at forms; it is suchness, immovable—these two phrases encompass it all.
The entire sutra is fundamentally intended for the salvation of sentient beings; therefore, it concludes with this exposition. This is the *pariṇāmanā* (circulation) section.

It marks the completion of the discourse on the sutra, wherein the merit of receiving and upholding it is praised, the great bodhicitta of the Bodhisattvas is inspired, and the rules for preaching the Dharma and the wondrous wisdom for contemplating the Dharma are revealed, so that the life of wisdom may be transmitted forever.

It is not that [the teaching] is severed. Regarding the upholding of the Dharma, this has already been explained in detail previously; however, as for the expounding of the Dharma, it has never yet been fully elucidated.
Therefore, it is shown at the conclusion of the sutra, which is precisely the point of entrustment.

Subhūti, if there were someone who took the seven treasures filling immeasurable asaṃkhyeya worlds (immeasurable asaṃkhyeya worlds being more than even the sands of the Ganges) and used them as an offering;
and if there were a son or daughter of good family who has resolved upon bodhicitta (the term "bodhisattva-mind" is used in the translations by Chen and Wei) and,
holding this sutra, were to receive, uphold, and recite even as little as a four-line verse from it...
To read and recite it, and to expound it for others—its merit surpasses that [of the former].

The general meaning of the *Prajñāpāramitā* has already been fully explained above. Now, the Tathāgata wishes for future generations to uphold and expound this sutra so as to transmit the life-force of wisdom;
therefore, he calls out and addresses them once more, comparing the merit of upholding this sutra with that of giving. In all cases...
It has been seen eight times. Each successive praise differs in its intent. To speak from the ultimate perspective of this sutra, it is most urgent for those who seek awakening.
For all Buddhas and the Dharma of unsurpassed Bodhi emerge from this alone. One only fears that people will regard it as mere words and not uphold it with their mind;
that they will delight in upholding the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) rather than the Bodhi [of the Great Vehicle].
Because they maintain the mind of *samyak-saṃbodhi*, they further point out that one does not grasp at signs; suchness is immovable.
What was previously explained—that not grasping constitutes the cause of signlessness—now shows that immeasurable merit constitutes the fruit of signlessness.

As it is said: "To uphold this sutra" means that one should uphold the mind thus generated—never retreating from what has already been generated, and diligently advancing toward what has not yet been attained.
This indicates that for those who have generated the bodhicitta, there is the gateway of *dhāraṇī*.
If one were to interpret it as "upholding the sutra," then since "receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting" follows immediately below, how could it be appropriate to state it redundantly?
To maintain this mind and seal it upon the sutras—even as little as a four-line verse—its various wondrous meanings are all one’s own original face.
To receive, uphold, read, and recite them gives rise to great wisdom; to expound them for others secures supreme eloquence.

Compared to those who uphold and explain them without having yet resolved their minds toward enlightenment, the difference is more than that between heaven and earth; therefore, the merit obtained is most supreme.
Victory! A detailed explanation: The fivefold comparison was previously conducted within the section on "Abiding"; the threefold comparison was conducted within the section on "Subduing the Mind.
This concludes that section. While the superiority of merely upholding the sutra has already been explicitly stated, the essential point of its exposition had not yet been revealed;
therefore, there is the single proof regarding "How to Expound It."
How does one expound it for others? One does not grasp at appearances;

one remains unmoving in accordance with reality (*tathatā*). "Reality" refers to suchness. "In accordance with reality" means being perfectly as-it-is. "Unmoving" precisely clarifies what is meant by suchness;
it signifies that its fundamental substance does not undergo change or movement. To grasp at appearances is precisely not to be in accordance with suchness. That is to say—
This movement does not grasp at signs; it is thusness (*tathatā*) itself, unmoving. It is also said: "The mind is suchness, and the environment is suchness;
therefore, it is called 'suchness-unmoving'. This is the meaning of being unstained. Even subtle thoughts and deliberations are all termed "stains," not necessarily only covetous desires.
The Sixth Patriarch said: "If the mind grasps at signs, or grasps at the sign of dharmas, or grasps at the sign of non-dharmas..."

That which has a dwelling place is not the mind; that the mind has no dwelling place is precisely True Suchness (*tathatā*). "Such" (*ru*) means that the myriad things are one and the same, giving rise to no discrimination.
It is like a single moon in the sky: though a thousand waves manifest its reflection, the reflections appear and vanish, yet the moon remains truly as it is.
Liu Daokai said: "The eight characters 'not grasping at marks, suchness unmoving' constitute the entirety [of this principle]."

The ultimate destination of the sutras and the central tenet of Prajñāpāramitā—throughout its thirty-two sections, as they are repeatedly examined and analyzed—is simply to perfect this non-appropriation of marks.
From the shallow to the profound, layer by layer, it is peeled away and revealed only to reach this state of suchness, immovable.
Shengxian said: "Non-appropriation of marks and suchness, immovable. This is the world...

The Honored One directly pointed to the fundamental nature and expounded it to instruct people, so that those who uphold the sutras may know where it leads and those who preach the sutras may grasp its essential purport.

The correct interpretation of the original text is as follows: If one claims that the Dharma taught by the Buddha does not grasp at signs and is suchness, immovable, then the one who expounds the Buddha-Dharma must likewise not grasp at signs and be suchness.
As with "immovable," when a practitioner collects the mind and engages with phenomena, they must in all cases not grasp at signs.
This state of being as-it-is and immovable is the intended meaning elucidated and expounded in the commentaries; it is not the primary meaning of the sūtra text itself. Thus says Ruru.
The expositor bases this upon the Buddha’s teachings to extensively elucidate their meaning.
This surpasses mere explanation by being free from all signs; this is the realm of the Buddha. Not abiding in signs is the realm of the bodhisattva.

Not giving rise to the conceptualization of dharmas is the practice of one who has resolved to attain enlightenment. However, since all signs arise from grasping, they ultimately converge in non-grasping.
This extracts the source of their illness. Regarding the term "marks" (*lakṣaṇa*), it encompasses all marks within the sūtras.
False marks are the opposite of true suchness (*tathatā*); the act of grasping and false movement are mutually causal.

Only by not grasping at marks does one accord with true suchness, remaining tranquil and unmoving; this is the wondrous realm of suchness-as-it-is. By not grasping at marks, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is inexhaustible.
To summarize: this does not adopt the heterodox views of annihilationism or eternalism; it does not adopt the phenomenal obstacles of ordinary beings;
and it does not adopt the ontological obstacles of the two vehicles. Therefore, through suchness (*tathatā*), one accords with the Tathāgata who is without coming or going;

through immovability, one realizes the Bodhisattva of the stage of Patience (*kṣānti*). The five natures are perfectly integrated, and all vehicles meet in profound harmony; thus, one may [attain] for oneself—

As it is said: "If one does not grasp at signs, how can one immediately accord with suchness (*tathatā*)?
This is because all signs belong to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). Conditioned phenomena are like dreams, illusions, and so forth; whereas true suchness has no coming or going.

It is simply by not grasping at phenomena such as dreams and illusions that one accords with the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) true suchness. Sentient beings, however, are greedily attached to the conditioned."
One should not grasp at things as being real. If one thoroughly understands that they are false and fleeting, like dreams or illusions, then there is nothing to crave;
